title: Is it time to cut ties with Cardinals DC Nick Rallis?
summary: The Detroit Lions blasted the Arizona Cardinals this past weekend, 45-21. Any time the opposition posts up close to 50 points on your club, it is a huge issue. Except for the 26-14 victory over the hapless Los Angeles Chargers on opening weekend, the Cardinals’ defense has surrendered 31, 36, 36, and now 45 points. […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - DECEMBER 21: Defensive coordinator Nick Rallis of the Arizona Cardinals looks on prior to a game against the Atlanta Falcons at State Farm Stadium on December 21, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Norm Hall/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions blasted the Arizona Cardinals this past weekend, 45-21. Any time the opposition posts up close to 50 points on your club, it is a huge issue. Except for the 26-14 victory over the hapless Los Angeles Chargers on opening weekend, the Cardinals’ defense has surrendered 31, 36, 36, and now 45 points. RELATED: SHOULD THE CARDINALS TRADE JOSH SWEAT? Maybe it’s just time to let DC Nick Rallis go. The Cardinals have allowed a league-high 162 points in just five games. Every American Football team at every level wants to average scoring 32.4 points a game. That is a dream situation. For Arizona, that dream is currently a nightmare. Our offense will be fine under Lafleur. Our defense needs a new DC! — {•¥•} (@___1_618___) September 28, 2026 The Cardinals’ 1-4-0 record is indicative of their inability to keep opposing offenses out of the end zone. Against the pass, Arizona’s defense has allowed the most passing touchdowns (14), tied for third with the fewest interceptions (3), ranked #32 in passing yards gained per attempt (9.1), second-worst defensive ranking (117.2), has allowed the third-greatest first-down conversion ratio (41.7%), given up the fourth most plays of 20+ yards (18), given up the fourth most plays of 40+ yards (3), and is ranked #14 in the most sacks (11). Versus the run, the Cardinals are ranked #9 in total rushing yards (633), #9 in rushing attempts (144), tied for #4 in most rushing touchdowns allowed (6), tied for #10 in most yards per carry average (4.4), and allowed the tenth most first downs via the run (35). According to FOX Sports , Arizona’s defense is ranked #26 overall. That is broken down into a #25 ranking for the passing defense and a #23 ranking for the run defense. What are the issues? Against the Lions, the Cardinals’ defense forced three straight three-and-outs to begin the game. Then, it was a jailbreak, with Detroit scoring six touchdowns and a field goal. They scored 24 points in the second quarter and 14 in Quarter 3. Huge passing gains were rampant. And the pass rush? Should we say the lack of a pass rush? Only DT Roy Lopez was putting some pressure into Detroit’s backfield and had a good game against the run. In the postgame press conference, Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur didn’t act disappointed or sad; instead, he was pissed. Regarding the defensive effort, he stated: “Obviously, not good enough. I know we’re better than that, but that doesn’t mean s*** right now.” Before being hired as the head coach of the Cardinals, LaFleur and Rallis had no connection with past employment. While LaFleur has been situated along the West Coast, Rallis was mainly with the Philadelphia Eagles, coaching with former Arizona head coach Jonathan Gannon. LaFleur simply kept him as his DC. But last year, the Cardinals defense wasn’t spectacular either. They finished the year ranked #26 overall, allowing an average of 363.4 yards a game. Both the run defense and pass coverage were in the bottom third in the league. When Gannon hired Rallis, he was considered one of the brighter minds in the game with plenty of youth behind him. In 2025, The Athletic featured him in its “NFL 50 under 40” list of ascending coaches and front office personnel. Right now, Arizona’s defense under Rallis is struggling to play at a level that gives the team a chance to win. What do four consecutive losses giving up 30+ points tell any Cardinals fan? No matter what this offense accomplishes, it is erased by the defense not being able to close out games late. And this is not simply a one-off. Last year, the Cardinals had a late lead and lost in seven contests. Remember when the offense was down 14 points to the Seattle Seahawks in Week 4 only to come back and tie the game? Seattle got the ball back with just 28 ticks on the clock, then went bip-bip-bip before kicking the winning field goal. All the defense had to do was contain, then take the game into overtime. Look at this year’s Seahawks game. Everyone in the league knows what to expect from Seattle WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba. He is a weapon, yet did Rallis give Smith-Njigba double coverage and force their offense to throw to other pass catchers? Hell no. What occurred instead was that the talented receiver had 155 yards and scored three touchdowns. He became the runner-up for “NFC Offensive Player of the Week.” Against the Lions, where was the run defense? RB Jahmyr Gibbs ran willy-nilly on his way to 151 yards on just 25 carries with two touchdowns, then rarely got any coverage from a linebacker when he went out for a short pass. He had five receptions for 56 yards. The Cardinals’ continued defensive struggles don’t seem to have an end game. Each week, it is going to be more of the same. Maybe a change at the top needs to be made and is in the franchise’s best interest to move on from Rallis. Most NFL coaches and GMs will not reveal anything pertinent to almost every situation. In the presser, LaFleur was asked if any coaching changes are on the horizon after getting blasted for 45 points. The question specifically was, “Do you need to make any changes to the defense coaching?” LaFleur’s response: “There’s a lot to fix right now, and I respect the question. I understand that, and I get it comes with the territory right now. My focus is on me fixing everything. None of it’s good enough. And again, anytime there’s a blowout like this, it starts with coaching. It’s not the players. It starts with us.” Like always, just Hollywood talk without anything that has legs. And no head coach is going to come right out and say that one of his coaches is probably going to kick rocks. There is respect in this league, and it is a rarity to throw others under the bus. Plus, it is a decision that needs to be thought out first and discussed within the organization and not be decided on the spur of the moment at the podium after a bad loss. And LaFleur is a guy who is going to point the finger at himself all day long. During last week’s press conference, Rallis was asked about the weekly 30+ points per game. He said: “Yeah, that sucks. Just focus on the process.” Come again? That’s it? No resolutions to the issue? Now, we get that the offense has its own set of problems and such; the defense is on the field more than ideal. Players get winded, especially in the final quarter. But Rallis didn’t offer any solutions whatsoever. And it isn’t going to get any easier. A glance at the schedule reveals upcoming games against the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Broncos, Dallas Cowboys, Seahawks, Rams, and then the Kansas City Chiefs. Raise your hand if you believe things will be different against these offenses. The Arizona Cardinals are sticking with defensive coordinator Nick Rallis, despite allowing 30 points in four straight games. Here's why. https://t.co/Ss8Xxwu9C8 — azcentral (@azcentral) October 13, 2026 In LaFleur’s first stint as an NFL head coach, he surrounded himself with veteran coaches on both sides of the ball. Rallis was already in Arizona, and it was an easy fix. But there is very little pass rush; the defensive backfield suffers from having to cover guys for way too long, minimal coverage from the linebackers on tight ends and running backs flaring out of the backfield, and the run defense is allowing 126.6 yards per game. Last season, they gave up 28.7 points on average per game, which ranked #29 in the league. DT Walter Nolen was brought in to solve the run defense and has been hurt repeatedly. Even though he is healthy this year, he has been a non-factor. DE Josh Sweat was the big splash signing and netted 12.0 sacks last year, yet is the invisible man with the pass rush this season. DE Darius Robinson is taking up space and getting a paycheck, and LB…

title: Cardinals Love is not practicing, game status uncertain
summary: The Arizona Cardinals begin the most difficult portion of their schedule. They will need all of their weapons in each game. This weekend’s contest is against division foe Los Angeles Rams. Both clubs are in dire need of a win. Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love is resting his ailing left ankle and has not practiced […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Jeremiyah Love #4 of the Arizona Cardinals carries the ball against D.J. Reed #4 of the Detroit Lions during the first quarter at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals begin the most difficult portion of their schedule. They will need all of their weapons in each game. This weekend’s contest is against division foe Los Angeles Rams. Both clubs are in dire need of a win. Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love is resting his ailing left ankle and has not practiced this week. In fact, it is expected that he won’t see the practice field at all. RELATED: CARDINALS OFFENSE ONE OF THE MOST BORING Arizona head coach Mike LaFleur stated that they are dealing with Love’s injury on a daily evaluation. For the ankle to heal completely, obviously, Love will need to stay off it, and the need to see him on the practice field is not a priority. At a post-practice press conference, LaFleur explained about why Love wasn’t practicing: “We all are in agreement as much as he wants to battle through, we’re all in agreement right now, it’s just, hey, just give it a little bit of rest and see as the week goes on what that’ll entail for Sunday.” Right now, his status for the Rams is not known, and could be a game-time decision. The Cardinals installed a new offense this year based on LaFleur’s past employment with the Rams and San Francisco 49ers’ schemes. Both franchises have very potent offenses, and it is assumed that at some point, Arizona’s will follow suit. But it won’t happen overnight, and the offense will need to have the right components in place. Like an exceptional quarterback and a great, not good, offensive line. Right now, both of these elements are missing. Love was selected with the third overall pick to supplement this new offense, but so far, he has looked very average. He has played in all five games with four starts. He has rushed for 245 yards on 67 carries, with nine first-down conversions, a single TD, and a pedestrian 3.7 yards per carry average. Love has also been active in the short passing game with 11 catches for 36 yards and another score. Jeremiyah Love's “This is probably gonna be the longest year of my life," comments hit hard when you realize he wasn't in for a single one of the Cardinals final 13 snaps on the potential game-winning drive pic.twitter.com/fO8NSzWiwm — Josh Norris (@JoshNorris) October 5, 2026 But the expectations were for Love to take the league by storm and become Arizona’s Emmitt Smith or Eric Dickerson. His play hasn’t wowed anyone so far, and he certainly hasn’t hit the big run. He got 90 rushing yards in Week 3 against the San Francisco 49ers on 21 carries. But at no time did he appear ready to hit the big run and take it to the house. In fact, his longest run of the year is nine yards. And he isn’t the best blocking back since he wasn’t expected to be while at Notre Dame. But that happens quite a bit with rookies, and then they are taught proper techniques. But Love is a fighter, and isn’t down on his rookie production. LaFleur offered: “I’m going to try to be as candid as possible with also knowing that everyone’s listening to this, too. He’s a tough dude.” Love injured his right ankle against the Las Vegas Raiders in preseason, which kept him out until opening weekend. Technically, it was a high ankle sprain, but it fully healed. Now, he injured his left ankle in the loss to the New York Football Giants, and the injury has lingered, as a lot of ankle issues do. Wasn't in there the last 13 snaps due to ankle injury — Jim 'Kountry' Shellenberger (@JShell74) October 5, 2026 Fragile ankles at the running back position are not a good thing. Ever. And for Love, he plays aggressively, especially with his cuts. His explosiveness has been affected since the Giants contest. Is this an issue going forward? LaFleur added: “You’d have to ask him that. I know how explosive he is. I know how explosive he wants to be. So, I mean, I think that’s a fair assessment in some aspects. Again, I don’t think it’s an overall hindrance, but again, the rest for him is going to be vital.” In the event that Love cannot suit up for the LA game, veteran Tyler Allgeier will start and become the bellcow back. Allgeier is in his fifth season and was an important free-agent signing over the offseason. While with Arizona, he has played in all five games with two starts, has gained 119 yards on 35 carries, has six first down conversions, scored once, and has a 3.4 yards-per-carry average. He has great hands and has caught 12 passes for 44 yards. Bam Knight is healthy and would back up Allgeier. Both are really good blockers when held in. Most likely, the coaching staff would bring up RB Evan Hull from the practice squad against the Rams.

title: NFL predictions: Falcons must win trenches against the Bears
summary: The Falcons fell to the Ravens in overtime on Sunday Night Football in Week 5, breaking a two-game winning streak where the offense averaged a blazing 40 points per game. Atlanta came back down to earth against an injured but still extremely well-coached Baltimore team, falling to 2-3 with the most difficult stretch of the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 31: Chicago Bears defenders tackle Drake London #5 of the Atlanta Falcons during the first quarter at Soldier Field on December 31, 2023 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Quinn Harris/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Falcons fell to the Ravens in overtime on Sunday Night Football in Week 5, breaking a two-game winning streak where the offense averaged a blazing 40 points per game. Atlanta came back down to earth against an injured but still extremely well-coached Baltimore team, falling to 2-3 with the most difficult stretch of the schedule still to come. It’s a disappointing result for the Falcons, but hopefully a learning experience for the new coaching staff. Attention now shifts to Week 6’s matchup with the Bears, who possess one of the league’s most fearsome offenses. Chicago is the only team in the NFL that has rushed for more yards than Atlanta, and should see starting quarterback Caleb Williams return to the lineup after a three-week absence. This is likely to be the toughest test yet for the Falcons defense, who are very shorthanded at cornerback and edge rusher. Unlike the Ravens, however, the Bears defense is quite vulnerable to both the run and pass. Despite Williams’ return and the Bears offensive prowess, the Falcons are just 1.5-point home underdogs in Week 6. The over/under of 51.5 suggests an offensive showcase, and Atlanta is going to need to put up points and control the clock to keep pace with Chicago. Falcons vs Bears Week 6 predictions This matchup presents a major opportunity for the Falcons to step up and win the trenches on both sides of the ball—similar to how they dominated both the Packers and Saints earlier in the season. The Bears have a good offensive line, but are likely to be missing bruising running back Kyle Monangai for the game. D’Andre Swift is a good runner himself, but Chicago has been most effective with the two-headed attack of Swift and Monangai—who is responsible for nearly as many yards and TDs as Swift. Caleb Williams will also factor in as a runner, but there’s no telling how he’ll perform in his first game back from injury. On the other side of the ball, the Bears will be without top edge rusher Montez Sweat due to a PED suspension. Veteran Dayo Odeyingbo is also in danger of missing the game with a quad injury. At linebacker, starter T.J. Edwards and reserve Keyshaun Elliott also missed practice for most of the week. That’s a lot of injuries piling up the in front seven against a Falcons team who would love nothing more than to run the ball. While former Falcons Grady Jarrett and Kentavius Street are performing well as pass rushers, neither has been an impact run defender. If Atlanta’s offensive line can bounce back and dominate the way they did back in Weeks 3 and 4, that’s a pathway to success for the Falcons. We all know this offense is a lot better when Bijan and Brian Robinson and getting chunk yardage on the ground, and that’ll be the most important thing to establish early in the game. Long sustained drives will also help keep Chicago’s offense off the field and the defense fresher over the long haul. On defense, this is another big test for a Falcons front that got beat up by the Ravens. I think Atlanta can get pressure, but they’ll have to also play disciplined football against the rushing threat of Caleb Williams. I’d expect a different approach this week than what we saw against Baltimore, perhaps with a QB spy involved on the majority of plays. It’ll be significantly easier to defend just D’Andre Swift versus Swift and Monangai, so that could also be a boon for the Falcons. At the end of the day, Atlanta’s depleted secondary presents some issues. I expect the Bears to have success in the passing game, and that means this could turn into a shootout. In that scenario, it’ll be hard for the Falcons to keep pace with Chicago. This will be the offense’s biggest test yet, as it might require a more pass-heavy approach from Penix throughout the game. All that being said, I think the Bears with Caleb Williams at the helm are possibly the most dangerous offense in football. Atlanta goes back and forth with Chicago throughout the game, but the defense can’t stop Chicago enough thanks to their secondary injuries. The Falcons fall to Chicago, 31-27, but do show some really nice things in the process. Rise up with Falcons fans on the SB Nation app! title: Ravens survey and discussion: grade the Cam Jurgens trade
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Ravens fans and fans across the country. Last week, the Baltimore Ravens made their biggest in-season trade since acquiring Roquan Smith in 2022, sending a 2028 second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles in […]
full_text: Sep 21, 2025; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA; Philadelphia Eagles center Cam Jurgens (51) against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Eric Hartline-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Ravens fans and fans across the country. Last week, the Baltimore Ravens made their biggest in-season trade since acquiring Roquan Smith in 2022, sending a 2028 second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for center Cam Jurgens. Reactions to the move varied across the NFL. Some praised Eric DeCosta for addressing the biggest hole on his roster with a proven player with an affordable contract that runs through the 2029 season. Others viewed the trade as a desperate overpay for a struggling player with a lengthy injury history. Lamar Jackson’s Week 5 absence and the Ravens’ subsequent overtime win over the Atlanta Falcons distracted fans from the trade over the weekend. But now that Jurgens is practicing with the team – albeit in a non-contact jersey as he progresses through concussion protocol – it is time to return to DeCosta’s blockbuster move. What is your grade on the trade? Nikhil’s take: This is an easy B for me. Let’s consider what we know: The Ravens need a center. This has only become more clear in Vega Ioane’s two starts at the position, which have featured excellent blocking but inconsistent snaps. Getting him back to his natural spot at right guard will allow him to focus on what he does best while Jurgens, a true center, handles the quarterback exchange. It’s fair to say that Baltimore’s Super Bowl chances were going to be undermined by their center woes. Instead of another stopgap solution, DeCosta went out and got a real starter. A second-round pick is a steep price. Starting-caliber offensive linemen – especially two-time Pro Bowlers at a position of desperate need – do not come cheaply. Ravens fans might point to DeCosta’s underwhelming results with his second-rounders during his tenure, but that does not decrease the value of the future pick. But Baltimore avoided giving away premium draft capital for a loaded 2027 class and instead sent their 2028 second to Philadelphia. Not ideal, but not a severe overpay, either. Jurgens’ contract provides offers even more value. The Ravens will owe Jurgens just under $1 million for the rest of this year and roughly $50 million over the following three seasons. That is a phenomenal value considering Tyler Linderbaum’s ridiculous $27 million AAV from the Raiders. What’s more, only Jurgens’ $16 million 2027 compensation is guaranteed, giving Baltimore a potential out to limit the damage should he not be the team’s long-term center. His injury history brings significant risk. Jurgens’ 2025 back surgery is by far his biggest red flag, but he has also dealt with two documented concussions and a knee injury in the last year, plus multiple issues in 2023. His health could be the biggest retroactive factor in grading this deal; for now, it is a clear risk that is worth taking. His play should improve at center. Jurgens has been among the league’s worst-graded offensive lineman this season, per Pro Football Focus, but he has been playing out of position at guard. Returning to his natural position should help him access the higher floor of play he established in his 2024 and 2025 Pro Bowl campaigns. Even if Jurgens isn’t among the league’s elite centers, reliable, above-average play would be a major boon to the Ravens offense. All told, this seems like a square deal between the two teams. The Ravens paid a pretty penny for a valuable asset, which is how NFL trades typically work! Baltimore’s short- and long-term return from this move could be massive, as could Philly’s. But more than anything else, I like that DeCosta finally and decisively took care of the one problem holding his team back more than any other. Late, perhaps, but better than never! Now, it’s your turn! Grade the Ravens’ trade for Cam Jurgens in the poll below and give us your reasoning in the comments section or in The Feed ! summary: The Ravens’ rookies are officially on a win streak as Baltimore moved to 4-1 after a thrilling Sunday Night Football overtime win in Atlanta, 30-23. Here’s how the rookies performed. OG Vega Ioane Oh, ho-hum, just a rookie offensive lineman in his fifth NFL game, starting at center for only the second time in his […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 11: Baltimore center Olaivavega Ioane (71) prepares to snap the ball during the NFL game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Atlanta Falcons on October 11th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Ravens’ rookies are officially on a win streak as Baltimore moved to 4-1 after a thrilling Sunday Night Football overtime win in Atlanta, 30-23. Here’s how the rookies performed. OG Vega Ioane Oh, ho-hum, just a rookie offensive lineman in his fifth NFL game, starting at center for only the second time in his collegiate and professional career and allowing zero pressures for two games in a row. It’s simply ridiculous how much this rookie has stepped up and impacted this offense. Beyond the three big weapons of Lamar Jackson, Zay Flowers, and Derrick Henry, Ioane is probably the next most impactful player on this offense considering all that he’s done. An offensive lineman has never won Offensive Rookie of the Year, but there needs to be real conversations about Ioane. . @Ravens @AtlantaFalcons @vegaioane17 seems like every big play goes behind Highway 71! Are the Ravens sure they wanna put him back at OG? #ravensflock @RapSheet #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/XlwmHIik9s — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) October 12, 2026 OLB Zion Young It’s been quiet for Young since the Cowboys game. He’s continued to excel against the run, but despite a larger opportunity with Trey Hendrickson out of the lineup, Young hasn’t rushed the passer well with just one win in the last two weeks. The second-rounder’s pass rush was known to need work coming out of college, and it’s clear he’s not quite there yet. But Young’s role as a run stopper has been well-earned and should continue to grow as the Ravens reserve Hendrickson and Mike Green for pass rushing snaps. WR Elijah Sarratt Sarratt went back to being a healthy scratch against the Falcons. With Ja’Kobi Lane’s return imminent, it will likely take an injury in the room for Sarratt to get another activation this season. TE Matt Hibner Hibner didn’t get any targets in this matchup but stayed active with 10 pass snaps and 20 run-blocking snaps. Hibner hurt his hand early in the game that saw him carted off the field. He eventually returned and continued to receive blocking snaps, though his hand injury could have factored into his lack of targets. It remains to be seen how Hibner’s role could grow with Druham Smythe out for the year and with Ja’Kobi Lane returning for to establish his own target share. The Ravens also signed veteran Nick Vannett from their practice squad to help fill Smythe’s role. TE Josh Cuevas Cuevas nabbed two catches on two targets for 26 yards, 22 of those coming after the catch. Cuevas’ role also remained similar to weeks past, just 19 snaps in the game, nine of them run blocking. CB Chandler Rivers Rivers’s snap count decreased from its recent rise over the last couple of weeks. Rivers played just 19 snaps, 18 of them against the pass. The Ravens clearly wanted Rivers off the field against obvious run looks in a concerted effort to contain Bijan Robinson for the game. Rivers seemed to struggle in coverage this week as well, which might have contributed to his lower snap count as well. P Ryan Eckley Eckley had four punts, averaging just 44.3 yards on his punts, but pinning three of them inside the 20. Eckley’s punting was vital to giving the Ravens’ defense a chance to force the Falcons to go on long drives and force field goals throughout the game. Wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane and running back Adam Randall remain on injured reserve, with defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny on the practice squad. Lane returned to practice on Wednesday and could be activated to play against the Cleveland Browns this weekend.

title: Brock Bowers is already the NFL’s best receiving tight end
summary: The week after they faced arguably the best receiver in football in Puka Nacua, the Buffalo Bills will see the NFL’s best receiving tight on Sunday when they face the Las Vegas Raiders. That is no slight to Dalton Kincaid, or George Kittle, Trey McBride, Sam LaPorta, or any of the other excellent tight ends […]
full_text: The week after they faced arguably the best receiver in football in Puka Nacua, the Buffalo Bills will see the NFL’s best receiving tight on Sunday when they face the Las Vegas Raiders. That is no slight to Dalton Kincaid, or George Kittle, Trey McBride, Sam LaPorta, or any of the other excellent tight ends in today’s increasingly tight-end happy league. Brock Bowers is a different beast. In his first professional season, Bowers caught an NFL rookie record 112 passes. Not just for a tight end. A rookie at any position. And he did so at a remarkable 2.02 yards per route run. It’s not as if the Raiders just funneled him targets to re-write the record books. He was legitimately efficient on his 592 routes and 148 targets that season, as he amassed 1,194 yards — the same yardage figure as CeeDee Lamb that year on only two more targets. This season, Bowers missed the first two games due to injury. In the three outings since his return, he has 10 catches for 116 yards and one touchdown on 12 targets, six catches for 86 yards and a score on 11 targets, and eight snags for 110 yards and a touchdown on nine targets. His yards per route run figure of 2.79 is tops in the NFL among tight ends. And he aligns everywhere, so he’s not a tight end by the classic definition. Entering this game, Bowers has run routes from the outside 40.1% of the time, the highest rate among all qualifying tight ends. It’s almost identical to the percentage at which Zay Flowers has run his routes on the outside. While certainly not the largest, nor most physical imposing tight end in the league, Bowers has maintained ridiculous reliability in traffic. He had a 53.3% contested-catch rate as a rookie. Then it was an outstanding 65.2% a season ago, and he’s 7-of-10 in those scenarios this season entering this contest. He’s not a huge tackle-breaker — only nine thus far in his NFL career. He gets open. He catches everything. Kirk Cousins has a 136.5 rating when targeting Bowers in his three games. And the tight end leads Las Vegas in all receiving categories. In a game after the Bills saw Puka earn 24 targets and catch 17 of them — albeit at a very minimal 8.1 yards per catch — Buffalo’s defense could be in for another individually high-volume, funnel-the-offense-through-one-player type of outing if they don’t specifically make it a top priority to limit Bowers in this game.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills injury report: DJ Moore DNP, Spencer Brown listed as Full Thursday
summary: The Buffalo Bills held their first full practice of Week 6 on Thursday, it was mostly business-as-usual on the injury front for the AFC East division leaders.   After a walk-through practice on Wednesday, the Bills posted a very lengthy injury report. The problem with reports coming off walk-throughs is that everything is just an […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 12: DJ Moore #2 of the Buffalo Bills warms up prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills held their first full practice of Week 6 on Thursday, it was mostly business-as-usual on the injury front for the AFC East division leaders. After a walk-through practice on Wednesday, the Bills posted a very lengthy injury report. The problem with reports coming off walk-throughs is that everything is just an estimate: this is what we think they would have been able to do if we had gone full force. Unfortunately, a lot of times that means some surprises on the next day’s reports — and when it comes to injuries, surprises aren’t usually a good thing. Not so on Thursday. The only change from Wednesday’s “pretend” practice report to Thursday’s “let’s put on the pads” practice report was Spencer Brown. The Bills’ starting right tackle had a full day of practice, but then, he told us he would. Brown said it was more of a spasm/tightness issue that forced him from Monday night’s game and he would be fine. He was right. Thursday injury report pic.twitter.com/9n3U6lo1ER — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 15, 2026 The only true questions surround cornerback Dee Alford, who was limited, and wide receiver DJ Moore, who didn’t practice. I would expect Alford to play Sunday. Moore will want to play, and his lack of practice isn’t an indicator of what he’ll be wearing on Sunday. If he gets any work in at all tomorrow, look for him to play. We’ll get game day designations on Friday, but I look for both Alford and Moore, along with wide receiver Joshua Palmer, to be listed as questionable once again, while defensive tackle Ed Oliver is likely to be ruled out for a second straight week. As for the Raiders, they also have a lengthy injury report. Thursday #BUFvsLV Injury Report https://t.co/KGcKYlXfjj — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) October 16, 2026

title: What could Josh Allen be working on mechanically with his throwing motion?
summary: After the Buffalo Bills win over the Rams in Week 5 on Monday Night Football, Josh Allen mentioned he“fighting mechanically some stuff right now” has sent me on a mission to find out what those mechanical issues might be. Before I begin, this was Allen’s direct quote on this topic at the during his postgame […]
full_text: After the Buffalo Bills win over the Rams in Week 5 on Monday Night Football , Josh Allen mentioned he“fighting mechanically some stuff right now” has sent me on a mission to find out what those mechanical issues might be. Before I begin, this was Allen’s direct quote on this topic at the during his postgame presser in Los Angelels: “Just early on, didn’t feel like I was in a rhythm [early], wasn’t taking some of the underneath stuff. Fighting mechanically some stuff right now that I’m working on. But I felt like in that second half I got into a rhythm. Guys made some plays. It’s awesome stuff.” When speaking with media at UC Irvine on Wednesday, Allen, who will have a pre-planned session with his QB guru Chris Hess while the Bills stay in California, was asked a follow-up question on his mechanics comment, and said this : “I think it’s every quarterback fights throughout the year. It could be as simple as one thing. Chris Hess is from this area. We had this on the books regardless. But it’s really good to have him out here, and maybe learn a thing or two, and try to find a way to tweak something and feel good.” And what follows here is just a guess. It’s a guess based on something I noticed early this season from Allen throwing the football. And yes, it feels strange critiquing Allen, one of the most gifted throwers of the football in NFL history. But here it goes. I think Allen’s throwing mechanics issue pertains to his release point dropping too low, close to a sidearm delivery. It hasn’t happened on every attempt, of course, yet there were a few misfires early this season in which it appeared Allen was releasing the football on the same vertical plane as his helmet or even lower. Like here against the Lions, when he missed Khalil Shakir deep down the field. I’ve slowed these All-22 videos to half speed, but I’ll admit it’s not especially easy to see how low Allen’s arm angle was on this throw: pic.twitter.com/4b9OW3Q6sZ — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 I was walking through the concourse when that play occurred and randomly had the ideal vantage point for Allen’s arm angle. I remember being struck by how sidearm it was. Check here, on a target for Keon Coleman down the field that fell incomplete against the Chargers in Week 3. This one is a lot easier to see: pic.twitter.com/7eNZ5Rpuwh — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 That’s almost fully sidearm, right? More recently, against the Patriots, on that strange drop by Joshua Palmer, on a throw that was well behind the receiver, Allen’s sidearm-ish delivery was very noticeable: pic.twitter.com/hDGuENrlmI — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 Watching that play live, I recall being surprised Allen, despite being under duress, wasn’t able to get the ball far enough down the field to hit a wide open Palmer in stride. That never happens. Now, Allen is a freak of nature. This we know. And a sidearm delivery doesn’t automatically equate to an inaccurate toss. Allen has shown he can throw a fastball for a strike from this lower arm angle, like the game-winning touchdown to Palmer against the Texans in Week 1: pic.twitter.com/7XV8XNEgEJ — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 Impressive. But here’s a second layer of speculation — I don’t believe sidearm is Allen’s desired arm angle. I’m certainly not going to be pretend I’m a biomechanics expert. But it’s not something he’s regularly done throughout his career. And I’ve seen the vast majority of his ridiculous displays of arm strength on throws in which he rotates his body and throws from a more natural three-quarters delivery in which his right hand releases the football at the top — or above — his helmet. There is more of a driving downward motion as opposed to a horizontal whip. Like here in the second half against the Rams: pic.twitter.com/DbtMvhed0w — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 Or on the short over-the-middle completion to Shakir in overtime: pic.twitter.com/6BUULqeyTB — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 Allen’s hand was much higher than the early-season misfires or even the touchdown to Palmer in Houston. After halftime against the Rams, his delivery looked a lot more “downhill.” Now, I must write that there are many contributing factors to a quarterback’s release point, particularly an improvisational savant like Allen. Is he scrambling? Is he rushed inside the pocket? Is he rolling left? Right? Distance of the throw and touch needed on the throw matter too. And, yes, it’s oftentimes easier to get rid of the football quicker with a sidearm delivery. Think of baseball infielders. We see a distinctive sidearm release all the time as they fire across the diamond or, more frequently, when they’re trying to turn a double play. No doubt you can get the ball out of your hands quicker throwing it sidearm. Conversely, think of an outfielder crow-hopping before launching a rocket to a base in hopes of nailing a runner trying to advance. They typically release the ball with a three-quarters or fully over-the-top delivery. The force from the front leg planting into the ground coupled with body rotation transfers energy through the kinetic chain up the body and ultimately into the throwing arm. And while a sidearm release can generate plenty of velocity, the higher the release point, the more empathically a thrower can “pull” his trunk downward right before release to increase the speed of the ball leaving his hand. A quarterback like Allen whose natural motion is more three-quarters or over-the-top almost assuredly doesn’t transfer that energy as efficiently when dropping the arm angle closer to sidearm. And he likely cannot create as much velocity when doing so compared to when he’s releasing the ball from higher on the vertical plane. This importantly impacts accuracy too. Allen is more accustomed to throwing from a higher release point. A dip near sidearm could very well impact the timing and coordination of his release. Writing on this reminded me of Allen’s touchdown to Jake Kumerow back in 2020 in Denver, when the Bills clinched their first AFC East title in 25 years. You know, the one Allen called the hardest he’s ever thrown a football in his life. Watch how close to over-the-top this release was on this throw. A visual clue to discern between sidearm and three-quarters or over over-the-top if you can’t see the arm because of how fast it’s moving — watch the head. If it moves downward right before the release, it’s the more fundamentally sound three-quarters or over-the-top delivery. If the head doesn’t dip, it’s sidearm. The head dip is a clear sign of the aforementioned body pulling down motion. You’ll see Allen’s helmet move downward on that throw against the Broncos: pic.twitter.com/hUagd8bjxI — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 15, 2026 So that’s where I land on this niche topic — I believe Allen is working on maintaining a higher release point for velocity and ball-placement purposes, which are quite important for an NFL quarterback. And sure, Allen can make accurate throws while dropping his arm angle close to sidearm. And in some instances, he might have to use that delivery. But I think he’s at his best — and taps into all of his arm strength and accuracy — when his release point stays higher.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Josh Allen is a master of picking his poison
summary: Sometimes you get a spark that needs to turn into something more. That spark came courtesy of the tweet from a familiar face in Matt Warren, as seen below. Numerous calls of “psycho” this week have surrounded quarterback Josh Allen as he reinforces his affinity for contact, including grinning wider than the Cheshire Cat after […]
full_text: Sometimes you get a spark that needs to turn into something more. That spark came courtesy of the tweet from a familiar face in Matt Warren, as seen below. Numerous calls of “psycho” this week have surrounded quarterback Josh Allen as he reinforces his affinity for contact, including grinning wider than the Cheshire Cat after getting into the mix of things. Matt Warren’s take? Josh Allen calling his shot when it comes to contact isn’t necessarily a bad thing. I liked the notion and figured if you liked his two cents, perhaps you’d like about a buck fifty or so from me. On the notion of being deliberate… Before we go too much further, here’s the tweet that sparked the whole thing. Been saying this for years. Allen gets to have more control over how he falls this way. I don't like all the choices he makes seeking contact, but him not doing the traditional slide is not a bad call. https://t.co/7U94jS1pwp — Matt Warren (@MattRichWarren) October 13, 2026 I want to get one point out of the way immediately and it’s possibly the best counterargument to the whole article. Yes, the entire point of a slide is to avoid contact entirely. Avoiding contact entirely is always superior to having an impact. The same thing applies to running out of bounds. No contact is ideal! That said, there’s only way to avoid contact entirely. Slide sooooo early that there’s zero risk of getting hit at all. Sometimes that’s the right all. All you need is the first down to secure the win by running the clock our? Get down right after you get it. How often is that the case? Sometimes. But we’re going to talk about those other times. Those other times competitive players are likely going to try to squeak out every yard they can and we’re going to cheer them on for that attitude. Sliding could still avoid contact, but it opens up the risk of getting hit. The primary reason I agree with Matt’s take is that you open yourself up to heightened risk of bad outcome due to one factor. Elevation. When you slide, by default you’re the lowest person on the ground with the most exposed part of you being your head. That’s not a great outcome if it gets hit and we’ve all seen enough of those to be worried about it. But how is barreling into the defender actually BETTER? Well first, Allen is a pretty tall guy. By being upright longer he’s far less likely to take a shot to the head. He’s not passive about the hits either. He squares up. Why is THAT good though, Skare? As a big guy, people are gonna tackle him low which risks knee injuries. By squaring up and dropping the shoulder he can lessen the risk of that as well. In simple terms, Allen is doing his best to dictate the outcome and take the hit to his shoulder, perhaps the area of the body best suited for it. Yeah, but why should we trust your opinion? I dunno. Maybe you shouldn’t. On the other hand, I do have some experience falling and choosing how to fall. Long time readers might recall my experience with judo and professional wrestling. Both, for obvious reasons, taught me quite a bit about falling and the benefit picking your spot. From judo, we were taught falling before anything else (more on muscle memory in a moment). We were taught not to improvise. So much so that the advice from Dr. Ashida if you were tossed into the air was this: Choose to fall well so you can live to fight another day. Don’t do anything unexpected. Shift your attention toward the fall and the fall only. From learning wrasslin’ it was quickly apparent that surprises are not welcome. That’s not to say every move in every match is scripted. Only that there are rules and formulas to make sure both parties know what to expect. Once you introduce chaos, injury risk skyrockets. I haven’t been in a ring in over 20 years. I still have shoulder tightness from not planning a leg drop well and landing poorly. Chaos is your enemy when gravity and collisions are in play. That shoulder could be a lot worse though if it weren’t for my next point; muscle memory and practice. Not quite ten years ago my family and I were going around town. Everyone else was riding bikes while I jogged so our dog could come with us. He’s a little doxie. A large dog had gotten loose in the neighborhood, thought our doxie looked like a chew toy and went through the back of my legs out of nowhere to get to him. Chaos had found me. I can’t thank Dr. Ashida enough for making sure I fell. Over. And over. And over. And over. He knew that when chaos came at us, our practice would come in and it did. I braced myself correctly and avoided anything worse than a couple scrapes from the concrete. No wrist pain. No elbow injury. No aggravation of my old shoulder injury. No concussion. Which brings me to my final point. When I fell I did what came naturally to me. Yes, “nature” in this case was in large part nature of a rehearsed variety, but not trying to break a habit was critical. This works as long as you have an effective habit. Allen’s tendencies have not led to a greater injury risk for him (knocking on wood). His habits are working. Allen is choosing his spots and reducing the chaos. Allen is leaning into habits he’s shown to be effective. I’m not about to change that. And if you don’t trust me, let’s end with a quick look at Allen and his habits to see if what I’m saying makes sense… pic.twitter.com/5pdmoE9TPi — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) October 15, 2026

title: Bills Week 6 rooting interests: Who can help Buffalo climb the AFC?
summary: That was a better outcome than the week before. It wasn’t easy getting there, but the Buffalo Bills outlasted the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night to keep their hold on the top spot in the AFC East — something they were in danger of losing after the New England Patriots took down the Las […]
full_text: That was a better outcome than the week before. It wasn’t easy getting there, but the Buffalo Bills outlasted the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night to keep their hold on the top spot in the AFC East — something they were in danger of losing after the New England Patriots took down the Las Vegas Raiders the day before. Now it’s the Bills’ turn to face the Raiders on Sunday afternoon in Las Vegas. Despite the win, the Bills slipped to the AFC’s fourth seed. The Kansas City Chiefs hold the top spot thanks to a bye week and no chance to lose. Baltimore, Jacksonville, and Buffalo all sit at 4-1, but only the Bills have a division loss, putting them on the bottom rung of that ladder. Here’s a look at how the conference stands right now: Kansas City Chiefs (4-0) Baltimore Ravens (4-1) Jacksonville Jaguars (4-1) Buffalo Bills (4-1) New England Patriots (3-2) Denver Broncos (3-2) Las Vegas Raiders (3-2) Cleveland Browns (3-2) Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) Cincinnati Bengals (3-2) New York Jets (2-3) Indianapolis Colts (2-3) Houston Texans (1-4) Miami Dolphins (0-5) Los Angeles Chargers (0-5) Tennessee Titans (0-5) So, we know we’re rooting for Buffalo, but there are plenty of other games around the league — most of them before the Bills kick off. Let’s take a look at this week’s rooting interests and see where we might be able to get a little help. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC East Buffalo Bills at Las Vegas Raiders Root: Bills It’s not like you needed to be told to root for here. The Bills need to keep winning, especially with New England refusing to go away. A win in Las Vegas would move Buffalo to 5-1 and keep them in control of the AFC East. And after watching what the Patriots did to the Raiders last week, there’s no reason Buffalo shouldn’t be able to take care of business. Go Bills! New York Jets at New England Patriots Root for: Jets Yes, we’re rooting for the Jets. New England is sitting just behind Buffalo in the division, and the Patriots have already benefited from defeating the Bills. A Jets victory would give Buffalo some breathing room in the AFC East. We don’t have to like these New York imposters. We just need them to win one football game. Miami Dolphins — Bye The Dolphins are still looking for their first win, and they won’t be getting it this week. At 0-5, Miami isn’t exactly threatening Buffalo’s division lead, so we can enjoy a week without having to think much about them. _____________________________________________________________________________ Rest of the AFC Seattle Seahawks at Denver Broncos Root for: Seahawks Denver is another AFC team we’d rather see collecting losses than wins. Seattle is an NFC opponent, making this a fairly easy choice. A Broncos loss helps keep another potential playoff contender from gaining ground. Houston Texans at Jacksonville Jaguars Root for: Texans Jacksonville is currently sitting above Buffalo in the conference standings, and that’s reason enough to want the Jaguars to lose. Houston is a division rival for the Jags, so a Texans victory would also tighten up the AFC South race. Plus, a second win for Houston will bolster the Bills strength of victory score. Baltimore Ravens at Cleveland Browns Root for: Browns Baltimore is currently sitting ahead of Buffalo in the AFC standings, so we need the Ravens to start collecting some extra losses. A Browns win would knock Baltimore down to 4-2 and give the Bills a chance to move ahead of them in the conference standings. And since it’s a division game, there’s always the possibility of an upset. Tennessee Titans at Indianapolis Colts Root for: Titans Indianapolis is the bigger concern in the AFC playoff picture, so we’ll take a Tennessee victory here. The Titans haven’t given us much reason to expect one, but that doesn’t mean we can’t ask. Every loss for a potential AFC wild-card competitor is useful. And, don’t forget, it would be helpful if the bottom feeder AFC teams were slightly better than the bottom feeder NFC teams when draft time rolls around next Spring. Pittsburgh Steelers at Tampa Bay Buccaneers Root for: Buccaneers Another easy AFC-versus-NFC decision. Pittsburgh is coming off a win over Indianapolis, and we’d prefer the Steelers not start building momentum of their own. Tampa Bay can help by sending them home with another loss. Los Angeles Chargers at Kansas City Chiefs Root for: Chargers Kansas City got to sit at home last week and watch everyone else play football. Now it’s time for the Chiefs to put that undefeated record on the line. The Chargers are also an AFC playoff contender, but Kansas City currently holds the conference’s top seed. We’re going to need someone to knock the Chiefs off that perch, and a division rival seems like a good place to start. Plus, I’m done rooting for KC – I hope I don’t have to again this season. _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC Chicago Bears at Atlanta Falcons Root for: Bears Buffalo hosts Chicago in December, so we’d like the Bears to start putting some more wins on their record before they make that trip. Chicago winning helps the Bills’ strength of schedule, and if Buffalo beats the Bears later this season, those victories will count toward strength of victory, too. The Bears are coming off a rough loss to Green Bay, so let’s hope they can bounce back against Atlanta. Arizona Cardinals at Los Angeles Rams Root for: Rams Buffalo just picked up a win over the Rams on Monday night. Now we’d like Los Angeles to start winning again, because every Rams victory makes Buffalo’s win look a little better in the strength-of-victory calculation. We wanted the Rams to lose last week. This week, we’re happy to cheer them on. Dallas Cowboys at Green Bay Packers Root for: Packers Green Bay is another team Buffalo has on the schedule, with the Bills headed to Lambeau Field in December. That means we’d like the Packers to keep winning between now and then. A Green Bay victory helps Buffalo’s strength of schedule, and if the Bills can beat the Packers later this season, all those wins become part of Buffalo’s strength-of-victory calculation. So, as much as it might pain some of us, we’re pulling for the Packers on Sunday night. Washington Commanders at San Francisco 49ers Root for: Commanders San Francisco is still undefeated, so we’re going to pull for Washington to change that. Neither team is on Buffalo’s schedule, so there isn’t much at stake for the Bills in this one. But there’s no reason to help another conference’s top team stay perfect. Carolina Panthers at Philadelphia Eagles Root for: Panthers Philadelphia has already lost to Jacksonville, and we’d be perfectly happy to see the Eagles take another loss. Carolina winning also keeps an NFC contender from getting too comfortable. But, there’s really no reason to get too worked up over this game. New Orleans Saints at New York Giants Root for: Saints This one isn’t going to move the AFC standings, and there’s no major reason for Buffalo fans to get worked up about the outcome. We’ll take New Orleans simply because we are tired of the Giants trying to claim they are New Yorkers. Plus, you know, history. But, in all honesty, this is one of those games where we can live with either result. _____________________________________________________________________________ Teams on Bye: Cincinnati Bengals, Detroit Lions, Miami Dolphins, Minnesota Vikings _____________________________________________________________________________ The Bills took care of their business Monday night, but the win didn’t move them up the AFC standings. In fact, they dropped a spot. That’s what happens when the teams around you keep winning, too. This week gives Buffalo a few opportunities to get some help. Baltimore and Jacksonville both have division games, Kansas City has to face the Chargers, and New England gets another chance to put pressure on the AFC East race. There are plenty of results…
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Panthers vs Eagles: Matchups to watch
summary: Last time the Carolina Panthers played the Philadelphia Eagles, they were heavy underdogs as a 3-9 team facing an Eagles team that was 10-2 and riding an eight game winning streak. But the Bryce Young-led Panthers were scrappy and hung tight with the Eagles in what was not the most aesthetically pleasing game. Young tried […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - DECEMBER 08: Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young (9) throws a pass in the first half during the game between the Carolina Panthers and Philadelphia Eagles on December 08, 2024 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Kyle Ross/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Last time the Carolina Panthers played the Philadelphia Eagles, they were heavy underdogs as a 3-9 team facing an Eagles team that was 10-2 and riding an eight game winning streak. But the Bryce Young-led Panthers were scrappy and hung tight with the Eagles in what was not the most aesthetically pleasing game. Young tried to pull off some heroics, escaping from a possible safety while getting his shirt ripped to complete a pass. He led the Panthers down the field late in a one score game. With less than a minute left, Young hit Xavier Legette with a deep ball to the middle of the field that could have won the game, but Legette let the ball hit the turf. The Panthers ultimately turned the ball over on downs and lost the game. The lead up to this game is a little different. The Panthers currently have the better record between the two teams, and the vibes around the Eagles especially low for a team that’s 2-3. All time great right tackle suddenly announced his retirement a couple weeks ago, and the Eagles followed that by trading long time starting center Cam Jurgens. And they’ve lost three straight games while all of that has been happening. The Panthers held up well in their matchups against the Lions, and that allowed them to pull off an electrifying win on Sunday Night Football. Let’s see what this week’s key matchups look like. Derrick Brown vs Tyler Steen and Markel Bell The Eagles offensive line has long been one of the strengths of the team, but this season they’re close to recruiting guys off the street to fill in the gaps. Markel Brown has had to fill in after the retirement of Lane Johnson, and he’s no Lane Johnson. Tyler Steen has been okay at right guard, but he got banged up last week and was limited in practice to start the week. Brown has been relatively quiet to start this season. The right side of the Eagles line is where they’re weaker, so it’s a prime spot for Brown to have his best outing of the year and wreck an Eagles offense that has had its fair of struggles. Devin Lloyd vs Dallas Goedert Tight end Dallas Goedert led the Eagles in targets against the Jaguars last week with all the injuries to the Eagles best skill position players. With Saquon Barkley and Devonta Smith both questionable this week, there’s a chance Goedert is once again the most established offensive weapon at Jalen Hurts’ disposal. He primarily operates in the short areas of the field. After whatever happened in Week 1, Lloyd has been outstanding in coverage when he’s played. If he can take away Goedert, he’ll take away Hurts’ safety blanket and make a whole lot more difficult for the Eagles offense. Tetairoa McMillan vs Quinyon Mitchell McMillan had the game of his life on Sunday Night Football against the Lions. He finished with 14 catches for 192 yards and two touchdowns against a very bad Lions defense. This Sunday’s test is a lot tougher. Quinyon Mitchell has been one of the better corners in the league almost since he arrived in 2024. Jalen Coker is back to help take away some defensive attention, but the Panthers are going to need to trust McMillan to win some one on one matchups against Mitchell to open up things for everyone else. Robert Hunt vs Jalen Carter The Eagles defense has been keeping them in games while their offense stumbles around. Jalen Carter is a big part of that. He leads the team with three sacks in five games, which is a very high number for an interior lineman. He’s coming off a dominant performance against the Jaguars in which he was credited with two of those sacks and 1.5 run stuffs. All of the Panthers interior linemen will be responsible for keeping Carter in check, but it’s likely going to be Robert Hunt that handles the bulk of that assignment. Hunt has been a little shaky this season. He’ll need to regain his form from past seasons to limit Carter. Eagles vs time zones The Eagles played in London last week, and with the NFL playing so many international games now, that doesn’t always mean a bye in the following week. The London trip certainly seems a lot less daunting now that the NFL forced a couple of teams to play a game in Australia, but it’s still not nothing to travel across six time zones to play a game early in the morning for the body clocks. We’ll see if the Eagles are suffering from any jet lag coming back stateside, especially since they lost the game in heartbreaking fashion before making the long flight home.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Jamari Sharpe
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: BLOOMINGTON, IN - SEPTEMBER 19: Indiana Hoosiers DB Jamari Sharpe (22) warms up prior to a college football game between the Western Kentucky Hilltopppers and Indiana Hoosiers on September 19, 2026 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, IN. (Photo by James Black/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Indiana Hoosiers cornerback Jamari Sharpe Bio Sharpe (6’1”, 187 lbs.) was a speedster wide receiver and track star in Miami, FL before finally switching to corner his senior year of high school. The nephew of former NFL corner Glenn Sharpe, was only a three star recruit and signed with Indiana, redshirting his freshman season in 2022. As a redshirt freshman, he broke into the starting lineup for most games. The following season saw the Hoosiers hire Curt Cignetti, and Sharpe’s role on the defense dwindled. Despite the fewer snaps, there was a noticeable jump in Sharpe’s technique and understanding of the defensive concepts. Last season, Sharpe won the starting corner spot opposite D’Angelo Ponds (who was a second round pick in last year’s Draft). Including Indiana’s bowl games, Sharpe tallied 50 tackles, six for loss, six passes defended, a fumble recovery, and a National Championship sealing interception against Miami. He has continued to play well this season despite missing a game early in the year due to injury. Strengths/Weaknesses Sharpe’s biggest strength is his zone coverage. He does an excellent job of reading the quarterback’s eyes and driving on throws with his elite athleticism. His track star speed allows him to be more patient because he is confident in his recovery on downfield throws. His improved technique under Cignetti goes beyond just coverage, as his tackling has become a lot more consistent (only charged with four missed tackles in 2025). His size/speed combination is exactly what NFL defenses look for in an outside corner. Sharpe’s production has not matched his coverage ability, leading some scouts to be a bit wary. He only intercepted one pass through the entirety of Indiana’s championship run, and that one came at the very end of the Championship Game. While he has been able to force several fumbles, his run defense is average at best. He’s a willing run defender, but isn’t a game changer on the outside. Projection Jamari Sharpe is a rangy zone corner with the size and speed to be effective at the next level. His growth under Curt Cignetti demonstrates a coachability and desire to improve that defensive staffs will love. Starting all 16 games for a national championship team will be looked upon highly as well. While his man coverage skills lag behind his elite zone skills, he does well enough to stay on the field regardless of the coverage called. A team like the Panthers, who run a lot of off zone coverage, would be a perfect fit for Sharpe. Ejiro Evero’s defense (if he is still the DC next season) would allow Sharpe to use his eyes and speed to their fullest advantage. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Jamari Sharpe is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: 2026 NFL QB Rankings- Quarter Pole Edition
summary: It’s the second installment of our 2026 quarterback rankings. We released our first set of rankings before the season started, and this second article comes out roughly 25% into the season. We will update this again at the midway point, 75% through the season, and at the end of the season. As always, critical to […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 12: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills smiles prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s the second installment of our 2026 quarterback rankings. We released our first set of rankings before the season started, and this second article comes out roughly 25% into the season. We will update this again at the midway point, 75% through the season, and at the end of the season. As always, critical to keep in mind, these rankings consider the QB’s career rankings. There are plenty of rankings that take a look at these rankings in a bubble and talk about only how QBs are performing this year only. These rankings look at their careers, so you’ll see less movement in the top 10, more movement as we move further down the rankings, and they are pretty volatile towards the bottom of the 50. But that’s critical to know when you look at Justin Herbert’s ranking. It also takes into account his previous years of success, and not just his struggles the first 5 games of the season. Yes, their more current performance outweighs performance from years ago, which is why you’ll see Aaron Rodgers where he is, and even guys like Joe Flacco. But without further discussion, here’s a look at the quarter pole edition of the 2026 QB Rankings. 1. Patrick Mahomes, Kansas City Chiefs (1) We wondered if the King was going to finally be knocked off his perch this time around, and Josh Allen certainly has made a case, but 9 TDs and 2 INTs in 4 games isn’t how you lose the top spot. 2. Josh Allen, Buffalo Bills (2) “Somebody tackle Josh Allen” is a song that’s taking over the social media airwaves, and it ain’t wrong. His pass/run combination is really like nothing we’ve ever seen. Allen can take over the top spot this year if he keeps it up, but he’s going to have to slay the dragon. 3. Lamar Jackson, Baltimore Ravens (4) It felt like people really wanted to pile on Jackson for a subpar season last year. I think we dropped him from 2 to 4 because we don’t like to overreact on this list. Jackson settling in at number 3 feels right. He’s still an elite playmaker with the football. 4. Joe Burrow, Cincinnati Bengals (5) The Bengals look like they are a playoff team and could challenge for a Super Bowl if things break their way. Burrow is obviously a big reason why. With an improved defense, it’s going to be on Burrow to make noise once again in January. 5. Matthew Stafford, LA Rams (3) Stafford rose to number three last year with his MVP performance, but so far this year, Stafford has shown signs of aging. He’s still a great slinger of the football and makes wow throws every game, but we are starting to see a little of Father Time catch up with him. It’ll be interesting to see how this season plays out. 6. Dak Prescott, Dallas Cowboys (7) After the top 5, it gets really difficult to rank QBs. Prescott hasn’t exactly grabbed this spot showing no mercy, but he’s having another quality Dak year while a lot of the guys around him have not played well. Dak climbs one spot as the bottom half of the top 10 starts shaking out this year. 7. Jared Goff, Detroit Lions (10) The Lions, as a whole, haven’t been great, but has anyone noticed that Jared Goff is averaging 300 yards passing per game and is on pace to throw 41 TDs with 0 INTs? He’s doing it with his third offensive coordinator in 3 years. Goff is showing he was not a Ben Johnson merchant. 8. Justin Herbert, LA Chargers (6) Justin Herbert is playing like one of the five worst QBs in the NFL, but because of his previous years, we aren’t going to just drop him 10 or 12 spots. If he continues to play like this, he will see himself fall out of the top 10 and maybe even the top 20, but we need to see more struggles over some more games before we are willing to say he’s not one of the better QBs in the league. 9. Brock Purdy, San Francisco 49ers (15) Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy have something going. Purdy is leading the league in QBR and has a QB rating of 119. He’s healthy after an injury-riddled 2025 and showing that he can be a top-10 QB in the league with Shanny by his side. 10. Caleb Williams, Chicago Bears (11) Caleb was poised to climb several spots, but the hamstring injury certainly derailed that. Caleb has had one healthy game in good conditions, and he led the offense to 59 points. It’s safe to say that he’s a top 10 QB in the league. The question is how close can he rise to top 5 by season’s end. 11. Jordan Love, Green Bay Packers (13) Love continues to oscillate on my list between about 8 and 13. He continues to show that he’s a borderline top 10 QB but can’t cement his status with his inconsistent play. He looked pretty dreadful the first few games of the season, but he showed against Chicago what he can do if he has a little more time to cook. 12. Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars (14) Lawrence may never reach the heights that he was expected to have when he was drafted first overall by the Jaguars, but Liam Coen has unlocked consistent play from Lawrence, and he’s safely established himself as a top-half QB in the league. 13. Sam Darnold, Seattle Seahawks (8) Darnold has had an odd start to his 2026 season. He’s been inconsistent, has turned the ball over, and honestly has been outplayed by his backup, Drew Lock. Darnold is a Super Bowl champion, and no one will take that away from him or how well he played in both 2024 and 2025, but he’s going to need to improve his play if he wants to be considered a top 10 QB in the NFL. 14. Drake Maye, New England Patriots (9) After his performance on Sunday, Drake Maye may be back, but with how poorly he played in his first four games, when his sample size is as small as it is, he’s going to have to tumble a few spots. If Maye gets back to his 2025 form, I fully expect him to cement himself in the top 10, but he needs to shake off how things started this season. 15. Jalen Hurts, Philadelphia Eagles (12) The Eagles may genuinely have a Jalen Hurts problem. He has a low completion percentage, which is fine if he was an attacking QB, but he rarely pushes the middle of the field and has one of the lowest Y/A at 6.1. The Eagles are building draft capital in 2028, and it’s not impossible to consider that they could go after a new QB if Hurts doesn’t improve. 16. Jayden Daniels, Washington Commanders (17) Daniels has the skills to be a top 10 QB in the league, but he continues to show that he can’t stay on the field, and he had another dislocation of his elbow that has forced him to miss multiple games. If Daniels continues to get hurt, he’s not going to be the guy the Commanders think he can be. 17. Bryce Young, Carolina Panthers (22) After a disastrous start to his career, Young continues to improve and is pushing to be a top-half QB in the league. I decided to slide him one spot in front of CJ Stroud, but it’s really going to be interesting to see how these two draft-mates have this year play out and where they stand by the end of the year. 18. CJ Stroud, Houston Texans (19) Ironically, the Texans defense has been the issue for them this year, not the offense, and Stroud has been pretty good. He hasn’t shown signs of being the guy from his rookie year but looks much better than the guy who has struggled the last couple of years. Stroud, at the moment, seems properly ranked. 19. Bo Nix, Denver Broncos (18) I’ve never seen a QB who can play poorly and bury his team only to play better and bail his team out. Nix is a roller coaster every game, and that inconsistency is preventing him from climbing the ranks. If he irons out his play, he has a chance to push to be a top 10 QB, but as long as the inconsistencies remain, this feels about the right spot for him. 20. Baker Mayfield, Tampa Bay Buccaneers (16) Mayfield did not play great before he was injured, and his offense, arguably, looks better with UDFA Jalon Daniels running the unit.…

title: Week 6 NFL Game Preview: Chicago Bears vs. Atlanta Falcons
summary: The Chicago Bears look to rebound from an ugly, humiliating loss to the Green Bay Packers while going on the road for the second straight week. This time, they should get starting QB Caleb Williams back. But he’s going to have a fight on his hands. The Atlanta Falcons have an explosive offense with stars […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 11: Atlanta running back Bijan Robinson (7) runs the ball during the NFL game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Atlanta Falcons on October 11th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Chicago Bears look to rebound from an ugly, humiliating loss to the Green Bay Packers while going on the road for the second straight week. This time, they should get starting QB Caleb Williams back. But he’s going to have a fight on his hands. The Atlanta Falcons have an explosive offense with stars Drake London and Bijan Robinson. Robinson is making a case for being one of, if not the , best running back in the league. Certainly among elite company like Kenneth Walker III, Jahmyr Gibbs, Derrick Henry and James Cook. Michael Penix Jr., the quarterback taken seven spots after Williams, is a great facilitator for Kevin Stefanski’s offense. He looks set to play despite a rib injury suffered late against the Ravens last week. Penix’s biggest issue over his first three seasons has been availability. Sunday will be his 16th start and 18th overall game. Let’s dive a little deeper into the Falcons and their history against Chicago. Atlanta Falcons SB Nation site : The Falcoholic Record: 2-3, second in the NFC South Last week: 30-23 loss in OT to the Ravens Game day, time, TV: Sunday, noon CT, FOX Spread: Bears -1.5 Bears all-time record against: 16-14 Historical meetings: The Bears and Falcons met in week 6 of the 2013 season with both teams at 2-3. The teams traded field goals, but Chicago found the end zone first with a 3-yard pass to Josh Morgan from Jay Cutler. This game ended up being a Bears-career high in passing yards for Cutler. He threw for 381 yards but just one touchdown. However, they had two 100-yard receiving games from Brandon Marshall (113) and Alshon Jeffery (136). Matt Forte rushed for two touchdowns. A late Matt Ryan interception helped seal it and the Bears won 27-13. Last meeting: Remember when there was very brief excitement that Matt Eberflus was building something? Week 17 of the 2023 season, the Bears moved to 7-9 when they stomped the Falcons 37-17 at Soldier Field. Taylor Heinicke threw three interceptions and was eventually benched for Desmond Ridder, who also threw a pick. Justin Fields threw a touchdown to DJ Moore, who had 159 yards. Fields also rushed for a touchdown, along with Khalil Herbert and Roschon Johnson. Herbert also had 124 yards. Injury report: The Falcons had three players on their Wednesday injury report. Did not participate CB C.J. Henderson (groin) Limited participation LB Divine Deablo (hamstring) DE Za’Darius Smith (concussion/neck) Offense: The Falcons offense ranks 13th in points and 10th in yards. Their rushing offense ranks second and their passing offense ranks 21st. The Falcons have gotten hot offensively since Michael Penix (67.5 pct. cmp./719 yds./3 TD/1 INT) came back. It helps to have Bijan Robinson (102 att./580 yds./4 TD), who leads the league in rushing. And Drake London (27 rec./488 yds./0 TD), who averages 18.1 yards per reception but somehow has no touchdowns. Bijan (18 rec./152 yds./1 TD) is actually their second-leading receiver. Followed by TE Kyle Pitts (10/109/1) and Jahan Dotson (8/149/1). Austin Hooper (5/40/1), Zachariah Branch (7/46/0) and former Bear Olamide Zaccheaus (4/17/0) are also role players. Behind Bijan is the other B. Robinson, Brian (51/210/4), who gets a fair share of carries inside the red zone. Defense: The Falcons defense ranks 21st in points and 16th in yards. Their rushing defense ranks fourth and their passing defense ranks 27th. S Xavier Watts (34 tkl/1 INT/2 PD/1 FF), LB Divine Deablo (16 tkls/1 PD/1 TFL/2 QB hits), CB Mike Hughes (25 tkls/1 TFL/3 PD) and CB C.J. Henderson (25 tkls/1 TFL/6 PD/1 FF) are the tackling leaders. S Jessie Bates III (24 tkls/2 PD/1 FR) and Za’Darius Smith (2.5 sk/4 TFL/3 QB hits) are two of the bigger names on the unit, but there is plenty of talent elsewhere, too. Cameron Thomas (2 sk/10 QB hits/1 TFL/1 FF) and Samson Ebukam (2.5 sk/9 QB hits/2 TFL) are among the leading pass-rushers. Gervon Dexter (0.5 sk/2 TFL/3 QB hits) is making himself comfortable in Atlanta’s defensive scheme, too. Key matchups: The defense is going to have its hands full with Atlanta’s playmakers. Bijan is tough for any team to contain. Combine him with London, who is a threat all over the field, and Dennis Allen’s unit will have its hands full. Until last week’s Ravens game, the Falcons have held opponents’ rushing attack in check. It was opponents’ aerial attacks that were doing damage. Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams will have to find the right balance to keep the Bears on the field, minimize Atlanta’s time of possession, while scoring as many points as they can. The Bears can hang in a shootout, but Chicago will want the ball last. Key stats The Falcons’ offense has turned the ball over in four of their five games. Atlanta has allowed nine passing touchdowns to three rushing touchdowns. The nine passing TD is tied for the fifth-most in the league. Opponents have the second-most pass attempts in the league against Atlanta, behind only Detroit. Atlanta has just one interception on the season, as well. The Falcons offense has the second-fewest pass attempts in the league and the second-most rushing attempts. While Chicago’s red zone offensive woes are well-documented, Atlanta ranks seventh in offensive red zone scoring, getting in 69.2 percent of their trips.
