Patrick Mahomes having a passionate rant towards Eric Bieniemy. 🎥 @sluggahjells pic.twitter.com/yJPg2xKs9B — The Whole Delivery (@TWDTV1) October 4, 2026 Sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson asked Reid about that moment at halftime, and he described it as “frustration and competitiveness ,“ according to Wolfson. On Thursday, ESPN’s Nate Taylor asked about the conversation during Bieniemy’s time at the podium. His answer offered insight into the coach-player relationship in Kansas City, between Bieniemy and Mahomes, or whoever else on the Chiefs’ offense. “I’m the one doing all the complaining for the most part,” Bieniemy said with a smile. “But I have no problems with guys venting their frustrations because I want them to; that’s part of the dynamics of the relationships that we have. “Sometimes, you’re going to agree with things, and sometimes you’re going to disagree with things, but if there’s something that has taken place out on the field, they may have a better point of view than what we do off the field, so I want them to feel comfortable coming to share that stuff with me,” Bieniemy said. The short video made it clear that Bieniemy was listening to Mahomes and making an effort to hear him out. It’s part of his coaching style and his overall mentality as a former player. “There is no issue of communication,” Bieniemy clarified. “We play in the arena; it’s all about survival… You’re inviting all of that because I’d rather him come and vent his frustrations at me than to vent it in a different place where it’s not going to be taken the right way.” The discussion occurred during the first half, before the team put up 20 points in the fourth quarter and put away a motivated Raiders team. Conversations like that can make the difference between a win and a loss. The Chiefs didn’t make it easy on themselves in Las Vegas or in the Week 3 win over the Miami Dolphins . The biggest factor toward that on offense has been the lack of short-yardage success. Bieniemy alluded to that when describing Kansas City’s offense so far this season. “We’re still working on establishing our foundation; we’re still working on establishing who we are as an offense,” Bieniemy shared. “I know that we’ve done some good things, but there have been some things that we’ve done extremely shitty that we need to improve upon.” The Chiefs rank ninth in third-down conversion rate and 12th on fourth downs , but the few failures have come at inopportune times. In Week 1, running back Kenneth Walker found a 60-yard touchdown run on fourth and short; in the last two weeks, the backfield hasn’t navigated the trenches as well. “One thing I always tell the backs is this: regardless [of whether] we block anyone, it’s our duty and our responsibility to find a way to move the ball, to find a way to move the chains,” Bieniemy said. “There are offensive linemen, tight ends, everyone is involved,” Bieniemy elaborated. “Right now, we’re just doing okay in short yardage. We have to be better collectively as a group.” Moving forward, the team should have left guard Kingsley Suamataia helping make room for the backs and possibly left tackle Josh Simmons as well. He is back on the practice field this week. Rookie left tackle Kahlil Benson has done an admirable job filling in; if he moves to the bench at some point, don’t be surprised if he’s still used to move the chains on third and fourth downs.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Steve Spagnuolo on Chiefs’ pass rush: ‘It’s a step away’
summary: Through Week 5, the Kansas City Chiefs have the fewest sacks in the NFL (4). Of course, the team doesn’t have the extra game that 30 other teams do, but the team also has a league-worst 2.6% sack rate. According to Pro Football Reference, the Chiefs rank in the middle of the pack in pressure […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through Week 5, the Kansas City Chiefs have the fewest sacks in the NFL (4). Of course, the team doesn’t have the extra game that 30 other teams do, but the team also has a league-worst 2.6% sack rate. According to Pro Football Reference , the Chiefs rank in the middle of the pack in pressure rate (24%) , so defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s unit just needs to finish more pass-rush reps. When Spags was asked about the pass rush during his press conference on Thursday, he pointed to the players being close. “It’s a step away,” Spagnuolo told local media. “It’s a half of a second of getoff; it’s a quicker counter move if you really want to get down into the detail. Our guys have been there; would we like to have more sacks? Yes, but I still like the fact that we get the quarterback off the spot, we make him throw off time or off balance, and if we can keep doing that, that’s a good thing.” “Our guys have a lot of pride, but we do talk about staying away from the “S” words: stats and standings,“ Spags shared. ”Try to deal in the “W” word: wins.“ In Week 4 against the Las Vegas Raiders , Kansas City hit quarterback Kirk Cousins 10 times, but didn’t register a sack. Defensive end George Karlafits accounted for over half of the hits on Cousins, including one at the end that led to an interception by rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa. “That’s a great illustration of being a relentless pass rusher,” Spags said about Karlaftis’ pressure. “We were covering a lot of people obviously; they had to throw to the sideline, but that’s him; most of his pressures and his success come because he is relentless. He did that way back when he was in college. Let’s keep doing that.” The team has a strong chance to reverse the trend in Week 6 against the Los Angeles Chargers , a home game against a quarterback who has been sacked 17 times in five games. Still, if the defense limits the Chargers’ offense and comes out on top, as the Chiefs did in their previous two games, Spags will be satisfied. The veteran coach pays attention to only one statistic. “We all want [sacks], but it’s a stat. You know the stat I like? The stat that we harp on is the one stat that helps our football team win the game, and that’s points allowed,” Spags preached. This season, Kansas City ranks seventh in points allowed (19.2), just under the 20-point mark that usually indicates whether an NFL defense is pulling its weight or not.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Tiering the AFC by who the Chiefs should fear the most
summary: Now that five weeks of the NFL season have passed, it’s time to rank and tier the AFC opponents based on who the Kansas City Chiefs should fear most for the rest of the season. Let’s get it started with the contenders: Tier 1: Could win the AFC 1. Buffalo Bills To me, four teams […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that five weeks of the NFL season have passed, it’s time to rank and tier the AFC opponents based on who the Kansas City Chiefs should fear most for the rest of the season. Let’s get it started with the contenders: Tier 1: Could win the AFC 1. Buffalo Bills To me, four teams can realistically win the AFC: the Chiefs, Bills, Jaguars, and Ravens. Of those three, the Bills remain the scariest. Buffalo’s offense remains high-powered, with quarterback Josh Allen, their run game, and improved weapons. Buffalo’s defensive line has more juice this year with the emergence of Gregory Rousseau and Deone Walker. Still, Buffalo’s back 7 is incredibly leaky and can sink them. 2. Jacksonville Jaguars The Jaguars are 17-5 since Liam Coen took over as head coach and are a legitimate threat. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence is playing elite football, and their offense is humming with a deep supporting cast of weapons. Defensively, their talent isn’t overwhelming, but it’s well-coached and has stars like pass rusher Josh Hines-Allen and cornerback Travis Hunter. Their roster has holes, but they have top-10 units on both sides of the ball and are well-coached. 3. Baltimore Ravens Baltimore’s been an interesting watch through five weeks. Lamar Jackson is playing great, and new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has done a great job designing the run game and weaponizing Zay Flowers. Defensively, their front has more juice with the signing of Trey Hendrickson and improvements from Tavius Robinson, Travis Jones, and Mike Green. However, like Buffalo, their secondary can be leaky, and they still have skill-position issues to sort through. It’s also a new staff in its first year, so it’s hard to gauge how they’ll do in the playoffs until we see them there, but they have enough talent to be a threat. Tier 2: Could win a playoff game(s) 1. Cincinnati Bengals You could definitely argue for the Bengals in Tier 1. Their offense remains elite with quarterback Joe Burrow, and wideouts Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Adding Dexter Lawrence and Boye Mafe has dramatically improved their defensive line. However, their linebacker and safety play are still dreadful and I don’t think they can mitigate that for three postseason games. 2. New England Patriots New England’s been weird to start the year, but they seem to be rounding into shape. Their defense has carried over its positive momentum from the postseason, and the offense is starting to look as explosive as they were a year ago. They’ll get wide receiver A.J. Brown back soon, which should make the offense even better. I’m still dubious on New England vs. elite teams, but they have enough talent to be scary. 3. Denver Broncos The Broncos have been a rough watch offensively all year, but it’s still time for them to catch a rhythm and play better. Their defense is still very good at rushing the passer and playing man coverage. They can be dangerous, but I don’t trust the offense at all, and the vibes seem off there. They can’t run the ball, and Bo Nix is not seeing it well and moving less after his injuries. Feels like last year was probably their best shot. 4. Houston Texans Houston is 1-4, so it’s surprising to see them here, but I still think they’re a dangerous team. Quarterback C.J. Stroud is playing great football, and their defense is still very good, though they haven’t played at the level they did a year ago. However, they’ve played the Bills, Bengals, and Cowboys, three top offensive units, which will make your defense look worse. Houston generally peaks later and their schedule lightens up, so I expect them to be hanging around in the AFC picture. Tier 3: Competitive regular season teams Pittsburgh Steelers Tier 3 teams are relatively competitive regular-season teams that could play spoiler for seeding purposes, but probably don’t have the juice as playoff teams. The Steelers are the top team in this tier. They’re trench talent on both sides of the line of scrimmage, but their secondary has played poorly, and quarterback Aaron Rodgers is too old to play well for 17 games. Las Vegas Raiders The Raiders got off to a 3-0 start and played well against the Chiefs, but the cracks showed against the Patriots. Their run game isn’t explosive, they lack wide receiver talent, and their pass rush outside of Maxx Crosby is shaky. They’ll be a competitive 7-8 win team, and three of those wins came right out of the gate. Cleveland Browns Cleveland started 3-1 and has shown more spirit than expected, but it’s still an offense led by Deshaun Watson, and they have one of the worst run games in the NFL. Like the Raiders, they’ve already hit their peak and will likely decline moving forward. Indianapolis Colts The Colts are a depressing situation because they traded their 2027 1st-round pick already and they aren’t a good team. Their offense is fine, but not the unit that was setting offensive records a year ago. Their pass rush is bad and they bleed too many passing yards in coverage. They’re just not a good team and I expect them to pack it in soon. New York Jets The Jets are playing hard and much better than a year ago, but they’re still limited in talent, and their coaching staff isn’t elite. But the Chiefs game against the Jets should be more competitive than I expected. Tier 4: Already doing mock drafts Los Angeles Chargers One of the shocks of the NFL season is how dead the Chargers already are, but they’re a terrible team. Their defense is fine, but not as good as when Jesse Minter was leading it. Their offense is atrocious. There’s a good chance their entire staff is fired and the players already look checked out. Nothing is going well. Miami Dolphins We saw the Chiefs play the Dolphins, and while they play hard, they lack any real talent. It’s hard seeing them win more than 2-3 games. Tennessee Titans The Titans are a dreadful watch with a terrible offense. Their staff is probably getting fired after their first year and they might have a new quarterback. It’s a train wreck in Tennessee.
author: Nate Christensen

title: Chiefs Market Movers: Who’s trending up or down out of the bye
summary: It’s been an interesting season so far—with the early bye week, it’s not quite a mid-season review, but it’s a great time to check in on some of the trends we’ve seen over the first four weeks. Your 4-0 Kansas City Chiefs are playing good defense and running the ball like it’s 1997. They have […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been an interesting season so far—with the early bye week, it’s not quite a mid-season review, but it’s a great time to check in on some of the trends we’ve seen over the first four weeks. Your 4-0 Kansas City Chiefs are playing good defense and running the ball like it’s 1997. They have an OPOY candidate (running back Kenneth Walker) and an MVP (quarterback Patrick Mahomes). The rookies are playing well, and the coaching staff changes seem to have helped. On the other hand, injuries, penalties, and pass-rush and pass-protection issues have been frustrating, and a couple of their wins were closer than they should be. Here are a few Chiefs who seem to be trending up or down. BULLS Running back Kenneth Walker III: The offseason narrative: Kansas City made only one significant offensive addition, and he’s a running back. The reality: it’s changed everything. Walker is leading the league in nearly every statistical category. He’s already racked up big plays of 60 and 76 yards, and has been on the field for three-fourths of the offensive snaps so far. The coaching staff has committed to a new-old-style offense with plenty of under-center handoffs, screens, and play-action passes. They found the perfect guy to execute on the field, and it’s paying off. The only question left is whether they can do this in January and February. Cornerbacks Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams: If the trend continues, we may have to talk about these guys every week. They’ve both shown the skill set and makeup to be an elite tandem in this league. Barring injury, my only concern is that the coaching staff tries moving one of them inside because of shortcomings there (see Bears below). Otherwise, these two are making Andy Reid, Steve Spagnuolo, and Brett Veach look very smart for letting those other guys walk. Offensive lineman Kahlil Benson: Going back to the premise of this series, we’re looking for those who are trending in one way or another, even if they aren’t the top-of-the-roster guys. Just think back to the expectations we had for a player, and how they have over (or under) performed compared to those expectations— or compared to their contract/draft slot. Given that context, it seems logical that we should be extremely bullish on Kahlil Benson. The guy wasn’t even considered a priority UDFA; he had to earn his roster spot via tryout and a strong offseason. Even then, there was lots of panic and doubt when he struggled in a couple of preseason games. He earned the starting nod and has more than held his own. Yes, the coaching staff is giving him more help than they normally allow a tackle, but by any measure Benson has performed well in the role he was asked to fill. As the season wears on, they’ll need him— whether he’s the starting left tackle, starting at another spot, or as depth—he is part of the solution. Others trending in the right direction this week: Emmet Johnson, George Karlaftis, Travis Kelce, Drue Tranquill, Kristian Fulton, Matt Araiza, Xavier Nwankpa , Felix Anudike-Uzomah BEARS Defensive tackle Chris Jones: It’s weird putting Chris on this list. He’s an elite player in this league, and will belong in the Hall of Fame. He’s made a fantastic living terrorizing quarterbacks from the interior of the defensive line. He’s been unblockable in key situations. But this season, he’s clearly fighting through injury and simply hasn’t been as disruptive as we’re used to. Jones doesn’t have a single sack yet this season, despite playing primarily in pass-rushing situations. Part of the issue could be his usage—the team has aligned him outside on most snaps. Chris Jones can do that—occasionally. But his bread and butter is destroying guards and double-teams on the inside. Maybe they’re trying to save him some wear and tear for later in the season? The entire Slot/Nickel Cornerback position group: It seemed obvious the Chiefs wanted to address this position coming into 2026, and they did, throwing a bunch of options out there. They drafted Jadon Canaday, signed Kader Kohu, brought L’Jarius Sneed back, and retained Chris Roland-Wallace and (gulp) Chamarri Conner. Sneed has been the guy thus far, playing 76% of the team’s defensive snaps at the position. The results have been predictably mixed— Sneed has been involved in some significant plays, including the forced-and-recovered fumble against the Dolphins. But teams have found lots of success with quick passes against Sneed. It’s one of those things that can wreck a pass defense— when QBs have a quick/easy option to complete a pass on one guy, it neutralizes a good pass rush. Fullback Khyiris Tonga: For a minute there, it looked like the Chiefs could dominate on third-and-fourth-and-1, but forward progress seems to have stalled over the last two games. Using defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga at fullback was a fun changeup, but teams seem to have completely caught on. Hopefully, Andy Reid was just setting up some future looks by handing the ball to Tonga a couple of times. They need to move the sticks better in these situations, and using an actual fullback may be part of the answer. Others trending in the wrong direction this week: Jack Cochrane, Rashee Rice , Kingsley Suamataia , Mike Caliendo VALUE (SLEEPER) PICKS: Defensive lineman Omarr Norman-Lott: ONL may be the forgotten man on this defensive front, but he may be close to returning and reminding folks why they missed him. A quick, stout interior defensive lineman who can rotate in on the pass rush, Norman-Lott can absolutely help. Left Tackle Josh Simmons: The fickle nature of NFL fans, media, social media, and other commentators is insane. Josh Simmons was the left tackle that we’ve always wanted in Kansas City. But then he missed the first four games with a back injury, and sentiment around Simmons plummeted—even faster than sentiment around the Chargers. Well, Simmons is back at practice after the bye week, and I’m sure many who have been sleeping on him will jump back on the bandwagon once he’s in the lineup. From what we know, he didn’t stop caring, and he didn’t forget how to play football. There’s a non-zero chance we’ll forget the Simmons criticism by the end of the postseason. Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa: It feels like an annual tradition with these Chiefs: acquire an athletic linebacker, bury him on the depth chart behind some one-dimensional coaches’ favorites. Then, we all complain that Spagnuolo needs a guy like that on the field. Why aren’t they playing this guy? Is this another case of a guy who “doesn’t understand the playbook?” If so, could the playbook be the real problem? Bassa appears to be that guy this season. Yes, it’s early, but (as mentioned above) Chiefs opponents have been picking on defenders with quick passes over the middle. Bassa is only a few games into his rookie season, but it’s time to give him a shot. He can be a playmaker— unless there’s something we don’t understand (there often is).
author: Matt Stagner

title: Patrick Mahomes has been testing Chiefs’ young wideouts
summary: When the Kansas City Chiefs come off of their bye week to host the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday, their receiving corps will look different than in previous weeks. Speedster Tyquan Thornton was lost for the foreseeable future when he dislocated his ankle making a spectacular play in Week 4’s victory over the Las Vegas […]
full_text: Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect When the Kansas City Chiefs come off of their bye week to host the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday, their receiving corps will look different than in previous weeks. Speedster Tyquan Thornton was lost for the foreseeable future when he dislocated his ankle making a spectacular play in Week 4’s victory over the Las Vegas Raiders . In addition, top wideout Rashee Rice left the game early with a hamstring injury. Rice was held out of practice on Wednesday . Rice and Thornton combined for 409 of the Chiefs’ 1037 receiving yards through the first four games of the season. Before Wednesday’s practice, head coach Andy Reid lamented Thornton’s injury but expected the team’s depth receivers to step up. Third-year pro Xavier Worthy also showed life in Week 4 by catching 4 passes for 70 yards after a very slow start to the year. “[Thornton] was having a very good year, and I’m sad to see what happened to him because of that,” Reid remarked. “He’s a great kid on top of all that. But one man’s loss is another man’s opportunity to jump in and do that. So, whoever that might be that’s got the call to make the play, that’s a positive. I’ve trusted all the guys, and Xavier’s still in there, too, going and he’s coming off a couple good catches in our last couple games.” Following Reid at the podium, quarterback Patrick Mahomes expressed confidence that young receivers Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen can rise to the opportunity now in front of them. “They’ve put in the work,” Mahomes explained. “Obviously, we’ve had the guys in front of them with Tyquan going out there and playing great football, and so they’ve had to put in the work at practice, and they’ve been doing that. So now their number gets called, and they’re going to step into the role and do their job. I’m excited for them. We’ll put them in position to succeed. I have a lot of trust in those guys, a lot of confidence in them, and so we’ll continue to push it forward.” "That's my guy right there, he trusts me, he trusted me in Training Camp, so I'm ready to work with him." — Cyrus Allen on getting ready to see more playing time with Patrick Mahomes. More on @fox4kc tonight. #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/lSCK2be7oP — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) October 14, 2026 Royals only has three catches for 17 yards on the year, and Allen has yet to make his first NFL catch. Mahomes believes that practicing as a bigger part of the game plan will allow for a stronger showing than what fans saw in limited Week 4 action after Rice’s injury. “It’s going to make it easier for them,” Mahomes predicted. “When you get thrown in, and you never know which position you’re going to be at and what route you’re going to run, it’s hard. That’s part of playing in the NFL is you don’t get those reps that you necessarily would have had in college and high school and stuff like that. So, I thought they did a great job of stepping in whenever their number’s been called. “But now they’ll have a full week of kind of getting those reps in, and we’ll put them in position to succeed where they can do their best things. And so, like I said, I have a lot of confidence in those guys. They did a great job at training camp, and when their number’s been called in the season, they’ve done a great job as well.” Mahomes has a good gauge on where the young receivers stand with Reid’s playbook because he has been testing them constantly since training camp. “I wouldn’t describe it as pop quizzes,” Mahomes revealed, “but you test guys, and you talk to guys throughout routes. So, in training camp and in early parts of the season and maybe in practice, when something happens, I go up to them and talk to what they’re thinking and kind of how I’m thinking. You hope what sticks with them is that they have these one-on-one conversations, either on the sideline or on the field, and so that when it happens in the game, they’re ready for it. That’s all you can do. You can’t prepare for everything, but at the same time, you can prepare for the reps that you do have. I thought we’ve done a great job of that, and we’ll do that this week as well.” Mahomes learned the technique he uses from one of the best: tight end Travis Kelce. “I think it started with Trav,” he recalled. “I think that was kind of the biggest thing when I first got into the league. He always would just talk to me after every play. So then, when we got to games, I would know what he was thinking, and obviously that’s kind of blossomed to what it’s blossomed to. So, I try to keep that going. I’ve done it with Rashee now. I’ve done it with a lot of these guys that we’ve kind of been through here, is that we have these conversations so that when we get in the game, we’re on the same page thinking. If we’re not, we talk about it on the sideline right after and try to be on the same page the next rep.”
author: Jared Sapp

title: Chiefs News: The Chiefs’ offense has been elite again
summary: Whether it’s big-time throws being made by quarterback Patrick Mahomes or gashing runs by running back Kenneth Walker, the Kansas City Chiefs’ offense looks like one of the NFL’s best once again after a multi-year stretch when that was not the case. But what’s different about this version of the Chiefs offense? Download the SB […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Whether it’s big-time throws being made by quarterback Patrick Mahomes or gashing runs by running back Kenneth Walker, the Kansas City Chiefs ’ offense looks like one of the NFL’s best once again after a multi-year stretch when that was not the case. But what’s different about this version of the Chiefs offense? Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news The Chiefs’ offense has been elite again — but for an entirely different reason | The Kansas City Star Here’s the oddity of the biggest change they made: They were basically the worst under-center team in the NFL a year ago. They totaled just 45.1 yards per game in the formation, second-to-last in the league. They averaged 3.0 yards per pass attempt while lining up under center, last in the league. Then they decided to do more of that. And what do you know, a year later, they lead the NFL in rush yards per play (6.3) in under-center formations, a half-yard better than second place, and rank second in pass yards per play (9.5), more than triple the efficiency of last season. Chiefs still have faith in pass rush, despite going without a sack since Week 1 | ESPN Entering this week, the Chiefs ranked 27th in pass rush win rate, generating pressure by beating the opponent’s pass protection within 2.5 seconds just 45% of the time. The concern for the Chiefs after their most recent game, a comeback win over the Las Vegas Raiders, is that quarterback Kirk Cousins, who they pressured on just 34.6% of his pass drops, was the least mobile passer they have faced so far this season. “We’ve done a good job of keeping the quarterback busy back there, though, with pressure, which is important,” coach Andy Reid said Monday. “Hands down, we want to have sacks. But the pressure on the quarterback ends up being an important thing, and I think our guys have been generating that.” Cyrus Allen and 7 more Kansas City Chiefs players who should play a bigger role after the Week 5 bye as injuries reshape the roster | A to Z Sports Briningstool has been the clear No. 3 tight end behind Travis Kelce and Noah Gray. His pass blocking leaves something to be desired (one pressure allowed on just two pass-blocking attempts), but he’s proven to be one of the team’s better run blockers at the position. In fact, he leads all Chiefs tight ends in run-blocking grade, according to Pro Football Focus. That includes both Gray and Kelce. With the running game becoming a much bigger part of the offense, getting your best run-blocking tight end on the field more often makes sense. Also, don’t put it past Kansas City to lean into more 13-personnel play-action looks. Briningstool made some acrobatic catches during training camp and the preseason. The story behind Chiefs rookie’s hot start? A Patrick Mahomes DM — and question to the GM | The Athletic Kansas City Chiefs general manager Brett Veach was in the Blum Student Union cafeteria lunch line when rookie running back Emmett Johnson caught him off guard. Johnson asked a direct question — and one Veach acknowledges now he wasn’t fully prepared for. “Y’all don’t think I can block, do you?” Chiefs Emerge as Potential Candidate for Week 8 Primetime Flex | Heavy Sports The Philadelphia Inquirer recently noted that the NFL is considering flexing the Eagles-Washington Commanders matchup out of “Sunday Night Football” in Week 8, as both teams currently have losing records. John Breech of CBS Sports examined the league’s other alternatives for the coveted primetime slot, but doesn’t believe there is a good option. Here is his case against the Chiefs-Broncos being flexed. Around the NFL Micah Parsons explains cautious return to play, doesn’t ‘care’ he’s missing Cowboys-Packers game | NFL.com “The biggest thing that people worried about with me, they’re like, ‘Man, why ain’t he back yet?’” he said this week on “The Edge with Micah Parsons” podcast. “If the Super Bowl was this week, I’m playing in the Super Bowl. But it’s just about me making sure I have all the small things fixed first.” Parsons underscored that the main concern isn’t injuring the repaired ACL again, but rather all the things that could go wrong by pushing to return early. Jaguars are first team since the merger not to allow a 40-yard rusher in first five games | Pro Football Talk Last year, the most rushing yards any player gained in a game against the Jaguars was 74, by Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. The Jaguars have now gone 23 consecutive games, counting last year’s playoff game, without allowing a 75-yard rusher. Opposing running backs have totaled 83 carries for 210 yards against the Jaguars this season, an average of just 2.5 yards per carry. That’s by far the best defense against running backs in the NFL this season. Lamar Jackson has ‘realistic chance’ to return vs. Browns in Week 6 | CBS Sports Jackson battled several nagging issues last year. Officially, an early-season hamstring injury cost him three games, and a back bruise caused him to miss another game late in the year. Unofficially, Jackson rarely looked like his normal explosive self. He had just 67 carries for 349 yards, both career lows, and his 5.2 yards per carry was his lowest mark since his rookie year, when he took over as starter midseason. Jackson’s pocket mobility evaporated, too, as he had a career-high sack rate. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Patrick Mahomes sees how the Chiefs’ offense can take it to the next level “It was easy once I saw Kenneth running the football,” Mahomes reflected about the offseason. “I was like, ‘We have to make sure we give him the best chances to succeed.’” “Obviously, he has run the ball terrific under center, and the offensive line has taken it upon themselves to fire off the ball and get that stuff down,” Mahomes continued. “I knew if we were able to do that, the play action game would open up even more. Then it’s about me just being the best quarterback for this team. It’s always going to be different, and this team was about being under center, getting him going and then play action off of it. I’m sure the defenses will adjust, and we’ll adjust off of that as well.” From The Feed Follow Arrowhead Pride on Social Media Facebook: Like our page Instagram: @ArrowheadPride X: Follow @ArrowheadPride AP Staff on X: See complete list

title: Chargers Injury Report: Little progress for injured Bolts Thursday
summary: From Wednesday to Thursday, there was very little movement, in any direction, for the laundry list of injured Chargers. title: Chargers land elite cornerback in new 2027 NFL mock draft
summary: After such a disastrous start to the season — and the presumed disaster that will likely follow over the next 13 weeks — it’s safe to say the Chargers could have numerous positions of need come next year’s draft. At this rate, the Bolts could be in line for a top three pick in next […]
full_text: WEST LAFAYETTE, IN - SEPTEMBER 26: Notre Dame Fighting Irish cornerback Leonard Moore (15) looks to the sidelines during the college football game between the Purdue Boilermakers and Notre Dame Fighting Irish on September 26, 2026, at Ross-Ade Stadium in West Lafayette, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After such a disastrous start to the season — and the presumed disaster that will likely follow over the next 13 weeks — it’s safe to say the Chargers could have numerous positions of need come next year’s draft. At this rate, the Bolts could be in line for a top three pick in next year’s draft. They could very well be in range of drafting Ohio State’s Jeremiah Smith, but everything seems to point to him going No. 1 overall and chances are the Chargers will not be there at the top unless this year us truly one of the worst in franchise history. Another name fans should get to know is Notre Dame cornerback Leonard Moore. He’s this year’s top cornerback prospect and arguably one of the best at the position to come out in recent years. He’s a complete, scheme-independent player who also reinforced his tackling entering the 2026 season. If a team does not need a quarterback in the top five, this is most certainly someone that will go that early. In a new 2027 mock draft from Bleacher Report’s Brent Sobleski, the Bolts end up picking Moore with the second-overall pick following the Titans drafting Jeremiah Smith ahead of them. Here’s Sobleski on how Moore fits with the Chargers: “The Los Angeles Chargers are in the midst of a disastrous season after starting 0-5. The team could go in a myriad of directions. In this instance, the Chargers add the best cornerback prospect since Patrick Peterson. Leonard Moore can immediately replace Donte Jackson, who is a free agent next year.” Other prospects that Sobleski believes could be on the table for the Chargers this year are LSU left tackle Jordan Seaton and Texas edge rusher Colin Simmons. Seaton is a bit odd as Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt still exist, but this could make sense if the Chargers really do not believe Slater and his injury issues will vanish anytime soon. I don’t think they’re getting out of his contract soon, either. Simmons is a real possibility given the talks of Khalil Mack either being traded before the deadline this season or simply retiring after the season altogether. The Chargers would be left with a duo of Tuli Tuipulotu and Akheem Mesidor, but their defense has always thrived with a trio of impact pass rushers. Drafting Simmons that high would be right on par with where they want to remain as a defense.

Trost is not yet activated from injured reserve, but this move means that the team has 21 days to either activate him or lose him for the rest of the season. His timing couldn’t be better given L.A.‘s current situation at tackle and this update is great news for the rookie third-round pick who’s been hurt since the preseason. Part of his high selection is Trost has the experience and versatility that can allow him to play as a rookie and help the Rams in 2026 . He also has the potential to develop at the NFL level like any player does. If Trost sees game action this year, then he’ll be doing both: Getting experience now, and developing for the future. As long as he can stay healthy. At this point, if a player is suiting up for the Rams, they have the potential to play. McVay said after the latest loss to the Buffalo Bills that all options were on the table. If Trost can stay healthy, he’ll be one of those options for the Rams. title: Rams make 2 practice squad moves to address special teams
summary: The Los Angeles Rams are making roster moves at a fast and furious pace, all centered around the special teams. That continued Wednesday with the officially announcements for signing edge Garrett Nelson, cornerback Damarion “Pepe” Williams to the practice squad, and kicker Blake Grupe to the roster. In corresponding moves, the Rams jettisoned edge Jamie […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams are making roster moves at a fast and furious pace , all centered around the special teams. That continued Wednesday with the officially announcements for signing edge Garrett Nelson, cornerback Damarion “Pepe” Williams to the practice squad, and kicker Blake Grupe to the roster. In corresponding moves, the Rams jettisoned edge Jamie Sheriff and kicker Harrison Mevis. While the addition of a place kicker was expected, the Rams inking of Nelson and Williams comes as a big surprise. It may simply be the normal give-and-take that occurs on the practice squad as the season marches along, but could the Rams brain trust really expect this pair of lower-tier players to add more to to the team than just filling in practice squad place settings? It is likely quite accurate and certainly fair to say that both are unknowns to Rams fans. Who are they and what do they bring to L.A.’s roster this season? Who is EDGE Garrett Nelson? Nelson had cup of coffee stops with five different teams and spent two seasons in the United Football League before signing with the Rams. The 26 year-old effort-based edge defender, has not recorded a single rep in NFL regular season play. At 6’3” 248 lb., he sports a well put together frame, shorter arm length at 31 5/8” and big 9 5/8” hands. Was an outstanding wrestler in high school and it shows in his contact balance and understanding of how to use leverage.. Originally signed by the Miami Dolphins as an undrafted free agent back in 2023. Let go in final cuts, he was quickly signed to the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad (PS) and released three weeks later. He was a member of the UFL’s San Antonio Brahmas in 2024 and 25 for their spring/early summer schedules. The fall of 2025 saw Nelson ping pong through training camp and practice squads. He started off with the Denver Broncos training camp, was let go in final cuts, and moved on to the New Orleans Saints PS until October, when he was again released. He settled in for the rest of the season, by re-signing with the Denver PS. 2026 has been just as busy. Nelson was inked to a reserve/futures contract by the Broncos in January, only to be cut in May. The Seattle Seahawks brought him in, but released him a day later. New Orleans claimed him off waivers for a second stint and again let him go at the end of August. He was a street free agent until the Rams added him to the PS this week. Finished his college days at Nebraska with 32 straight starts. Played both standing and with a hand in the dirt, tallying 167 tackles, 26 for loss, and 12 sacks. He also tabbed four each of passes batted down and passes broken up in coverage. Substantial amount of NFL preseason film on Nelson. He’s one of those players with the “hair on fire” play style. He’s a linear player, not a loose-limbed guy with twitchy agility and change of direction. Better as a run stopper than pass rusher. Not an explosive mover, but has good get off and hustles in pursuit which helps him appear to play faster. While his arm length is just okay, Nelson works hard and does a good job of setting the edge and taking on blockers. He keeps his outside shoulder free to keep the action turned in and gets a wide base and his hips into holding a gap. Has good awareness following the ball and straight line pursuit looks good. He’s the guy who going to hustle after every runner and get his share of hustle tackles. On the negative side, If linemen get a hold, he struggles to disengage and can be moved, nor is he going to quickly get lateral into position to block a path. As a pass rusher, Nelson doesn’t show a full toolbox of moves, pretty much limited to bullrushes. Pretty accurate striker, but not a great hand fighter with chops and swipes. Although he gets off the snap, there’s no shake and bake to get his opponent off balance, nor the dip and bend to get around the corner. He does however, have the ability to mirror the quarterback when stymied and pursue for clean up sacks. There’s film of him on kick block and kickoff coverage. That could be his main path to getting on the field. With his 4.93 forty time he’s not a burner, but he hustles every minute on the field banging into guys and actually zoning in on returners pretty well for a bigger guy. Watching him on kickoff coverage, there’s no reason to think he could not also get work done getting down range on punts. Former @HuskerFBNation EDGE Garrett Nelson has signed an UDFA with the @MiamiDolphins . 🐬 pic.twitter.com/x0cpwvk1Nh — Nebraska On BTN (@NebraskaOnBTN) May 1, 2023 Who is CB Damarion “Pepe” Williams? Fiesty, aggressive slot corner who showed promise coming out of college, but hasn’t been able to secure a role in the NFL. Williams has been with three previous outfits before joining the Rams and hasn’t participated in any measurable regular season action since 2022. At 5’10” 182 lb. with 29 5/8” arms and 8 3/4” hands the 28 year-old lacks prototypical NFL cornerback frame, but he play’s with an attitude and physicality that’s much bigger. He was a First Team JUCO All-American before moving up to D1 football. Drafted by the Baltimore Ravens at #141 of Round 4 in the 2022 NFL Draft. As a rookie, Williams saw action in 14 games. In 2023, he made the opening roster, but only played in one game, losing the season to injury. He suffered an ankle injury and the screws set to stabilize ended up cracking the bone, forcing a second surgery. In 2024, the Ravens waived him and signed him to the practice squad, but cut him loose for good in October. The Seattle Seahawks added him to their PS for the rest of the season and offered him a reserve/futures contract at its conclusion. Seattle let him go in 2025 final cuts. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers grabbed Williams up and followed the same protocol, PS followed by futures contract for 2026. Two month’s ago, Williams was again injured and placed on the Injured Reserve List, rather than stay there all season, he accepted an injury settlement and became a street free agent until the Rams signed him to their PS Wednesday. After his aforementioned junior college tenure, Williams advanced his game to the University of Houston. He started 33 of 34 games over three seasons, garnering 167 tackles, 10.5 for loss, picked off three passes, and broke up 24 more. At both the JC and university levels, Williams provided special teams work as a returner of punts and kickoffs. The biggest thing that stands out on both his college and pro film is his willingness to stick his nose in tackling. Despite the lean frame, Williams plays with an aggressive, combative nature,. Taking into consideration his size and skillset, he appears best suited in the pro game to slot/nickel work and zone coverage, looking in at the play in front of him and making the best use of his anticipation, read/react, and downhill burst skills. He has however, in his history, shown the versatility to line up anywhere in the secondary. With a 4.53 forty, he’s not liquid fast, but showed stellar burst and the ability to maintain it on 1.53 10-yard and 2.59 20-yard splits. Williams is not a long strider to close ground on longer routes, his is short area speed. While he shows good ball skills and plus hand/eye coordination, he appears to have some ball tracking issues when lined up outside, turning his back to run the quarterback, and running downfield with opposing receivers. Because of he’s quicker than fast, he can provide sticky coverage underneath. With his competitive nature and willingness to tackle, there would appear to be a path to play time as a gunner on special teams. Again, he does have return work in his college background, but I couldn’t find a record of any as a pro. It’s hard to project him into many cornerback snaps, simply because the Rams have gotten solid coverage out of the current unit. BIG pressure on 3rd and 10 by Damarion Williams 😤 📱: Stream #PHIvsBAL on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ORHtcnltUr — NFL (@NFL) August 10, 2024 Moving the needle?…

title: Should Rams bring back Joe Noteboom as A.J. Jackson insurance?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams need insurance at left tackle behind Alaric Jackson, and if they want to look outside the current roster there are a few veteran free agents left who can fill that need. One of the most intriguing names left on a bare market is the one Rams fans will remember the best: […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams need insurance at left tackle behind Alaric Jackson, and if they want to look outside the current roster there are a few veteran free agents left who can fill that need. One of the most intriguing names left on a bare market is the one Rams fans will remember the best: Joe Noteboom. Two years after his last start with L.A., should the franchise bring him home? Why the Rams need a little help from old friends Jackson will only miss one game due to suspension, costing him this Sunday’s home game against the Arizona Cardinals, down from his original two-game suspension that was handed down after he punched Buffalo Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb Monday night. That’s a good thing, because the Rams don’t want to be without their left tackle more than they have to be. But Jackson has also proven he’s not the most reliable player on the roster, and this is a team that can’t afford any holes along its offensive line as it tries to keep pace in the NFC race. While David Quessenberry is fine in a pinch, Los Angeles would be better off with a reasonable replacement who can rotate in should Quessenberry struggle. At this stage of the year, however, limited options for free agent acquisitions include the likes of Taylor Decker, Noteboom and not much else. Decker was a hot topic this offseason the last time Jackson found himself in hot water. He had a long, productive career with the Detroit Lions and is certainly familiar with quarterback Matthew Stafford. The biggest questions about Decker, however, revolve around what he would cost and whether or not he would want to come back. I’m just being a Dad! lost a lot of time with the kiddos last few years. — Taylor Decker (@__taylordecker) October 1, 2026 Noteboom is intriguing mostly because he’s a familiar face. After being selected in the third round of the 2018 draft, he played 81 games over seven seasons in Los Angeles, starting 36 of them. Injuries have hampered him throughout this career; just search for him in the TurfShowTimes archives and you’ll see plenty of examples of that. The Rams let Noteboom walk following the 2024 season, and he spent last year with the Baltimore Ravens on a one-year deal worth just over $2 million. He ended up starting once in 10 games played. He’d be a cheap option and he knows the system, but is that enough to assuage any other concerns tied to him? Ravens offensive line pass-blocking grades and pressures allowed against Houston: – Joe Noteboom: 18.5 / 5 pressures – Andrew Vorhees: 55.5 / 2 pressures – Tyler Linderbaum: 74.9 / 0 pressure – Daniel Faalele: 43.4 / 1 pressure – Roger Rosengarten: 67.1 / 1 pressure — Pedro H. Rhormes (@rhormes_) October 6, 2025 After that, the Rams would be looking at several other also-rans at the position. Cam Robinson never met the hype he had as a prospect (both in high school and college) but has at least been functional for most of his career, and was still signing decently sized contracts into his most recent deal. Kelvin Beachum is already 37, and while he’s been equally unspectacular he’s been in the league well over a decade for a reason. That’s the bulk of the feasible options. Jackson is a good player and a core piece of what the Rams want to do, but this is now multiple suspensions he’s faced (plus another in college), not to mention the off-field legal issues. While the hope is obviously that he can simply stay on the field the rest of the way after his suspension ends, the Rams need to consider adding as much depth at that spot as possible.

title: What fans criticizing Sean McVay are forgetting about the Rams
summary: The Los Angeles Rams are 2-3 and once again the finger pointing is at Sean McVay and his handling of special teams, play calling, and clock management. It’s a common story in the McVay era, but it’s not nearly as bad of a tale as what the Rams were like before McVay rescued this franchise […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams are 2-3 and once again the finger pointing is at Sean McVay and his handling of special teams, play calling, and clock management. It’s a common story in the McVay era, but it’s not nearly as bad of a tale as what the Rams were like before McVay rescued this franchise from the dark ages. As fair as it could be to criticize McVay for his failures, it’s unfair to ignore his successes. And since L.A. hired him to replace Jeff Fisher in 2017, he’s had a lot more wins than losses. The old Rams went through a lot of losses. I’ll take some special teams gaffes over 32nd ranked offenses. Sean McVay watching his special teams unit pic.twitter.com/r8mbI9lcPG — Kafka, Esq. 🧌 (@metalgearobama) October 13, 2026 Yes, special teams is bad It’s fair to say that the Rams continuously fail at the third phase of football. Through five weeks, L.A. is once again ranked dead last in DVOA on special teams. Special Teams EPA through Week 5 1. MIN +26.5 2. SEA +25.4 3. NYG +21.8 The Super Bowl favorite LA Rams sit 32nd (–28 EPA), and SF is 26th despite having the second‑highest SB odds. pic.twitter.com/MLxcPJOLDf — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) October 13, 2026 And for yet another season, the Rams have changed kickers . This time at midseason, just as they did in 2020, 2023, and 2025. There’s little question that since firing Bones Fassel, McVay hasn’t gripped the importance of special teams. The Rams have lost 28 pts on Special Teams. We've played 5 games. MY GOD https://t.co/2GD023zRTm — Marcus Whitman (@TFG_Football) October 13, 2026 That being said, the Rams are also top-7 DVOA on both offense and defense. And that’s without Myles Garrett. That’s largely without Jaylen Watson or significant contributions by Aaron Donald. That’s with Puka Nacua missing two games. So should we forget what McVay has done to help the Rams while we’re criticizing him for what Harrison Mevis did to set them back? Let's set the record straight on some poor NFCW statistical narratives. DVOA ranks: 49ERS Offense: #1 Defense: #4 Special teams: #24 Overall: #1 SEAHAWKS Offense: #26 Defense: #2 Special teams: #8 Overall: #8 RAMS Offense: #6 Defense: #7 Special teams: #32 Overall: #10 — David Lombardi (@LombardiHimself) October 15, 2026 Sean McVay completely turned the Los Angeles Rams around as soon as he was hired in 2017. Prior to McVay’s arrival, the Rams had not made the playoffs since 2004 when they were the then St. Louis Rams. McVay arrived and immediately took L.A. to the playoffs in his first year. The next year, they were in the Super Bowl. McVay’s changing of the Rams’ culture is among the most dramatic turnarounds in the NFL you’ll find. The (roughly) decade before McVay The Rams went 8-8 in their ’04 season, and somehow beat the Seattle Seahawks in the Wild Card Round. St. Louis would go on to lose in the Divsional Round to the Atlanta Falcons. They never made it back to the playoffs until McVay’s arrival. From the span of 2005 to 2016 , the Rams lost, and they lost a lot. They won 60 games with 131 losses. Zero contention. Zero hope year in and year out. The (roughly) decade after McVay Then, in 2017, Les Snead took a risk and hired McVay, the youngest NFL head coach at the time. McVay rewrote the book on what the Rams could be. From 2017 to 2025 , McVay and the Rams won 92 regular season games to go along with 57 losses. Two Super Bowl appearances, one Super Bowl win. Plenty of the hope year in and year out. I think it’s time for Sean McVay to LET GO. Let go of the past mistakes. Let go of the games that got away. Let go of the need to call the perfect game. Sometimes it feels like he’s so worried about making the wrong decision that he gets in his own way. The Rams have the #1… pic.twitter.com/KuqRWiNZXe — SamTalksRams (@SamTalksRams) October 14, 2026 A new day The Rams went from being a doormat to a perennial contender. It took a team effort, but no single person may have made that turnaround happen more than McVay. Before McVay, the Rams weren’t taken seriously as a Super Bowl team, they weren’t even taken seriously as a team that could win any given Sunday. It was the dark ages for the franchise and their fanbase. Now, the Rams contend every year (one losing season aside). McVay’s led them to a Super Bowl win. McVay is the best head coach in the history of the Rams. Fans should be frustrated with lack of continuity on special teams. No one should be more frustrated than McVay, but with history as a guide, McVay will get this team right. He’s done it before. If McVay doesn’t get it right, he’ll lose some of his shine, but not all of it. Not until the Rams find another head coach who does it better.

Going into Week 6 isn’t the ideal time to tweak your special teams, but it happens, and the Rams either overcome it or they don’t. Even if L.A. doesn’t fix its third unit for the 2026 season, they have to keep trying for their future. So, like the moves or not, the Rams are trying out some things, and that’s what they’ll have to keep doing until the get it right, if they get it right. Keep trying. The Rams have been trying to fix or improve their special teams on a consistent level for a while now. It’s a massive storyline that likely won’t be going away anytime until the issues are fixed. If the issues are fixed. Rams Make Flurry of Roster Moves as Kicker Blake Grupe Headlines Three Additions (sports.yahoo) “Additionally, the Rams signed cornerback Damarion Williams to give them some depth on the practice squad. Williams was a fourth-round pick by the Baltimore Ravens in 2022. Given Jaylen Watson’s injuries, the Rams need some cornerback depth. Williams spent time with the Seahawks in 2024 and has also been with the Buccaneers over the last two years. Williams is a smaller cornerback at 5-foot-10 and 180 pounds, with arms measuring less than 30 inches. However, he may bring some special teams value. You read that right. Los Angeles is going back to the Jets to solve its kicking problems. The jokes write themselves. Grupe, meanwhile, hasn’t even attempted a kick for the Jets so far this season.“ Bradley Chubb Addresses Postgame Altercation After Defeating The Los Angeles Rams (buffalobills.com) “Watch Bills outside linebacker Bradley Chubb speak following the Buffalo Bills practice at UC Irvine in Newport Beach, California on October 14, 2026.” Rams’ Alaric Jackson has suspension reduced to one game (sports.yahoo) “Jackson appealed the suspension. “Hearing officer Derrick Brooks, jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFLPA, has reduced the two game suspension of Los Angeles Rams offensive lineman Alaric Jackson to one game,” Michael Signora, the NFL’s senior vice president of football and international communications, said on social media. His touchdown pass to Brandin Cooks and ensuing two-point conversion were fantastic examples of his never-quit playstyle that, to this point, hasn’t hurt him much. title: Week 5 miss aside, Matt Gay’s accuracy a plus for Raiders special teams
summary: Perhaps, a Cup of Joe would do the Los Angeles Rams some good. That’s in reference to the Rams wire-to-wire loss to the Buffalo Bills this past Monday Night Football in a game where special teams continues to haunt head coach Sean McVay. From both a coverage and kicking perspective (namely blocking up front for […]
full_text: (Photo by Edward Monigan IV/Getty Images) | Getty Images Perhaps, a Cup of Joe would do the Los Angeles Rams some good. That’s in reference to the Rams wire-to-wire loss to the Buffalo Bills this past Monday Night Football in a game where special teams continues to haunt head coach Sean McVay. From both a coverage and kicking perspective (namely blocking up front for the place kicker), McVay’s squad continues to struggle with the 37-34 overtime loss to the Bills the latest example. As the issues pile up, it’s becoming abundantly clear the last time the Rams had a quality special teams unit was when Joe DeCamillis ran the group from 2021-22 (that first year was when Los Angeles won the Super Bowl with McVay at the helm, by the way). Of course, DeCamillis is now the Las Vegas Raiders special teams boss. And his kicker during the productive two-year run with the Rams? You guessed it: Current Raider Matt Gay. Outside of Gay’s double-doink where his 49-yard field goal attempt hit the upright after crossbar against the New England Patriots this past Sunday, the 32-year-old kicker regained the accuracy he showcased under DeCamillis in the 2021 and 2022 season (stats). Currently, the Utah product is 10-of-11 on field goal attempts (a long of 59 yards), and 11-for-11 on extra point attempts with a team-leading 44 points for the Raiders this season. That point total is good for fifth most in the NFL (Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader leads the league with 58 points heading into Week 6 action). Gay’s 11 made field goals has him in a three-way tie for third-most in the NFL and his 91.7 accuracy percentage is above the league average of 84.8 percent. Those percentages are skewed five games into the 2026 season with 10 kickers not missing an attempt thus far. 59-yard field goal ‼️ A new career long for Matt Gay! LVvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oynUzQH41x — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 Raiders punter AJ Cole III — Gay’s kicking battery tag team partner — is his usual booming self sending 19 total boots into orbit for 948 yards. The 30-year-old’s 49.9 yards per punt average is sixth-best in the NFL while his net yards per punt average (which includes both return and touchback yardage subtracted from the sum) is 43.3 which is 11th-best amongst his league contemporaries (league average is 42.2). Cole’s 72-yard punt is his longest of the year (the Cleveland Browns’ Corey Bojorquez paces the league with an 81-yard blast) and of the Raiders punter’s 19 boots, seven have dropped or been downed inside the opponent’s 20-yard line and two were touchbacks. Cole is also an integral part of Gay’s place kicking operation as the holder and has done well in that regard, as is long snapper Alex Ward getting the punter the ball to place on field goals and on punts. That provides a window into exploring the Raiders’ coverage and return units. We’ll start with coverage of punt and kick returns first. Kickoff-wise, DeCamillis’ coverage group boasts the eighth-least yards per return average at 24.6. In total, teams have 21 kick returns against Las Vegas for 516 yards with the Miami Dolphins running back Jaylen Wright’s 79-yard kick return in Week 1 the longest given up by the Raiders. The lowest mark in the NFL is 20.3 yards per return by the Dallas Cowboys (22 returns for 446 yards). The Tennessee Titans have the lowest kick returns against (five) and yards (129) amongst the 32 teams in the NFL. The Raiders’ punt coverage unit is allowing the fifth-highest yards per return average (14.0) with a total of six returns for 84 yards (a long of 27 yards). In comparison, the Seattle Seahawks are atop the league with three returns with zero yards allowed. The team behind them are the Carolina Panthers (three punt returns, 31 yards) and Buffalo Bills (three returns, 32 yards — also the Raiders’ opponent this weekend). The punt coverage unit had a gaffe in Week 4 against the Chiefs, but DeCamillis had a fiery retort to that: It appears DeCamillis was firing back at Chuck Pagano, who criticized the call on @PatMcAfeeShow . Pagano prefaced his comments by saying he has a lot of respect for DeCamillis. DeCamillis' Broncos scored an 83-yard punt return touchdown against Pagano and McAfee's Colts in a… https://t.co/mKzCm16V4m pic.twitter.com/8IBBZqS2Co — Sam Warren (@samwarren83) October 9, 2026 Las Vegas’ return units are both productive in both kick and punt departments, but as elite edge rusher Maxx Crosby is keen to say: More is required. Namely, the team must avoid fumbles on kick returns from here on in as the Raiders coughed the ball up twice already this season — one by running back Dylan Laube (Week 3) and another by wide receiver Dareke Young (Week 4) that occurred when both return men approached a traffic jam of blockers/gunners. But when the Silver & Black hang on to the football and don’t get it punched out on kick returns, the team boasts the third-best yards per return average at 28.3, just behind the Minnesota Vikings and Colts (both at 29.8). Laube owns the third-highest yards per return average at 30.3 so far this season and has 10 kick returns for 303 yards (long of 53). Young has returned five kickoffs for 127 yards (25.4 average) while wide receiver Deven Thompkins has three kick returns for 80 yards (long of 32). The Buffalo Bills’ Ray Davis is out in front with a 32.1 yards per return average (he has a long return of 70 yards) on kick returns while the Colts’ Anthony Gould is second with a 30.7 average. The league average is 26 yards per return. Flip it to punt returns and Las Vegas does own the fourth-highest average at 14.3 yards per return. That’s a little skewed too, though, as the Raiders total six returns for 86 yards. Rookie wide receiver Malik Benson has five returns for 68 yards (13.6 average) while Thompkins had one return for 18 yards against the New England Patriots this past Sunday, boosting that team’s overall average to 14.3. The Minnesota Vikings are tops in this department with 11 punt returns for 238 yards and a touchdown (long of 86) with a staggering average of 21.6 yards per return. All that is compiled by Vikings wideout Myles Price — who also has 17 kick returns for 506 yards (long of 68). More impact returns (and hanging onto the football) from DeCamillis’ group will bolster Klint Kubiak’s offense. And of course, Gay’s performance does too, while Cole’s punting helps Rob Leonard’s defense. A return to complementary football would a tremendous boon for Las Vegas — especially with a tough schedule before the team’s late Week 13 bye.

title: Shaky Las Vegas Raiders’ offensive line faces up-and-coming Buffalo Bills’ pass-rush duo Greg Rousseau, Deone Walker in Week 6 key matchups
summary: Week 6 is an opportunity for the Las Vegas Raiders to bounce back after back-to-back losses, including last week’s blowout in New England. However, that certainly won’t come easy against the 4-1 Buffalo Bills, who currently have the best Super Bowl odds (+750) of any AFC team, according to FanDuel Sportsbook. In other words, if […]
full_text: (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 6 is an opportunity for the Las Vegas Raiders to bounce back after back-to-back losses, including last week’s blowout in New England . However, that certainly won’t come easy against the 4-1 Buffalo Bills , who currently have the best Super Bowl odds (+750) of any AFC team, according to FanDuel Sportsbook . In other words, if the Raiders are going to prove to be a legitimate playoff contender in 2026, they need to win the key matchups below. Raiders’ OL vs. Rousseau, Walker Part of the reason for Las Vegas’ two-game skid is that quarterback Kirk Cousins has been under pressure more frequently. According to Pro Football Focus , Cousins was pressured on 33 of his 101 dropbacks ( 32.7% ) in Weeks 1 through 3, and he’s faced pressure on 34 of 83 dropbacks ( 41.0% ) in the last two games combined. Two of the biggest culprits on the Raiders’ offensive line are left guard Spencer Burford and left tackle Kolton Miller. Granted, Burford only gave up one pressure against the Chiefs, but he surrendered five and posted a 0.0 pass-blocking grade against the Patriots. Also, the five-year veteran has yielded the most pressures ( 18 ) of any guard in the NFL for the season so far, meaning pass protection has been an issue for him beyond the last two games. That’s forced the left tackle to give his guard more help, contributing to a slip in Miller’s production. He was beaten for just five pressures in Weeks 1 through 3 combined before losing 12 times in the last two weeks . To be fair, not all of Miller’s issues are tied to Burford. The former has plenty of room for individual improvement, too, specifically with how he handles power rushers. Meanwhile, the Bills’ defense has an up-and-coming pass-rush duo with edge-rusher Greg Rousseau and defensive tackle Deone Walker. Rousseau has posted six sacks in five games, which is two shy of tying a career high, and leads his position with 35 pressures, per PFF . Now, the 26-year-old has primarily lined up as a left outside linebacker or on the right side of the offensive line so far this season. However, he’s had more snaps on the right side every game since Week 2, topping out at 19 snaps against the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football . Given Miller’s struggles and the fact Rousseau primarily wins with power, the left tackle’s weakness, expect Buffalo to at least test Vegas’ blindside protector with its best pass-rusher on Sunday. On the interior, Walker has spent almost as much time as a right defensive tackle ( 89 snaps ) as he has on the left side (93) this season. So, he’ll likely be testing Burford, or whoever is in at left guard for the Silver and Black. On paper, that’s a favorable matchup for Buffalo since the 2025 fourth-round pick heads into the game ranking third among defensive tackles with 21 pressures . Granted, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak hinted at some offensive line changes during his press conference on Monday. That could mean Burford will be on the bench this Sunday. But regardless of who is in the trenches, the offensive line has to have an answer for Rousseau and Walker. The Bills defense has been bad this season, tying for the most points per game allowed ( 32.8 ) and giving up the fourth-most yards per game (396.2). So, if the Silver and Black can keep those two defensive linemen in check, their offense should be able to move the ball and put points on the board. Leonard vs. Brady Sure, play-callers could be a “key matchup” every game, but this one feels more or extra important for Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard. Leonard started hot, keeping the Miami Dolphins and Los Angeles Chargers to 13 and 14 points, respectively, in his first two games ever as a coordinator. However, the book is out on his tendacies and Vegas is averaging 34.0 points per game allowed over the last three weeks. The Silver and Black are feeling the effects of having a first-time defensive play-caller. It wasn’t as prevalent against the New Orleans Saints, but the Kansas City Chiefs and New England Patriots seemingly had the answers to the test with perfect play calls for what the Raiders were running, especially on money downs. Now, an offensive coordinator turned head coach, Joe Brady, comes into town. During his three seasons as Buffalo’s offensive coordinator, Brady’s offenses ranked fourth, 10th and fourth in yards , and sixth, second and fourth in points. After getting promoted to head coach in the offseason while retaining offensive play-calling duties, he hasn’t skipped a beat with the No. 4 offense in terms of yards and No. 1 in points so far in 2026. Those aren’t exactly encouraging numbers for a struggling first-time defensive coordinator, but Leonard has to start making adjustments. The foundation of his scheme is solid (it’s very similar to Mike Macdonald’s with the Seattle Seahawks), showcasing a lot of creativity. But it might be time to reverse course and simplify the play calls because he’s losing the element of surprise. For example, Sumer Sports has the Raiders rotating safeties 44.0% of the time, the second-highest rate in the NFL. Changing up the pre- and post-snap looks works when the opposing quarterback isn’t expecting it or is caught off-guard. But when it’s that frequent, they can just expect the picture to change and take advantage of defenders being out of position since the defenders have to sprint to their spots rather than lining up in them. It’s all part of the chess match, which Leonard is still learning at this stage in his career. But if Las Vegas is going to pull off an upset on Sunday, he needs to be a quick study. Stukes vs. Allen Josh Allen was the NFL MVP two years ago and has looked like one of the early favorites to win the award for a second time in 2026. To put it in perspective, he’s averaging 30 more passing yards ( 219.5 to 249.8 ) and 16 more rushing yards (31.2 to 47.8) per game than he did in 2024. Also, he leads the league with eight rushing touchdowns and has seven scores through the air so far this season. Allen is one of those quarterbacks where if a defense tries to take away everything, they’ll end up taking away nothing. He’s become so dynamic that the strategy shifts to just trying to limit the damage and then forcing him into a mistake or two. One way to do that is to get the MVP candidate to play hero ball and force passes downfield. The Wyoming product has always been known for his arm strength and gunslinger mentality. This season, he’s tied for sixth with 23 pass attempts of 20 or more yards past the line of scrimmage, per PFF , but isn’t having much success. Allen has only completed nine of those attempts for a 39.1 completion percentage that is tied for 22nd among qualifying quarterbacks (minimum five deep passes). Also, six of his seven “turnover-worthy plays” have come on deep shots for the highest TWP rate (22.2%) on said throws in the league. Meanwhile, another aspect of the Raiders’ defensive regression is that they’ve only turned the ball over once in the last two games — a forced fumble against the Patriots — and haven’t had an interception since Week 3. Given Allen’s propensity to push the ball downfield, the spotlight will be on Vegas’ free safety, Treydan Stukes. Stukes only has one pick so far, stepping in front of a deep pass from Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis in the season opener. Also, the rookie is coming off the worst game of his young career, making a few coverage mistakes in New England. However, the Arizona product was known for his ball skills in college, recording seven career interceptions , including four last year. Additionally, he’s been a solid first-year defender in the three other games he’s played during the campaign. That being said, the Raiders need Stukes to be on his “A-game” and take advantage if/when Allen gives him an opportunity to create a momentum-shifting play.

full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders want to do a lot differently Sunday when they host the Buffalo Bills than what they did in a 45-17 road loss at the New England Patriots on Sunday. Chief among those changes is getting tight end Michael Mayer more involved. The fourth-year tight end played a season-low 65 percent of the Raiders’ offensive snaps Sunday. While he didn’t play as much, Mayer, who signed a a three-year, $45 million contract extension last month, wasn’t involved much when he was on the field. He was targeted just once and he finished with one catch for two yards at New England. Mayer had 20 catches for 169 yards on 24 targets in the first four games. Kubiak blamed himself for Mayer not being more involved in Week 5. “Just myself. Didn’t give him enough opportunities,” Kubiak said of Mayer’s lack of involvement. “We gave him one early in the game. Getting back to that approach against Buffalo, which has struggled in pass defense this season, will be vital.

title: Miami Dolphins’ painful season could be beginning of something special
summary: If we’re being honest, watching the Miami Dolphins in 2026 has not exactly been an enjoyable experience. The losses are piling up, the offense continues to struggle, and there are already rumblings from the team’s fanbase about the job head coach Jeff Hafley is doing. But there is a silver lining to all of this, […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: (EDITORS NOTE: Tonal effects have been applied to this image.) Jacob Rodriguez #10 of the Miami Dolphins takes the field at Hard Rock Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images If we’re being honest, watching the Miami Dolphins in 2026 has not exactly been an enjoyable experience. The losses are piling up, the offense continues to struggle, and there are already rumblings from the team’s fanbase about the job head coach Jeff Hafley is doing. But there is a silver lining to all of this, and it starts with the rookies. Miami’s 2026 draft class is getting thrown into the fire, and that experience could pay significant dividends as the Dolphins move forward. Through five games, Hafley’s club leads the league in snaps from rookies, with over 2,000 such cases heading into their bye week. The Cleveland Browns are second — but are a staggering 600 snaps behind Miami in that department. First-round offensive guard Kadyn Proctor has played 293 offensive snaps, appearing on 100% of Miami’s offensive plays. Second-round linebacker Jacob Rodriguez has logged 311 defensive snaps, while first-round cornerback Chris Johnson has played 304 defensive snaps. Fifth-round safety Michael Taaffe isn’t far behind, with 287 defensive snaps to his name. That’s a massive amount of responsibility for a group of players who were playing college football just months ago. Rodriguez has already established himself as a major contributor in the middle of Miami’s defense — and is in the running for the NFL’s Defensive Rookie of the Year award. Johnson is getting valuable experience against high-end NFL receivers, while Taaffe is learning how to operate in a professional secondary. Proctor, meanwhile, is receiving the kind of weekly education that only comes from facing elite NFL defensive linemen. Will they make mistakes? Absolutely. They’re rookies. But every missed assignment, every difficult matchup offers another opportunity to learn. When the 2027 season rolls around, these players won’t be entering training camp as inexperienced newcomers trying to figure everything out. They’ll have an entire NFL season under their belts. They’ll understand the speed of the game, know what their coaches expect, and have a much clearer idea of what they need to do to improve. That doesn’t guarantee they’ll become stars, but it gives Miami a chance to build around players who have already experienced the initial growing pains of a rebuild. Now, imagine pairing that experience with a few quality free-agent additions. Miami currently has over $110 million in projected cap space for 2027 according to Spotrac. The Dolphins won’t spend recklessly. Instead, they’ll pluck a couple of young, high-character standouts in search of a new home. General manager Jon-Eric Sullivan needs to identify a few difference-makers to add to his roster while allowing Miami’s young core the opportunity to continue to develop. Of course, the Dolphins still have plenty to prove this year. But losing in 2026 doesn’t mean the season will be a complete waste. Miami is finding out which young players can handle daunting NFL responsibilities, and those answers could prove invaluable moving forward. If Sullivan gets the next offseason right, this painful year could become the foundation for something special. The Dolphins might not be ready to contend today, but the hope is that the experience these rookies are gaining now will help Miami get there a whole lot sooner than some expect. Keep the faith. Trust in Jon-Eric Sullivan. Fins up.
