title: Patriots mailbag: How can Drake Maye attack the Jets?
summary: The New England Patriots are looking to keep their winning streak alive as they welcome the New York Jets to Gillette Stadium. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. How would you attack the Jets defense? – Maye The Force Be With You What’s different about the Jets this year that would help them […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are looking to keep their winning streak alive as they welcome the New York Jets to Gillette Stadium. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. How would you attack the Jets defense? – Maye The Force Be With You What’s different about the Jets this year that would help them avoid another drubbing like they got at the end of last year? – paulnewman As he did with his defenses in Detroit, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn wants his defense to play man coverage and blitz. Through the season, New York ranks second in blitz rate and 10th in man coverage rate. However, that approach could be costly against Drake Maye, who has excelled against the blitz and can exploit man coverage by pushing the ball downfield or making plays with his legs. If the Jets lean heavily on single-high coverages, expect Maye to take his shots, as he did last week. The most notable change for the Jets this season has been Glenn’s increased versatility on defense. New York is leaning more heavily into split-safety coverages, including a significant increase in Cover 6, and could feature those looks Sunday to limit Maye’s deep-ball opportunities. While there isn’t much to fear from the Jets’ offense from this perspective with Christian Gonzalez available to limit Garrett Wilson, New York has also overhauled its defensive personnel this offseason, potentially setting the stage for a low-scoring divisional battle. Rookie David Bailey has gotten off to a fast start on the edge, while veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick is still making plays in the backend. With Henderson being out a few weeks, how do you see the offense compensating for that? More Stevens, Corey Kiner increased load, or perhaps getting our younger WR’s more involved by adding more 4-5 WR sets & spreading out opposing D’s? – KissBillsRings With Henderson out for sometime, could we see Larison called up? – jpd985 We’ll see if Henderson misses time after somehow logging a pair of limited practices this week. If he’s out Sunday, Rhamondre Stevenson should be expected to carry the load, as he did in the regular-season opener when he played 60 snaps with Henderson sidelined. Behind Stevenson, Larison would likely be elevated from the practice squad again, as he was in Week 1, with Kiner handling the change-of-pace carries. While the fumble is something a depth running back can’t afford, I thought Kiner actually ran well against the Raiders last week. If Yahoo’s stats are right, the Pats are 11th in the league in rushing yards/game at 121.6, and 16th in the league in rushing yards/attempt at 4.1yd/att. So they’re persistent? With Gilliam and Henderson laid up, and a Jets team begging for jumbo packages running down their throat to wear down their talented defensive line, what do the Pats have to do to improve rushing efficiency? – WannaBe Pats GM More of what they’ve done the last two weeks. After a slow start on the ground this season, the Patriots have changed things up and become less predictable scheme wise. They’ve spiced up their go-to ground game with more motion and window dressing and have leaned into new schemes as well. With much being written about how Maye couldn’t handle the 2 high safety looks from last year’s playoffs and the first few games of this season, what has changed? Did BUF and LV not play those looks or have worse personnel? Or are there signs that Maye is starting to handle that better? – Palm_Fronds_and_Shamrocks Maye ranked near the top of the league in several metrics against Cover 2 last regular season. However, given his exceptional deep-ball efficiency, it was — and still is — viewed as one of the best strategies for limiting explosive plays. The issues in the playoffs seemed to stem more from the quality of opposing defenses than from the schemes themselves. Maye hasn’t had many issues against those coverages in recent weeks, although it was puzzling to see Las Vegas opt for the opposite strategy and play single-high man coverage on more than 50% of its drop backs — a risky approach against a quarterback like Maye. Were you excited to finally see the Patriots use Pop Douglas & Kyle Williams correctly against the Raiders leading to 3 TD’s and 156 Yards combined? – For Pats Sake The usage didn’t really change for DeMario Douglas and Kyle Williams last week. Douglas scored two touchdowns against busted coverages and ran a pair of really strong routes. Williams, meanwhile, finally got opportunities to make plays downfield against a Las Vegas defense that played single-high safety on more than 50% of its snaps. He capitalized. Considering the injury bug that hit our team until now, who would be the 8 IR players you think should be brought back during the regular season? What about the extra two players, after we go into the playoffs? Would you wait with the last 2-3 spots closer to the playoffs to see if a certain position needs more help than others (say CB instead of WR)? – Maxxwell This is something the Patriots will have to manage moving forward when it comes to their roster. They have already used two return designations on Marcus Bryant and Brenden Schooler, with A.J. Brown set to take the third. Of the remaining players on injured reserve, Mack Hollins and Reggie Gilliam should be considered likely candidates for two more spots. From there, the Patriots can remain flexible with the final three regular-season return designations, plus two additional spots in the playoffs, as no other player on IR appears to be an immediate priority to return. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

title: A.J. Brown brings ‘fresh juice’ to Patriots offense
summary: After spending the designated four weeks on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain he suffered in Week 1, New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown has been cleared for practice. He did not participate fully on Wednesday or Thursday, though, making his status for Sunday against the New York Jets uncertain. Still, offensive coordinator […]
full_text: After spending the designated four weeks on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain he suffered in Week 1, New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown has been cleared for practice. He did not participate fully on Wednesday or Thursday, though, making his status for Sunday against the New York Jets uncertain. Still, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels noted how it was “good to see him back out on the practice field,” and that Brown returning could provide a “fresh juice” to the guys in the wide out room. “This happens quite a bit for us,” he said. “You miss a guy for a week, two weeks, sometimes longer than that, and then you have an opportunity to get him back during the course of the season, it’s always good. It brings some fresh juice to the guys and to the unit. We know what he can do when he’s out there and he’s healthy. We’ll see how the rest of this week goes and ultimately what ends up happening.” The Patriots have gotten inconsistent production from the top of the receiver group in Brown’s absence. This may be partly because there isn’t a weapon that demands extra attention or has the same presence as him. Since Brown hasn’t played much this season, McDaniels doesn’t have much data to describe how the offense changes with him in it. But he compared it to the way Stefon Diggs drew attention in 2025 against the Jets. “Last year they doubled Diggs in the Jet game a couple times,” said McDaniels. “So, anytime they put two people on one person, then someone else has a single opportunity.” As good as it would be for Drake Maye and the New England offense to get their top target back as soon as this Sunday, it was made clear that it was no guarantee from the Patriots’ medical team. McDaniels was asked about having Brown back, which he quickly corrected to “when” they get him back, definitively showing that there is still an argument that Brown is not ready to go yet. Brown himself said that his status is “still up in the air” and that it is “a coach Vrabel decision” on if he steps on the field for the first time since the third quarter of the season opener against Seattle.

title: Patriots Hall of Famer Jon Morris passes away
summary: Jon Morris, a member of the New England Patriots Hall of Fame, has passed away. He was 84. The Patriots announced his death on Thursday. “Jon Morris was one of the great players who helped build the foundation of our franchise,” said Patriots owner Robert Kraft in a statement. “For generations of Patriots fans, he […]
full_text: Jon Morris, a member of the New England Patriots Hall of Fame, has passed away. He was 84. The Patriots announced his death on Thursday. “Jon Morris was one of the great players who helped build the foundation of our franchise,” said Patriots owner Robert Kraft in a statement. “For generations of Patriots fans, he represented the toughness, dedication and pride of those early teams. It meant so much to me to call Jon in 2011 and tell him he had been selected to our Hall of Fame, ensuring that his contributions would always be remembered.” Morris was born on April 5, 1942 in Washington D.C. and played college football at Holy Cross. He was drafted by both the NFL’s Green Bay Packers and the then-AFL’s Boston Patriots in 1964, eventually deciding to come to New England. Over the next 11 seasons through 1974, he saw action in 130 games with 125 starts for the club and was voted AFL All-Star on six occasions as well as the Patriots’ first ever NFL Pro Bowler in 1970. Injuries hampered him late during his Patriots career, and he was traded to the Detroit Lions in 1975. Morris added 42 more starts during his three years in Detroit, and later played 10 games as a reserve for the Chicago Bears. He retired from pro football in 1979. After his playing career, Morris spent nine years as a radio color commentator for the Patriots. He later also worked for NBC. Morris was named a member of the Patriots’ Team of the 1960s, as well as their 35th and 50th anniversary teams. In 2011, he was inducted into the franchise’s Hall of Fame.

title: Will Campbell streamlines stages of grief after latest knee injury
summary: Coming out of college, durability was one of Will Campbell’s many strengths. Not even halfway through his second season with the New England Patriots, he has missed time due to injury twice already. The second of those injuries happened against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, and it did leave the 22-year-old not only in […]
full_text: Coming out of college, durability was one of Will Campbell’s many strengths. Not even halfway through his second season with the New England Patriots, he has missed time due to injury twice already. The second of those injuries happened against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, and it did leave the 22-year-old not only in pain. It also, by his own admission, left him quite angry at the situation. “Just mad. That’s really all it was. I was just pissed off,” Campbell told reporters at his Gillette Stadium locker on Wednesday. For Campbell, hurting his right knee after getting rolled up on from behind is unfortunately nothing new. The same thing happened to him during his 2025 rookie season in a game against the Bengals. He missed the next four contests as a result of that particular injury before returning for the regular season finale and later New England’s playoff run. However, he was a shell of his former self upon coming back from the torn MCL he had sustained. This year, the ordeal appears to be far more favorable for the player. It has allowed Campbell to quickly jump from anger to acceptance — two distinct stages of grief, as coined by everybody’s favorite Swiss-American psychiatrist, Elisabeth Kübler-Ross — rather quickly. “It’ll be all right,” Campbell said. “I could definitely tell a difference from this year to last year.” Campbell exited the Patriots’ Week 5 game versus Las Vegas in the second quarter. He gingerly walked into the locker room after the injury and was quickly announced as questionable to return to the game. Despite that label, he made his way back to the sideline shortly thereafter. He expected a return to the game — “I thought I was going back in,” he said — but the team decided to roll with rookie Caleb Lomu instead. Campbell was last seen riding a stationary bike, and did not come out with the rest of his teammates after halftime. He eventually was ruled out. Despite the injury and subsequent reports that he had suffered a knee sprain that would force the team to take a “week by week” approach , Campbell has decided to look at the glass as half-full rater than half-empty. “As s—ty as it is, it’s part of this game. It’s part of playing the position that we play, and stuff happens. You just have to hope the chips kind of fall your way,” he said. “It always could be worse. Just going to take it day by day, not going to put any expectations on anything, and just trust my body, see how I’m feeling, ramping up and things like that, and see what happens.” What has happened already is Campbell appearing at practice . While limited, he managed to participate in the session with his teammates. That does not guarantee a spot on the game-day squad, or indeed the 53-man roster, for the upcoming game against the New York Jets and beyond, but it is a positive step in the right direction.

title: Drake Maye reacts to A.J. Brown return to Patriots offense
summary: As Drake Maye took the Patriots’ practice field Wednesday, he saw a familiar, but new face: wide receiver A.J. Brown. “It’s always a warm welcome in the huddle to have him back in there,” Maye said. “So, looking forward to seeing him progress, and it’s always great seeing him back out there. I think you […]
full_text: As Drake Maye took the Patriots’ practice field Wednesday, he saw a familiar, but new face: wide receiver A.J. Brown. “It’s always a warm welcome in the huddle to have him back in there,” Maye said. “So, looking forward to seeing him progress, and it’s always great seeing him back out there. I think you would have to ask him how he felt, but I think it’s good to see him back out there, that’s for sure.” Brown returned to practice on Wednesday for the first time since being placed on injured reserve following Week 1. The Patriots now have a three-week window to activate him to the roster. When he returns, Brown will provide a significant boost to New England’s offense. “You know what he can add. He’s been a player in this league,” Maye said. “It’s not like we haven’t seen him as a player in this league, and there aren’t many like him that roam around in this league. So, I’ll just try to do my part to give him some chances and keep on spreading the ball around for guys that are open. “We’ve had a lot of guys step up. So, I’m looking forward to keeping that rolling and adding another piece whenever he feels like he’s ready to get out there.” In Brown’s absence, free-agent addition Romeo Doubs has taken on a larger role while young players like Efton Chism III and Kyle Williams have made the most of their opportunities. Maye believes Brown’s return could create even more opportunities for the rest of the receiving corps. “I think it definitely opens up other parts of the field and other parts of the game for guys,” Maye said. “I think you see it in the NBA; it’s probably the closest thing that I can think of. When they start doubling the best player once they get past half court, then they’re just leaving a corner 3 open or leaving a guy open for a dunk.” The Patriots’ offense got off to a slow start after losing Brown in the season opener. However, the unit has found its stride over the past two weeks, with Maye throwing seven touchdown passes and adding another score on the ground. Although Brown has been unable to contribute on the field during that stretch, the veteran, whose locker stall is directly next to Maye’s, has remained engaged off the field. “He’s just a pro. I think you will see by the way he carries himself and how he cares about players. I’ve been impressed,” Maye said. “He’s not been at the games, but you can see how closely he’s watching the games and little things he picks up on. You can tell he’s really watching and that he cares. He’s just a great teammate from what I have experienced here with him, and he’s looking forward to getting back. “I know he’s just got a big smile. He’s got a contagious smile, and it’s good seeing that in the locker room. I enjoy being near it every day.”

title: Our Offense vs. Their Defense: New York Giants
summary: The New Orleans Saints are traveling to New York/New Jersey to take on the Giants. The Giants are actually doing very well under first-year head coach Jim Harbaugh, especially considering they lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season. The Giants are 3-1-1 on the year right now and are feeling very confident. The Giants’ […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 05: Cesar Ruiz #51 of the New Orleans Saints and Erik McCoy #78 line up for a play against the Atlanta Falcons during the first half of a game at Caesars Superdome on October 5, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are traveling to New York/New Jersey to take on the Giants. The Giants are actually doing very well under first-year head coach Jim Harbaugh, especially considering they lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season. The Giants are 3-1-1 on the year right now and are feeling very confident. The Giants’ defense is led by Dennard Wilson, who was with the Titans last season. The Saints struggled against the Vikings’ heavy-pressure defense, and Wilson and the Giants will bring a lot of the same. The two most blitz-heavy defenses last week were the Vikings and Giants, respectively. The Giants are not as formidable as the Vikings, but they are still a very good defense nonetheless. Currently, they rank 15th in total defense and seventh in passing defense. The advantage the Saints would like to exploit would be against their run defense, which ranks 25th in the league. They are also a top-10 scoring defense, allowing only 21.2 points per game. They rank third in the league in interceptions with six and have eight total takeaways on the season. The Saints’ offense does not match up too well against this defense. The struggles they experienced last week in the Dome could very well plague them again on the road. The best way for the Saints to attack this team would be through the running game, but that’s something the Saints have yet to figure out how to do consistently. New Orleans will have to find a way to get the offense into third-and-manageable situations. The Giants rank 27th in the league in third-down defense, and if the Saints can find a way to stay ahead of the chains, they could potentially find themselves in the red zone. If they make it into the red zone, this is another area where the Giants’ defense struggles. They allow touchdowns on 69.2% of opponents’ red-zone possessions. Third-down and red-zone conversions are actually strengths for this Saints offense, as they currently rank sixth in third-down conversion rate and third in red-zone touchdown conversion rate. The problem is that they are either giving the ball away or putting themselves behind the chains with pre-snap penalties and poor execution in the running game. The Saints have a chance, but which Saints team will travel to New York? Will it be the team that went to Baltimore and upset the Ravens for their lone win of the season, or the team that embarrassed themselves against the Falcons?

Changing the identity of the Giants’ defense | ESPN.com This week’s opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants prepare to battle the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. Bring on the blitz! Changing the identity of the Giants ’ defense | ESPN.com This week’s opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox). Saints QB Tyler Shough has been just a touch above average against the blitz, with a 0.1% completion percentage above expectation (CPOE). He has five touchdown passes and two interceptions against the blitz. Wilson’s track record doesn’t show a heavy lean on the blitz. His Titans defense blitzed just 22.8% of dropbacks over the previous two seasons, the 22nd-highest rate. He sent DB blitzes 9.3% of dropbacks, which was 25th over that span. Perhaps that changes a bit with the Giants short-handed on pass rushers. It might be the best way for them to survive. Giants embracing the underdog role Dennard Wilson was asked about the Giants being underdogs against the Saints: "Everybody counts us out. We like playing with a chip on our shoulder." pic.twitter.com/FssaD8qvwG — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 15, 2026 Giants adamant Kayvon Thibodeaux is making a bigger impact than modest stats indicate | New York Post Sunday was almost a homecoming game for Kayvon Thibodeaux. The Saints called the Giants about trading for Thibodeaux during April’s draft but found the asking price — believed to be a third-round pick — too high. Watching from afar as reports surfaced, including from The Post, Thibodeaux posted an image from “Fast & Furious” to social media with the tagline, “You thought you could leave without saying goodbye.” Jameis Winston ’ s starting dream is alive as the Giants roll into a game against the Saints | FOX Sports When Jameis Winston signed with the New Orleans Saints in 2020 initially to back up Drew Brees and then to be in the mix to succeed him at quarterback, he was long removed from winning the Heisman Trophy in college and being the top pick in the draft. He did not give up on being a starter in the NFL again, like he was early in his career with Tampa Bay. “I dreamt of it,” Winston said. “And now it’s here.” Giants WR reveals details of intense exchange with Jameis Winston: ‘You know how to read lips?’ | NJ.com Winston wanted Mooney to flush the drop and refocus — echoing what Mooney had told Winston in the wake of his own mistakes. Said Mooney: “That was his opportunity to tell me, ‘As much as you tell me to f— it, this is my time to tell you: F— it. It’s OK. Just move on. I’m coming back to you right now.’” It wasn’t just the drop that had Mooney annoyed in that moment when it appeared he was rolling his eyes at Winston. In reality, Mooney said, he was aggravated about how the afternoon had unfolded. “It was just how the game was going for me,” he said. “I got face masked. I got poked in the eye. When I had a ball, I got ran into, and I thought it was a [pass interference]. It’s just that things weren’t going well for me.” ‘Big, fast, physical ’ Giants tight end emerges as special teams playmaker | The Record Theo Johnson entered the NFL harboring dreams of becoming one of the league’s top tight ends. The former New York Giants coaching staff used to show him highlights of Rob Gronkowski, pulling him out of meetings to bring him upstairs, just to break down Gronkowski video for inspiration and motivation. Now in his third season, Johnson isn’t giving up on that goal just yet. Confident Giants kicker Dominic Zvada: ‘If nothing has changed, nothing should change’ | New York Daily News Zvada said he spent Monday dissecting what went wrong and now has no need for a rear-view mirror as he prepares for the New Orleans Saints. A return to MetLife Stadium and to a turf field might help his footing, and he is no less confident than he was last week. “I really just try and focus on what I can control,” he said. “That’s kind of how I’ve been able to have success early in the season is by just focusing on not the score or where we’re at in the game or anything like that. It’s just focused on going out there, having that mental checklist in my head and lining up and kicking the ball through the uprights. That’s really all I need to focus on. I’m kind of just forcing myself to focus on that, and when you force yourself to focus on that, everything else just kind of fades out. And then you’re just kind of in your own world. So it’s nice.” New York Giants ’ John Harbaugh: Isaiah Likely a ‘ unique kind of athlete ’ | USAToday.com “When he was being evaluated, he went in the fourth round; I think it was late fourth round. Nobody really could get their arms around him. He made all these plays in college, but it just looked different. You see it out here, it turns out it’s really good what he does,” Harbaugh said. “He’s elusive; he can get away in man and zone coverage. He’s got a great feel; he’s got great hands, he has an amazing catch radius. He’s an elusive runner, a good, strong runner. So, all those things that are football. He’s also, and this was in college, he was crazy good as a perimeter blocker. He would launch guys through the air, like five yards through the air sometimes at Coastal. He’s a really good perimeter blocker here too. He’s translated really well, and I think he’s been able to really express that here this year. The kind of player he is, and it’s just great to see.” From Big Blue View Abdul Carter held out of practice for 2nd straight day ‘Peanut punch’ prevalence has gotten Giants’ attention 5 takeaways from Matt Nagy: Good things coming in Giants’ running game? title: Fantasy Football 2026: Week 6 preview — Start/sit and more
summary: Welcome to Week 6! Week 5 was a wild one, with three games going to overtime (including the Sunday and Monday night games) and the London game featuring two lead changes in the final eight seconds. What will we get this week? A better question might be “who will we get this week”? One injured […]
full_text: The Giants trio is cooking | Getty Images Welcome to Week 6! Week 5 was a wild one, with three games going to overtime (including the Sunday and Monday night games) and the London game featuring two lead changes in the final eight seconds. What will we get this week? A better question might be “who will we get this week”? One injured quarterback returned in Week 5 (Jayden Daniels), and what a return it was – the 2024 offensive rookie of the year reminded of us of why he’s elite when healthy – he ran for over 100 yards and two touchdowns, and broke 30 fantasy points! Four more banged-up quarterbacks started the week off as questionable to return in Week 6 – Lamar Jackson, Caleb Williams, Baker Mayfield, and Michael Penix, Jr. Whether they return will impact lineup decisions for fantasy managers. Mayfield was ruled out on Thursday. Daniels wasn’t the only QB to break 30 fantasy points last week – two others joined him. Eight QBs cracked 25 fantasy points, and 14 scored at least 20. Wow. I wrote a lot this summer about the incredible depth of quality at the QB position for fantasy this season, and we’re seeking that play out. Stats of the Week : The NFC East didn’t get any wins in Week 5, even though there was a divisional game. 2. The Eagles (2-3) are under .500 for the first time since the 2021 season. 3. Every team in the AFC North is over .500, while no teams in the NFC South are over .500 4. Wow category: With two more TDs on Sunday, Jahmyr Gibbs passed another Lion (Barry Sanders) for the most TDs by a player before turning 25. Gibbs has 58 TDs in 54 regular season games played. 5. Ick category: With two more fumbles on Monday night, James Cook now has 11 since the start of last season. No other running back has more than five fumbles in that span. 6. Jaylen Warren became the first player since Herschel Walker (1986) to have an 80+ yard TD catch and a 50+ yard TD run in the same game. OK, Week 6, here we go! Note: The HOU@JAC game is in London – set those lineups early! Bye Weeks: CIN, DET, MIA, MIN Week 6 Rides, Fades and Sleepers For those who are familiar with this column, you know the drill. For everyone else: The Rides, Fades, and Sleepers is an analysis of players that I think are primed for an especially strong or poor performance, often as compared to consensus expectations. This isn’t a straight-up Start/Sit exercise. As a general rule, start your studs. I’ll rarely list the most obvious names at a position as “Rides” because those players are almost always expected to have strong performances. You don’t need me or anyone else telling you to start Josh Allen . While this analysis is intended for season-long play, it works for DFS formats too. Half PPR scoring and Expert Consensus Rankings (ECR) are used for the column. Each week, I’m picking a Ride, Fade, and Sleeper of the Week. The rules: The Ride of the Week can’t be a truly elite option, the Fade can’t be someone who nobody is starting anyway, and the Sleeper must be an actual sleeper, from down in the rankings. Last week, my Rides, Fades, and Sleepers did pretty well, and my featured picks cooked. My Co-Rides of the Week (Jared Goff and Jacoby Brissett) both cracked 25 fantasy points, my Fade of the Week (Jalen Hurts) scored just 13 fantasy points (QB21), and my Sleeper of the Week (Jameis Winston) also broke 25 fantasy points and finished as the QB6. You can check my work here . *** Ride of the Week: Jordan Love (vs. DAL). I went back and forth between Christian Watson and Love. Don’t worry, Watson is on the Ride list too. Love is consistent so far this season, with exactly two TD passes in all five starts. I think he’ll have at least three this week. He has at least 29 pass attempts in each start, so the volume is there. His best weekly finish on the season was last week, when he finished as the QB8. He has a great chance to improve on that this week against Dallas’s suspect secondary. I’m sure Joey Porter, Jr. will help, but Dallas is allowing the sixth most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to opposing QBs, and they don’t have a pick yet this season. With four teams on Bye and multiple QBs banged up, Love is a clear QB1 option this week, even in shallow leagues. Reminder: Green Bay and Dallas played to a 40-40 tie last season (Love had 300+ yards, three TDs, and zero picks in that shootout). Fade of the Week: Omarion Hampton (@KC). I get it – you used a second round pick on Hampton, and confirmation bias makes it hard to bench him. But at this point, you have to consider it. Ask any gambler: Throwing good money after bad rarely works out. The Chargers are a mess, their offensive line is, well, offensive, and he’s not seeing enough work to give you any confidence that a breakout game is coming. His snap share has been under 50% in each of the last three contests and hit a season-low 30% last Sunday. He hasn’t topped 15 touches in three straight games. It’s also a tougher matchup. KC is only allowing opposing RBs an average of 69 yards per game, which is third best in the NFL. Heard enough? Hampton is ranked as the RB25 this week and I think that’s generous. He’s a clear sit for me. Sleeper of the Week: Jameis Winston (vs. NO). For the first time ever, I’m running back a sleeper of the week. Even after last week’s bounty, he’s once again the 17 th -ranked QB on the board, and once again I think that’s too low. Jameis is feeling it (two straight games with three TD passes, and at least 20 fantasy points), and Malik Nabers is looking more and more like his old self. Jameis is benefitting from a soft landing after the Dart injury – four straight games against losing teams, with three of them at home. The Saints are middle of the pack against QBs, but that’s in large part because they’re so easy to run on. Fire up Jameis with confidence if you need him. Quarterback: Elite option this week – Josh Allen, Matt Stafford, and Brock Purdy; the analysis starts below them. Rides: Dak Prescott (@GB). The 52.5 Vegas total for this game is the second highest on the board this week, and the Cowboys will have had ten days to stew over their embarrassing home loss to the Bucs. Green Bay is allowing the second fewest FPPG to opposing QBs, but part of that is who they’ve faced. Dak should find success in what figures to be a shootout, like the aforementioned game between these teams last season. Others ranked in the Top-15 this week who I think will outperform their ranking: Jayden Daniels (@SF) , Drake Maye (vs. NYJ) , and Kirk Cousins (vs. BUF). Sleepers: Jacoby Brissett (@LAR) doesn’t have a great matchup, but as was the case in last week’s blowout loss to the Lions, volume while chasing points should get him to some decent garbage-time totals. Brissett is averaging just under 40 pass attempts per game. If you need a second QB in a Superflex, or a streamer for someone who is hurt or on a Bye, there are some OK options, including Michael Penix, Jr. (vs. CHI, if he is able to play), Jalon Daniels (vs. PIT), and (gulp), Deshaun Watson (vs. BAL). If you’re really desperate, Tanner McKee (vs. CAR) could have some success throwing on Carolina’s banged up secondary. Fades: I don’t see how anyone can start either Justin Herbert (@KC) or Bo Nix (vs. SEA) right now, and especially when they have bad matchups, as is the case this week. Too many QBs are outscoring them each week. It’s been ugly, folks. Among QBs who’ve started at least three games, Nix is currently the QB25 and Herbert is the QB29. If you drafted one of them to be your starter, (a) I’m sorry, and (b) I hope Plan B is in effect. Where is the Texans’ vaunted defense this season? They played much better last week, but that was against Cam Ward and the Titans. The Jaguars will be a much sterner test. I think they’ll give Trevor Lawrence (vs. HOU) some problems in the London game. He’s not a sit for me, but I have him outside my Top-10 this week. Bryce Young (@PHI) has been fantastic this season, and he’s well-rested coming off a Bye. I don’t love…

full_text: Abdul Carter | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), and edge defender Abdul Carter (calf) all worked on the side with trainers Thursday during the media viewing portion of New York Giants practice. All three, along with cornerback Colton Hood (concussion) and safety Tyler Nubin (neck) were officially listed as “did not practice.” For Thomas, who has been managing his injury since Week 2 against the Los Angeles Rams, this has been his weekly routine. He has yet to miss a snap due to the injury. If Carter is not able to play Sunday against the New Orleans Saints, that would be a massive blow to a Giants’ defense already without star edge defender Brian Burns (torn ACL) for the season. Carter has 2.0 sacks, and is tied sixth in the NFL among edge defenders and linebackers with 14 quarterback pressures. Carter leads the league with 11 ‘quick’ quarterback pressures, defined as pressures achieved in less than 2.5 seconds. If Eluemunor cannot play, Marcus Mbow would start at right tackle and rookie J.C. Davis would be the swing tackle. Linebacker Malik Harrison, who was just added to the 53-man roster this week, was added to the injury report with a groin issue. He was a limited participant. Safety Jason Pinnock, who missed last week’s game due to a concussion, was a full practice participant. That is good news, especially with Nubin trending toward not playing. title: NY Giants’ RB Cam Skattebo explains taking gloves off late in game vs. Commanders
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Keen-eyed Big Blue View observers noticed that late in the fourth quarter and overtime of Sunday’s game against the Washington Commanders, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo had removed his gloves and was playing bare-handed. “I was drenched,” Skattebo said. “I was soaked in water and mud, and it was […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Keen-eyed Big Blue View observers noticed that late in the fourth quarter and overtime of Sunday’s game against the Washington Commanders, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo had removed his gloves and was playing bare-handed. “I was drenched,” Skattebo said. “I was soaked in water and mud, and it was just part of the way the game went. I played fifty-plus snaps, and I was soaking wet. I was falling on the ground, I was blocking a lot, everybody’s wet. When I got up from fumbling my arms were covered in dirt, mud, and water. “I had more confidence in holding onto the ball without gloves than I did with gloves, and it bit me in the ass. If I feel that way I’m still going to take the gloves off and protect the ball the best I can.” Skattebo said he could have gotten a new pair of gloves, but felt he would have had the same issue. “Whether your hands are wet or not you’ve gotta protect the football,” Skattebo said. “I didn’t do that, and I understand where everyone’s coming from, so I’m gonna take the heat, go back on the field, and give it the best shot.” Skattebo sat on a stool at his locker on Thursday and answered questions from a number of reporters. “That’s [protecting the ball] a main job in this league,” Skattebo said. “If you protect the ball you’ll be OK, and if you don’t you’re not going to have a job. “Working on that and making sure I protect the ball is my No. 1 focus right now.” Skattebo said “it’s fine” if some people are not sold on him as a true No. 1 running back. “I understand that. I’ve given the ball up three times, four on paper, and I understand that,” Skattebo said. “I totally agree with them for feeling that way. Over time it’s going to change. “I’ve been a No. 1 back my whole life. I’ve been a four-down back my whole life. It’s not gonna change. I’ve just gotta continue to get back to myself, start feeling comfortable again, and being able to take care of the ball and run the ball like I know how to run the ball.”

title: 5 takeaways from Matt Nagy: Good things coming in NY Giants’ running game?
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The fact that the New York Giants have not run the ball as well as they expect to, or need to, so far this season has been well-documented. Like it was in these two Big Blue View posts: The question is, what are the Giants going to do about it? Offense […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The fact that the New York Giants have not run the ball as well as they expect to, or need to, so far this season has been well-documented. Like it was in these two Big Blue View posts: The Giants may need to change how they think about offense 5 Giants-Saints storylines: Optimism in the midst of ‘crazy town’ The question is, what are the Giants going to do about it? Offense coordinator Matt Nagy said on Thursday that getting more from the run game, 24th in the league at 3.7 yards per carry, was a “work in progress.” “We think we have some answers. I’m not going to get into that publicly, but I do believe that we’re on our way into doing some things, and so that’ll be good,” Nagy said. “We look forward to seeing what comes from it, but these guys are trying. It’s not for a lack of trying from the coaches with the scheme or from the players with execution. We just got to keep staying with it, trust with what we’re going with, and be able to be balanced when we play football. We can’t just be all run or all pass. We got to be able to stay balanced. I think that’s probably the biggest thing.” How much do the Giants need to adapt in their approach to the run game? “You got to be able to be flexible with the players, with your scheme, with the coaches. You can’t be stubborn,” Nagy said. “That’s probably going into this whole process one of our greatest strengths as coaches that I’ve noticed since I’ve gotten here is we got some coaches that really want to do what’s best for the players and for us. And then the players, too. I think it’s very important for the players to have a voice in this thing and us to be able to communicate clearly with them and say, ‘Hey, what are some things maybe that we’re doing that we’re not good at or you don’t like?’ And then vice versa, what are some things that we need to do that would help us out? That’s, to me, what good football coaching and communication is. So, that’s what we’ve done, and now we know.” For Nagy, first down runs are particularly important. “We have to be better on first down running the football,” Nagy said. “We can’t stay in this second and eight, second and 10, second and seven, but we know that. So, what are we going to do about it? How are we going to fix that? And that’s our number one challenge.” The J.J. McCarthy package McCarthy was on the field for five plays against the Washington Commanders. McCarthy’s longest run was 2 yards, and the only successful play — a screen pass to Malik Nabers — was wiped out by penalty. The Giants have no intention of abandoning it. “It is a change of pace,” Nagy said. “There’s three plays that we had him in there where it’s the old “if” thing. We had one piece of the play that was just off a little bit. One of them was the penalty, right? Then there’s two other plays that we had that could have been really big plays, and they weren’t for one reason. And so, without getting into the scheme part of it, we’ve told the guys and we’ve told J.J., like, ‘Listen, you’re doing what you’re supposed to do. We like that package.’ We can’t be predictable with it when we use him and when we’re going to do it, but he needs to stay with it. That can be an advantage for us.“ Nagy said the Giants also need to balance familiarizing McCarthy with the full playbook, and that they don’t take too many practice reps away from starter Jameis Winston. “We’re going into week three with him, so we’ll continue to see where that’s at,” Nagy said. “In the meantime, we don’t want to lose sight that he needs to learn this offense as a quarterback, not as a package guy. That’s very important. So, we’re trying to keep that going, too, to where he can understand that. But you’ve got to be careful with how many reps you take away from him Jameis.” More tempo? The Giants leaned into tempo in the second half vs. the Commanders. Nagy said it was “absolutely” something that helped. “I think that helped us last week. I know it helped us,” Nagy said. “So, when you look at something like that, you say to yourself, ‘Okay, that was some good stuff.’ We’ve got to be able to say now how much do we want to do of it, when do we want to do it, and then how do we make ourselves not be predictable when we are in it? About those fumbles Despite Cam Skattebo having fumbled in three straight games, and all three of the Giants usually active backs having had some type of fumbling issue this season, Nagy expressed confidence. “I’ll never lose confidence in those guys. We don’t want that, but I will never lose confidence in those guys because they’re going to make plays for us,” Nagy said. “You’re obviously talking about Skatt (running back Cam Skattebo), speaking to him specifically. Love the guy to death. I know how much he cares. I know how much he wants it. Everyone here is seeing what this NFL has become right now with that peanut punch. It’s across the board.” ‘Massive jump’ for Malik Nabers Star wide receiver Malik Nabers has had back-to-back 100-yard receiving games. Against the Commanders, Nabers had 11 catches on a season-high 20 targets. “Probably the first week or two, you could see he was a little hesitant, which is natural,” Nagy said. “I haven’t thought about that at all when he’s out there playing now. To me, that’s a massive jump. When you don’t see it in practice, when you don’t see it in the game, you see that growth. Whatever that date is or that day, to me it’s day-to-day for him, but man he’s looking good.”

title: NFL predictions: Will underdog Giants upend the Saints?
summary: Can the New York Giants, 3-0 at MetLife Stadium this season, continue their winning ways at home on Sunday when they face the New Orleans Saints? Below, how the Big Blue View staff is predicting the game, as well as the rest of the NFL Week 6 action. Chris Pflum Just how beaten up are […]
full_text: Can the New York Giants, 3-0 at MetLife Stadium this season, continue their winning ways at home on Sunday when they face the New Orleans Saints? Below, how the Big Blue View staff is predicting the game, as well as the rest of the NFL Week 6 action. Chris Pflum Just how beaten up are the Giants? That’s the question on my mind as we get ready for this game. I think I’m less concerned with Abdul Carter than I am with Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor. Even though Thomas hasn’t been healthy since Week 1, the Giants have still fielded one of the very best tackle duos in the NFL. And while Marcus Mbow has played well in his outing, he’s struggled with power in the past. That’s a bit of a concern given the Saints have a pair of good-sized and powerful defensive ends in Chase Young and Carl Granderson. That said, the Saints’ defense has been pretty porous and their win rates haven’t been great this year. As long as the Giants can protect Jameis Winston, there should be opportunities to move the ball and score. On the flip side, the Giants’ defense has been playing with a similar aggression as the Vikings’ defense that held Tyler Shough to 3.8 yards per attempt, and their offense to 142 total yards. The Giants’ pass rush has been dynamic over the last two games, and they’ve been opportunistic in creating turnovers. The Giants’ athletic blitzers could cause many of the same problems for the Saints as the Vikings’ did — at least assuming Abdul Carter’s calf injury is minor. I’m still going to pick the Giants to win the game, but my confidence level depends on the the Giants’ health. Pick: Giants Tony Del Genio This is an uncomfortable matchup for the Giants. The Saints have been sub-.500 in three of the past four seasons, yet they have beaten the Giants three years in a row. The Giants’ last victory was in overtime in 2021, when Daniel Jones passed for 402 yards in the Superdome. The losing quarterback in that game was…Jameis Winston. History aside, my discomfort stems from what I see as a non-ideal matchup of strengths and weaknesses. Tyler Shough is a very experienced quarterback even though this is only his second year in the NFL. His receiving corps is better than what the Giants saw last week, most notably Chris Olave, second in the NFL in receiving yards. Shough was flummoxed by Brian Flores’ blitzing Minnesota defense last week. If that sounds like good news because Dennard Wilson has become fond of the blitz himself, it’s not. Flores’ defense works because the zone defense and deception he uses behind it induce quarterbacks to throw quickly to receivers they think are open, but aren’t. Dennard instead is playing a decent amount of Cover 0 and leaving cornerbacks to stay with receivers in single coverage. Can the Giants’ cornerbacks cover receivers like Olave? The answer to that may decide the game. I’m more optimistic about the Giants on offense…if they can protect Winston. Chase Young is back to his early form, and with Carl Granderson on the other side form a good 1-2 punch against…whom? Neither Andrew Thomas nor Jermaine Eluemunor practiced on Wednesday. If Winston sees a lot of pressure, it could be lights out for the Giants. Given time, though, he may be able to exploit the Saints’ second and third levels. And maybe the Giants can find a way to finally run the ball effectively against one of the worst run defenses in the league. I choose to be optimistic this week. A little, anyway. Pick: Giants David Hartman I’m more than a little surprised that the 1-4 Saints are favored over the 3-1-1 Giants this Sunday, and especially with the game being played at MetLife. Then again, while the Giants are 2-0-1 in their last three outings, all of those games were effectively decided on the final play of the game. New York is a bounce (and brain fart) or two away from also being 1-4. The Saints are Big Blue’s fourth straight opponent who, like them, picked in the Top-10 of the 2026 draft, with three of those four games at home. This game is the end of the easy stretch of New York’s schedule. New Orleans can throw the ball, but they can’t run it or stop the run. They rank 30th in the NFL in rushing offense and 29th in rushing defense. Kellen Moore’s offense is fast-paced — they’re second in the league in plays per game (74). Dennard Wilson’s defense will need to stay fresh, and play better than it did last week against Washington. Sustained drives by New York’s offense should help with that. I like the Giants to win fairly convincingly in this one, and for the first time in a month, I don’t think you’ll need to wear a heart monitor to watch the fourth quarter. They should be able to establish the run and work some play-action off of that, and I think they’ll be able to rattle Tyler Shough with their pass rush, as the Vikings did last week. Jameis Winston didn’t throw any picks last week (although he did lose a fumble) and while it’s a lot to ask for a repeat, I think he’s showing pretty good command and very good rapport with his main weapons. They’ll get a lift from the home crowd too. Pick: Giants James Hickey The Giants come home Sunday to face a the New Orleans Saints, a team that has been put on notice by their owner just this week that improvements are needed. I do not know about you, but when my boss tells me something like that, my work goes up a notch. As Jon Runyan noted this week, the Giants could easily be 1-4 and they are a beat up team coming off their tie in Washington— there is a real chance that their offensive tackles could be a first- and second-year player at some point on Sunday. When teams are evenly matched, I always go with the more desperate team and the Giants using up all of their luck last week. Pick: Saints 27, Giants 10 Valentine’s View Like others above, this game makes be a bit queasy from a Giants’ perspective. They have lost to the Saints three years in a row. The 1-4 Saints are likely better than their record, and are under fire from ownership . They will come to MetLife Stadium desperate to turn their season around. The Giants are 3-0 at home this season, but you are fooling yourself if you think they will win every game at MetLife. The Saints are vulnerable defensively and middling offensively, but the Giants have plenty of their own issues. I think the Giants can find a way to win this game. Perhaps that comes down to the belief in themselves the Giants have developed vs. a Saints team that has underperformed expectations. I feel like, at least for now, things have been bouncing the Giants way. If Abdul Carter can’t play, though, my view on this game might change. title: ‘Peanut punch’ prevalence has gotten Giants’ attention
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The ‘Peanut Punch’, with would be tacklers punching at the ball with a closed fist in an effort to jar the ball loose from ballcarriers, has become the rage in the NFL. “The league is more of a punch-out league than it’s ever been before,” head coach John Harbaugh said on […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo carrying the ball in overtime vs. Washington. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The ‘Peanut Punch’, with would be tacklers punching at the ball with a closed fist in an effort to jar the ball loose from ballcarriers, has become the rage in the NFL. “The league is more of a punch-out league than it’s ever been before,” head coach John Harbaugh said on Wednesday. Cam Skattebo’s overtime fumble Sunday against the Washington Commanders, which cost the Giants an opportunity to win that game, came on a punch-out by Washington defensive tackle Daron Payne. “Everyone here is seeing what this NFL has become right now with that peanut punch,” offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said on Thursday. “I mean, it’s across the board. You see it the next night in that Rams-Buffalo Bills game. Guy [Buffalo defensive end Greg Rousseau] had two of them. “So it’s a different style of game. They’re being taught to punch the ball out.” With defenders punching at the ball like never before, what are ballcarriers to do? How do they protect the ball? “You emphasize it. You practice it, which we do every week,” Nagy said. “Coach Harbs is just – he’s so good with that. We make sure every practice that we are – we have a bunch of different drills that we work. We work it and you have to speak it into existence. “So that’s the part sometimes that can get frustrating is you end up getting to a point where you practice it, you emphasize it, but yet it still happens. So you just can’t – you can’t just stop doing that. You have to make sure you keep emphasizing it. We’ll show clips.” Nagy did address the Skattebo fumble. “This weekend more than ever at the end of the game situationally is a part of it,” Nagy said. “So you just have to be careful of – there’s that fine line of making sure that after the game everyone – Skat knows everyone’s upset at what happened. He gets that. “So there’s that fine line of knowing, listen, the next day on Monday or Tuesday when you show it, explain it. But you don’t beat it down … he’s just got to do it. It’s simple. Do it. Just cover the ball, two hands, especially in that moment, and then we just got to emphasize it as coaches.” Kickoff and punt returners are also dealing with tacklers trying to punch the ball out. “It’s something we talk about. We talk a lot about it, right?,” said special teams coordinator Chris Horton. “And it is happening. It is happening a lot. You see a lot of these plays. But it’s just a reminder that defenses are attacking the football. “So when we’re carrying the ball, we spend a lot of time about being intentional about protecting the football. Where should the ball be?” Tyrone Tracy had a ball punched out Sunday vs. Washington as he was going out of bounds on a kickoff return. “We talked about body, ball, boundary,” Horton said. “Well, if I’m running to the left, the ball needs to be on the left side. That way that guy can’t punch that ball. If he does punch it, hey, we’re on the sidelines probably going out of bounds. But through contact, we got to make sure that we are intentional about protecting the football.”

title: Giants vs. Saints matchup: Can the Giants’ defense shut down the Saints’ offense?
summary: The New York Giants enter Week 6 as the leaders of the NFC East and return home after a Week 5 tie to face the New Orleans Saints. This game marks the third time in three weeks that the Giants will underdogs to a last place team, as the 3-1-1 Giants are 1.5-point underdogs at […]
full_text: The New York Giants defense lines up across from the New Orleans Saints offense before a play. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants enter Week 6 as the leaders of the NFC East and return home after a Week 5 tie to face the New Orleans Saints. This game marks the third time in three weeks that the Giants will underdogs to a last place team, as the 3-1-1 Giants are 1.5-point underdogs at home to the 1-4 Saints. The Giants come into the game still looking to have their first complete performance since starting QB Jaxson Dart was lost for the season. the Giants are 2-0-1 since Dart was lost in Week 2, but have escaped losses by the skin of their teeth each time. The Saints, meanwhile, are reeling after a 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings that saw the Vikings shut down the Saints’ offense. Can the Giants take lessons from the Vikings’ league-leading defense and get off to a fast start against New Orleans’ offense? Stats that matter What the Saints do on offense When it comes to the passing game, Kellen Moore’s offensive philosophy has historically been a blend of the Air Coryell and West Coast schemes. He’s added modern twists and updates to those venerable schemes, but the foundation is the use of a West Coast quick game with Air Coryell style vertical concepts when opportunities present themselves. They mix and match condensed and spread formations, while also asking Shough to work from under center as well as out of the shotgun. They typically use motion on nearly every play, as well as use bunch or stack sets to help secure clean releases for their receivers. The West Coast roots of the offense are evident in the structure of Moore’s passing play design. He frequently calls route concepts designed to create traffic or conflict at the second or third levels, and create receiving windows that his pass catchers can exploit. Moore’s passing concepts frequently seem to feature half-field reads against the Minnesota Vikings, though that could be an attempt to counter the Vikings’ blitzing defense (more on that in a bit). Shough is capable of making full-field progression reads and the offense does ask him to do so, however half-field reads and quick-game passing concepts seem to be the bread and butter. In that vein, there are instances where Shough can lock on to receivers or stare down spots from the snap, which could be an opportunity for the Giants’ opportunistic defense. The Saints’ offense makes relatively frequent use of their tertiary receivers in the passing attack. Wide receiver turned tight end Juwan Johnson is Shough’s third-most targeted option, averaging just over 6 targets per game, while Alvin Kamara is fourth and averaging four targets per game. Both players serve as primary options in passing plays as well as check-down targets. Moving to the running game, Kamara is the starter after Travis Etienne Jr. landed on the injured reserve after Week 3 with a hamstring injury. Kendre Miller is the change-up to Kamara as a power back, but both rnners have struggled to consistently produce. The 31-year old Kamara has averaged 3.1 yards per attempt this year, while Miller has averaged 2.9 per attempt. But while Kamara was the starting running back, he only carried the ball three times against the Vikings. Miller, meanwhile, carried the ball 10 times. Schematically, the Saints based their running game on outside zone concepts against the Vikings’ blitz schemes, however they did mix in gap schemes with pulling linemen. Both their line and Miller were more effective executing their outside zone runs. Shough hunting The Giants’ pass rush has been absolutely ferocious over the last two games. Abdul Carter might be the most fearsome pass rusher in the NFL right now, boasting an incredibly impressive 36% pass rush win rate despite being doubled on 40% of his rushes. His 2.22-second time to pressure is the fastest in the NFL, and he’s generating pressure — and quick pressures — at an elite rate. It isn’t a surprise that Carter also leads the NFL in pass rush wins with 31. But while Carter is the player that that teams need to account for on every play, he isn’t carrying the by himself load both Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux generated three quick pressures apiece, while linebacker Arvell Reese, and defensive tackles D.J. Reader, and nDarius Alexander each contributed two quick pressures. Cornerback Dru Phillips led the team with five quick pressures (and two sacks) of Jayden Daniels. The difference over the last two weeks has been the adjustment by Dennard Wilson to use the blitz to unleash the his pass rushers. Over the last two weeks, the Giants have sent five (or more) rushers 57% of the time, and 61% against the Washington Commanders. The Giants’ blitz rate since the second quarter against the Arizona Cardinals is (distantly) second only to that of the Minnesota Vikings. I bring that up because the Vikings gave us a blueprint for how to attack Tyler Shough and the Saints’ offense. The Vikings sent extra rushers on 21 of 25 drop backs against the Saints, limiting Shough to just 96 yards passing (3.8 per attempt), with 2 interceptions and 1 sack. Pressuring Shough is an excellent way to disrupt the Saints’ passing offense. Shough is, generally, an efficient quarterback who’s a favorite of offensive coaches. He is generally faithful to the structure of the offense and play design and typically doesn’t put the ball in danger. He’s a good athlete who also has a live arm that allows him to access all areas of the field. However, Shough is, in the words of former scout Nate Tice, “Very Tua-coded” as a passer. Shough takes care of the ball, but he’s also prone to throw the ball away as a first resort. He’s below league-average in interception rate, he’s also below league average in yards per attempt and touchdown rate. He also currently has the 10th-fastest time to throw of all quarterbacks, as he would rather get the ball out or throw it away than extend the play or hold the ball for a deep pass. The pressure and difficult coverage reads created by the Vikings’ defense brought out Shough’s tendencies to throw the ball away rather than risk going backward or turn the ball over. That’s a tendency the Giants can, and should, look to exploit with their athleticism and aggression on defense. There are, of course, differences in how Wilson and Flores deploy their blitz schemes. Flores has woven the blitz (or five-man rushes) into the very fabric and structure of every aspect of his defense. Everything is predicated on pressure under a two-deep shell, either true Quarters coverage or Cover-2. The goal of Flores’ scheme is to create free runs for his rushers while not allowing the offense to access the deep or intermediate area of the field. This is even true for his run defense, and the Vikings frequently use the blitz to “gap out” opposing offenses and disrupt their runs. Wilson’s blitz schemes, meanwhile, are based on using sticky press-man coverage to take receivers away while his hyper-athletic linebackers do their thing. The Giants lead the league in Cover-0 usage , calling pure man coverage at a league-high 11%. To put that in perspective, Steve Spagnuolo and the Kansas City Chiefs led the NFL in Cover-0 usage last year at just 7.6%. That’s particularly impressive considering the Giants’ defensive adjustment is only seven quarters old. While the Vikings’ defense has been much better than the Giants, the Giants have a marked advantage in athleticism at all three levels. That could allow them to severely disrupt what the Saints want to do on defense and harass (or attack) Shough. However, the difference in structure presents two potential areas of concern against the Saints. The first is the presence of wide receiver Chris Olave. Olave was a lone bright spot for the Saints against the Vikings, and his precision route running gives man cover corners fits. He’s also a savvy veteran who knows how to manipulate defenders to expand receiving…

J.J. McCarthy’s Giants debut offered a glimpse: What’s next? | NJ.com Still, don’t be surprised if Harbaugh gives McCarthy another shot Sunday in a similar package to what Nagy used in Washington. After all, Harbaugh said he liked the look of the plan Nagy and Co. had for McCarthy. “I do, and I think we’ll grow,” Harbaugh said. “We just have to see. It just all depends. We’re in a situation now where it’s by any means necessary. So we’re all on board for whoever, however. Sometimes, it’s going to work. Sometimes, it’s not. We had a chance in a couple of those to make big plays.” You weekly “Did you see that play the rookie made?” highlight Watch Arvell Reese take the block with one hand and tackle the ball carrier with the other 😮 @arvxll | @Giants | @OhioStateFB pic.twitter.com/70gR1Gi23X — NFL (@NFL) October 14, 2026 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Lions move into top spot | PFF 17. New York Giants (up 3). The Giants benched John Michael Schmitz Jr. ahead of Week 4, with Bryan Hudson replacing him in the starting lineup. The move has paid off so far, with Hudson notching PFF grades above 70.0 in both starts. Hudson has allowed just one pressure from 102 pass-blocking snaps, producing a 96.8% PFF pass-block win rate across those two starts. title: New York Jets: In search of a turning point
summary: The New York Jets face off against the New England Patriots in Foxborough, Massachusetts this Sunday. Foxborough has been a house of horrors for the Jets over the last two decades. The Jets beat the Patriots in Foxborough 17 – 3 in January of 2024. Prior to that the Jets had not won a regular […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - OCTOBER 15: Members of the New England Patriots and New York Jets say a prayer on the field after the Patriots' 24-17 win at MetLife Stadium on October 15, 2017 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Abbie Parr/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets face off against the New England Patriots in Foxborough, Massachusetts this Sunday. Foxborough has been a house of horrors for the Jets over the last two decades. The Jets beat the Patriots in Foxborough 17 – 3 in January of 2024. Prior to that the Jets had not won a regular season road game against the Patriots since the 2008 season. That’s a very long time between road victories against the Patriots. It’s been more than just understandable road losses to a Patriots team that has been among the best teams in the NFL for much of the last 25 years. The Patriots have made a point of embarrassing the Jets. The Jets lost to the Patriots on the road 54 – 13 in 2021. In 2018 it was a 38 – 3 loss. In 2017 it was 26 -6 and in 2016 the Jets lost on the road 41 – 3. It has been a long, ugly, futile stretch of failure on the road for the Jets against the Patriots. On Sunday, the Jets get a chance to change all that against the defending AFC champs. In the process, the Jets can get to .500 on the season and forge ahead of the Patriots in the AFC East standings. A Jets win would give both teams a 3-3 record, but the Jets would have the better record head-to-head, in the AFC East division, and in AFC games. A win would also give the Jets a golden opportunity to begin to make some noise in the race for a playoff spot. Following the Patriots game the Jets have a six game stretch that includes games against the Miami Dolphins, Las Vegas Raiders, Kansas City Chiefs, Buffalo Bills, Los Angeles Chargers, and the Miami Dolphins again. The Jets are certainly in no position to overlook anyone, and most teams will likely see the Jets as a great opportunity for a win. Nonetheless, at least on paper, three wins in that six game stretch seems eminently doable, and four wins aren’t out of the question. If the Jets can somehow manage a big upset on Sunday, it’s not difficult to see a path to a .500 or better record after 12 games. That would at a minimum keep the Jets on the periphery of a playoff push over the last month or so of the season. If the current Jets regime wants to finally change the Jets’ status as a laughingstock of the NFL, this is as good a chance as any to start down that path. The Jets have been here before. In 2024 the Jets were 2-3 going into a big division game against the Buffalo Bills. They almost won before falling 23 – 20. That set up a death spiral as the Jets proceeded to lose six out of seven games, rendering the rest of the season irrelevant. In 2023 the Jets beat the New York Giants in overtime to get to 4-3 on the season. They promptly lost five straight as they slid into irrelevance. In 2022 the Jets blew out the Chicago Bears 31 – 10 in late November to get to 7-4 on the season. They were serious playoff contenders. They never won another game that season. In 2018 the Jets beat the Indianapolis Colts to get to 3-3. They went 1-8 the rest of the way. In 2017 the Jets beat the Cleveland Browns 17 – 14 to put the finishing touches on a modest three game winning streak and get to 3-2 for the season. They went 2-9 the rest of the way. Modest early season success for the Jets has too often been followed up with horrendous late season collapses. Some day the Jets will reach a turning point. Some day the Jets will not only find some early success. Someday the Jets will then follow up by winning the games that appear winnable. Someday the Jets will begin to string together mid season victories into late season contention. Someday the Jets will make the playoffs again. The Jets have an opportunity here to turn the page on years of agony and heartbreak. A turning point is not always easy to see in the midst of a bad team’s struggles. The Jets have been a bad team. They have struggled. Eventually that will end. Perhaps sooner than anyone thinks. There is an opportunity here to vanquish some ghosts. A signature Jets win against an opponent that has absolutely crushed the Jets in Foxborough for decades just might be the beginning of something new for the Jets. One victory by itself would of course be meaningless. Upsets happen. Sometimes a great opponent just doesn’t get up for a game against a weaker opponent. The key for the Jets, if they manage an upset on Sunday, would be to take care of business in the following weeks. If that were to happen, suddenly the Jets might not be laughable losers. The opportunity is there. The challenge is daunting. Someday the Jets will win one of these games. And someday the Jets will parlay such a win into something bigger and better. Someday the Jets will find a turning point and not look back. Why not Sunday?

EPA/Play For EPA, I’ll use Ben Baldwin’s […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - OCTOBER 11: New York Jets offense huddles during the game against the Cleveland Browns at MetLife Stadium on October 11, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images DVOA DVOA measures a football team’s play-by-play efficiency compared to the league average, adjusted for opponent strength and game situation. Through five weeks, the Jets rank: 22nd Overall 17th in Pass Offense 19th in Rush Offense 11th in Pass Defense 26th in Rush Defense 16th in Special Teams Overall, these metrics are fairly consistent, ranging anywhere from average to mediocre. Which, honestly, is a big step forward from last season. EPA/Play For EPA, I’ll use Ben Baldwin’s Weighted EPA from RBSDM. EPA captures the net value of an individual play by calculating the change in a team’s expected points from before the snap to after the whistle. It’s also fairly predictive. Through five weeks, the Jets rank: 19th in Passing EPA 22nd in Rushing EPA 19th in Overall Offense 9th in Overall Defense 13th in Passing Defense 10th in Rushing Defense ESPN Analytics From an efficiency standpoint, the Jets rank: 20th Overall 23rd in Offense 14th in Defense 11th in Special Teams Overall Takeaways Overall, the Jets show up fairly consistently across all of these performance metrics. That shouldn’t be surprising, as most of them are correlated to some extent. Still, a few takeaways stand out. The Rushing Offense Needs to Be Better The Jets’ rushing offense needs to be a bit better. We saw glimpses of what it can do against Cleveland, but I’d venture to guess that not many people in the organization thought the passing offense, with Geno Smith on essentially a minimum level deal, would outrank the rushing offense through five weeks. There’s still room for this unit to improve, and getting more consistent production on the ground would go a long way toward helping out the passing offense as well. The Defense Has Been a Nice Surprise The Jets’ defense has been a nice surprise overall. Going into the season, I think we expected the defense to be much improved (how could it not be?), but there were still major questions about the secondary in general and how much the edge room would be able to contribute immediately. The weather has likely contributed to the overperformance, but this hasn’t been a unit that has relied on turnovers yet, either. If they can start forcing some interceptions, there could be room for this unit to keep up its strong level of play. So, What Are The 2026 Jets? Overall….we still don’t know. What we do know is that through five-weeks, the Jets have been meh…which honestly represents a big upgrade from what we saw in Aaron Glenn and Darren Mougey’s first year. While I don’t think anyone is running to call the Jets good, there has been a noticeable improvement and if you’re a fan looking for progress with this new regime I think it’s hard to argue there hasn’t been some. Whether it’s enough meaningful progress for Aaron Glenn to keep his job? I don’t know yet. But if the Jets continue to play like this, they should be able to largely compete the majority of weeks, even if they’re not quite a playoff-caliber team yet.
