title: Jayden Daniels showed real leadership in latest remarks on Commanders tie
summary: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels stood before his teammates this week and addressed the end-of-game disaster that resulted in a 27-27 draw with the New York Giants.   His message was simple.   I’m the quarterback. The buck stops here.   “You stand up there and be a man,” Daniels told on-site reporters Thursday during his […]
full_text: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniel s stood before his teammates this week and addressed the end-of-game disaster that resulted in a 27-27 draw with the New York Giants. His message was simple. I’m the quarterback. The buck stops here. “You stand up there and be a man,” Daniels told on-site reporters Thursday during his weekly press conference. “Everybody’s a part of it but it’s ultimately on me. I said my two cents and let the guys know it will never happen again and that we’re going to move forward from that.” That private meeting wasn’t the last time he took accountability for that Week 5 tie. Daniels took full responsibility for letting the clock run out in overtime despite a chance to beat New York with a field goal. “Ultimately it’s on me,” Daniels said. “I know DQ is getting a lot of (flak) for it or whatever but, regardless, I’m supposed to be calm with everything and control everything and I failed (uphold) the standard I hold myself to and the standard of this organization. “It’s something for me to (move on from). I’m not saying I’m proud of it or anything. It wasn’t a loss. We tied, but it was a failure. I hold myself to a higher standard than that. Moving forward, I’ll grow from it and learn from it and it’ll never happen again.” Daniels exuded leadership in that moment, an important move for the secure high-ranking Commanders outside of owner Josh Harris . That doesn’t mean everything that went wrong Sunday was all Daniels’ fault. It certainly wasn’t, but he wouldn’t let others take the fall. He understood and accepted the outside criticism — ‘it’s warranted’ — because he’s the man in the arena. “The coaches could call a play and have it be chaos and havoc on the sideline, but ultimately I’m the one who controls that huddle,” Daniels said. “It’s on the field and all eyes are on me. I just didn’t execute to my standard.” Daniels defended head coach and the respect for him within the locker room and the organization. He spoke for nearly 15 minutes on Thursday and didn’t shy from a single question or even give a stock answer. That doesn’t mean he should entertain all this forever, but it was a smart move by Daniels that should create a break from the immediate aftermath of Sunday’s events. (Well, maybe after David Blough talks on Friday). He stood up for his offensive coordinator as well. “I think he communicated the situation, the play and everything like that,” Daniels said. “It’s ultimately on me. DQ got the heat, (David) Blough and myself. Don’t even put it on the coaches. I have to be more aware and manage the game right. I did not do that. It doesn’t matter what happens on the sideline between the coaches or anything like that. I have to manage the game right.” Everybody inside Commanders HQ was surely watching that presser. It’s worth viewing in its entirety with the video below. Here’s betting it resonated well. Just like Quinn, accountability was taken. Insight was provided. Now we’re moving on. “I feel like I was able to grow as a person from this and I was always told, growing up, don’t make the same mistake twice,” Daniels said. “I made it once and I won’t make it again.”

title: Washington Commanders open practice window for reserve linebacker on IR
summary: Jordan Magee is getting back to practice. That’s a plus for the Commanders, who formally opened his 21-day window to return off injured reserve. He was placed on IR following a hamstring strain suffered in a Week 1 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. He’s an important depth piece and core special teams player who was […]
full_text: Jordan Magee is getting back to practice. That’s a plus for the Commanders, who formally opened his 21-day window to return off injured reserve. He was placed on IR following a hamstring strain suffered in a Week 1 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. He’s an important depth piece and core special teams player who was missed while he was out. Washington’s linebacker depth was tested during that stretch with Frankie Luvu missing time and Leo Chenal suffering a fractured neck that ended his season. Magee should be the primary backup if he’s able to return off IR. If he isn’t activated before the end of this 21-day window, he’ll be placed on season-ending injured reserve. The Commanders have return to play guidelines that generally involved a ramp-up period, though it varies in length based upon the nature of the injury and a player’s health status. Getting Magee before a Week 6 clash with San Francisco is probably an unfair expectation, but it’s not impossible. A return after the bye, though, seems more likely. Also, head coach Dan Quinn said that cornerback Trey Amos and running back Jeremy McNichols, who are also on IR and in the midst of their practice windows, are expected to be full participants in practice this week. Same with safety Nick Cross, who is on the active roster. The Commanders brought defensive lineman Deatrich Wise back from IR last week and he was a key player up front.

Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Commanders Roundtable Will Daron Payne become a trade deadline target? The trade deadline arrives at 4 PM on Tuesday, Nov. 10 [right after the Week 9 Rams game] Through five games, Payne has totaled 11 tackles while registering one sack and fumble in week five against the New York Giants. He’s drawn criticism for lackluster efforts at times through the opening weeks of the season, though the defensive line depth has taken hits. Defensive end Charles Omenihu was sidelined in week five after suffering a groin/ankle injury the week prior, while Deatrich Wise Jr. has yet to make his season debut despite having his 21 day practice window opened last week. Yet the absence of Johnny Newton also looms large after he was placed on the reserve/injured list due to a torn pectoral muscle suffered during preseason, leaving a potential hole in the meantime if Washington opts to make a move on one of the organization’s longest tenured players. After entering 2026 with limited draft capital, the Commanders own their picks in all seven rounds in 2027 while Payne could draw a potential late day two or early day three pick. Yet with a chance to add assets in exchange for an expiring contract, especially for a player with questions surrounding his future in 2027 and beyond, general manager Adam Peters could cash in on arguably the most attractive trade deadline asset. Whether he stays, goes or even draws a second extension remain undecided, but only for a matter of weeks. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Amik Robertson looked like another slot corner; Washington got more Not every free agent pays off, but Adam Peters knocked it out of the park with the signing of cornerback Amik Robertson , who has an NFL-leading eight passes defensed through five games. Robertson also has 33 tackles and one forced fumble, but you can’t put a number on what he’s brought to the field. Robertson has recorded a pass defensed in four consecutive games: two against Dallas, four against Seattle, one against Indianapolis, and one against New York. His best individual game was against Seattle: six tackles, four passes defensed, and a forced fumble. After the Seattle game, defensive coordinator Daronte Jones praised Robertson’s toughness and confidence : “Obviously, there’s a lot of room for growth, but in terms of his confidence, I like where he is with that.” When the Commanders signed cornerback Amik Robertson on March 12 , following two seasons in Detroit, I thought, okay, another slot corner. My first reaction was confusion since they already have Mike Sainristil, but after watching some film, I quickly saw why the staff wanted Robertson. Five games into the season, Robertson is starting on the outside alongside Rasul Douglas. Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Chat live during every game Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . The Athletic (paywall) Penalties and poor 2nd-half pass defense are causing Washington to swap wins for losses (or ties) The Commanders have a minus-34 scoring differential in the second half of games this season to rank 31st in the NFL through Week 5. Of their 12 red zone drives, only three have come in the second half. They’re tied with the Eagles for the fewest in the latter half of games, three fewer than any other team. Penalties have stalled many drives and negated points. Washington had 16 accepted pre-snap penalties (15 on offense) in the first five weeks of the season. Thirteen of those were on third downs, and eight of those third-down pre-snap penalties came in the second half. Yet, the defensive issues are even more glaring. That unit has improved in some areas, notably against the run; it ranks eighth in the league with 95.4 rushing yards allowed per game, up from 30th last season, when the Commanders gave up 141.8 yards per game. But in multiple games now, they’ve jumped out to strong starts and failed to maintain that level of play for a full four quarters. The last quarter of regulation has been especially costly for Washington. Commanders opponents have averaged 4.8 yards per play (10th-fewest in the NFL) and 10.8 points (tied for 15th) in the first half of games this season. But in fourth quarters, they’re allowing 7.5 yards per play and 11.0 points, both ranking 31st. Washington is also one of only four teams that haven’t recorded a single fourth-quarter sack this season. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Commanders vs. 49ers preview | A trip out west To read more of this article, CLICK HERE A to Z Sports The quarterback comparison gives the Commanders a reason to believe Jayden Daniels is a better quarterback than Brock Purdy. I’d argue he’s a full class better. Daniels is an A while Purdy is a B. The difference, for me, is what Daniels can create when everything around him breaks down. Purdy has been excellent within Shanahan’s offense, but Daniels has the mobility and off-script playmaking ability to turn a busted play into a first down or a touchdown. That’s the kind of quarterback advantage that matters when the opponent has the stronger roster. Is a class better enough to overcome a franchise that is 8-22 in its last 30 Monday Night Football games? It could be just enough to keep this from being an impossible matchup. I won’t call it a win. I’m a pragmatist about this team. But San Francisco is banged up, and Purdy has played a near-perfect season by Brock Purdy standards without hitting the wall yet. For Washington to pull it off, Daniels needs a near-perfect game. The receivers need one or fewer drops. The offensive line has to give up two or fewer sacks. With a bye next and Philadelphia waiting on the other side of it, there is no bigger game on the schedule right now. It’s also been a season of firsts that should never repeat. Antonio Williams’ called-back touchdown against the Colts. Stefon Diggs jumping on the pylon and hurting Washington on a two-point try. Daniels, Quinn, and Blough each taking a third of a share for botching the end-of-game procedure against the Giants. Those firsts have to become learned, unrepeatable behavior now. San Francisco is a wagon. Washington still has a quarterback capable of catching a team off guard, and if anyone in this league is fighting for his life more than Quinn, point him out to me. It’s going to be very difficult. It is not impossible. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Niners Nation 5 questions with Andrew York of Hogs Haven: How is Adam Peters viewed three years in? Assessment of Adam Peters so far Overall, he’s been good and he’s definitely improved the overall talent of the roster (which was abysmal when he was hired), but it definitely seems like he’s learning on the job and he’s made a few noticeable mistakes so far. title: Commanders Film Session: How Jayden Daniels powered Washington in his return
summary: Jayden Daniels’ return to the lineup against the New York Giants was nothing short of impressive. While his legs helped keep Washington’s offense afloat, accounting for 103 rushing yards and two touchdowns, his efficiency as a passer was just as dangerous. Daniels’ 199 passing yards may not jump off the stat sheet, but he completed […]
full_text: Jayden Daniels’ return to the lineup against the New York Giants was nothing short of impressive. While his legs helped keep Washington’s offense afloat, accounting for 103 rushing yards and two touchdowns, his efficiency as a passer was just as dangerous. Daniels’ 199 passing yards may not jump off the stat sheet , but he completed 68% of his passes, finishing with 17 completions . His decision-making, aggression and ball placement kept the offense moving and demonstrated how dangerous he can be when he’s operating at full strength. As Washington prepares for Monday night’s matchup against the San Francisco 49ers , who enter the game ranked sixth in the NFL in total defense by yards allowed per game, Daniels will need to maintain that dual-threat ability to give the Commanders a chance to secure their second win of the season. Mental processing and pocket patience On the first drive , Washington lines up in 12 personnel (one running back and two tight ends) against the Giants’ base 3-4 defense. After gaining 13 total yards on its first two plays, Washington faces second-and-8. Daniels does an excellent job processing the Giants’ coverage both before and after the snap. The Commanders run a switch-release concept with their tight ends against a Cover 4 structure, with two deep safeties. Ben Sinnott does an excellent job driving the cornerback upfield and away from Chig Okonkwo, who takes the inside release and runs a seam route. The Giants maintain their coverage structure after the snap, leaving the middle of the field open and giving Daniels an immediate answer. With the offensive line providing adequate protection, Daniels has enough time to stay with his primary read. He simply needs to deliver the ball beyond the linebacker and into Okonkwo’s path. His recognition of the coverage and ability to exploit the space allow Washington to capitalize on the defensive look. Leverage processing and elite placement Washington returns to 12 personnel on this next play , which comes at the start of the fourth quarter with the Commanders facing first-and-10. Daniels’ trust in Terry McLaurin is evident, but this completion stands out because he quickly processes defensive leverage and delivers the ball with precision. Washington runs a dagger concept involving Ben Sinnott, Treylon Burks, and McLaurin. McLaurin wins at the top of his route, gaining inside leverage against his defender as he breaks toward the middle of the field. Meanwhile, the Giants use edge rusher Kayvon Thibodeaux to account for the seam threat, dropping him into hook coverage. Daniels recognizes that Thibodeaux’s positioning leaves him unable to contest McLaurin’s dig route effectively. At the top of his dropback, Daniels delivers an on-time and accurate throw into a tight window and gets the ball out on schedule. It’s an excellent example of his ability to read leverage, trust his receiver and attack a defense before it can close the throwing lane. Reading progressions On the next example, Washington uses 11 personnel from an empty formation. Daniels begins his progressions toward the boundary, where McLaurin and Antonio Williams run corner and hook routes, respectively. The Giants’ deep-third and flat defenders effectively eliminate those initial options, forcing Daniels to work his progressions further. That’s where the route combination between Okonkwo and Burks becomes important. Their routes create a two-level read, putting linebacker Tremaine Edmunds in a position where his decision determines Daniels’ next move. Edmunds stays with Okonkwo, opening the middle of the field for Burks. Daniels recognizes the opening and delivers an accurate pass to Burks for a first down. It’s another example of his composure and processing ability. He doesn’t force the ball to his initial reads, instead allowing the coverage to dictate where he goes next. Daniels delivered an impressive performance against the Giants, making Washington’s final overtime sequence all the more frustrating. His ability to threaten the Giants’ defense as both a passer and a runner gave the Commanders chances to win, but the game ended in a tie. The encouraging takeaway for Washington is that a healthy Daniels gives the team a chance to compete every week. His performance against New York showed that he can win with his arm, punish defenses with his legs, and consistently make the decisions necessary to keep the offense on schedule. The challenge now is turning those flashes into a more complete offensive performance, especially with a tough matchup against San Francisco ahead. In the full Trap or Dive film session below, I break down Daniels’ performance against the Giants, including his work as a passer and runner, as well as the areas where Washington’s offense fell short under first-year offensive coordinator David Blough. Comment and let us know your thoughts on the state of the Commanders offense. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

title: Which NFL teams have never won a Super Bowl?
summary: Some NFL teams have scored multiple Lombardi trophies, but which franchises have never won the Super Bowl? Check out more information now.
full_text:
It's been 60 years since the NFL and AFL rival football leagues announced their merger and established the Super Bowl, the annual league championship that has been claimed by 20 different franchises since 1967.

 Of the 12 organizations that are still looking to capture the elusive Vince Lombardi Trophy, four of them -- the Cleveland Browns , Detroit Lions , Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars -- have never reached the big game.

 The 2026 NFL season will culminate with Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, the home of the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers . The Rams, who won Super Bowl XXXIV in 2000 and Super Bowl LVI in 2022 (at SoFi Stadium), opened the campaign at +500 odds to win it all .

 Let's take a closer look at the 12 franchises that have never won the big game (along with their number of Super Bowl appearances):

  

 

 Cleveland Browns (0) 

 There was a time when the Browns were the class of the NFL, winning seven championships with three runner-up finishes in their first 10 years as a franchise. However, it's been a different story in the Super Bowl era, particularly over the last three decades . Cleveland reached the AFC Championship Game three times after the 1986, 1987 and 1989 seasons but lost all three to John Elway and the Denver Broncos -- often in heartbreaking fashion . Over the last 30 years, Cleveland has posted more winless seasons (one) than division titles and Super Bowl appearances combined (zero).

 

 Detroit Lions (0) 

 The Lions are one of the NFL's oldest franchises (founded in 1930), yet they have zero Super Bowl appearances and arguably the worst postseason résumé in league history. That's why their 2023 run to the NFC Championship Game was such a big deal for Detroit fans. The Lions won their first playoff game since 1992, ending the NFL's longest active drought (and the fifth-longest all-time, right behind the team's previous 33-year winless run from 1958 to 1991). The Lions seemed poised to make their first Super Bowl appearance, but the San Francisco 49ers erased a 17-point deficit and defeated Detroit to punch their Super Bowl ticket.

 

 Houston Texans (0) 

 The Texans are the newest franchise in the league, having joined as an expansion team in 2002, so Houston's inclusion on this list shouldn't come as much of a surprise. Still, it's been a tough couple of decades for the Texans, who have never reached a conference championship. However, that could change in the coming years, as rookie quarterback C.J. Stroud already looks like a potential superstar, while head coach DeMeco Ryans is a rising star himself and has Super Bowl experience from his time as an assistant coach in San Francisco. Their 45-14 wild-card win over Cleveland during the 2023-24 season helped Texans fans feel hopeful.

 

 Jacksonville Jaguars (0) 

 The Jaguars have had a checkered history across nearly 30 years of existence. Shortly after they joined the NFL in 1995, they found immediate success, making the playoffs four times in their first five seasons -- including two trips to the AFC Championship Game. However, both ended in a lopsided defeat, and Jacksonville reached the playoffs just twice in the next 17 years before making another run to the AFC title game in the 2017 season -- only to blow a double-digit lead in the fourth quarter to Tom Brady's Patriots, squandering the team's best shot to reach a Super Bowl so far.

 

 Arizona Cardinals (1) 

 Having been in existence since 1920, the Cardinals are the oldest franchise without a Super Bowl victory, though they did win two league championships (1925, 1947) prior to the Super Bowl era when they were based in Chicago. Arizona came oh-so close to its first Super Bowl victory in 2009, when star receiver Larry Fitzgerald scored a go-ahead touchdown with 2:37 left in Super Bowl XLIII. The Pittsburgh Steelers responded with one of the most impressive game-winning drives in Super Bowl history, scoring in the final seconds to sink the Cardinals' title hopes.

 

 Los Angeles Chargers (1) 

 Few teams have done less with more than the Chargers, who have consistently boasted elite teams that come up short in the postseason. The franchise did reach the Super Bowl once in 1995, falling victim to Joe Montana 's 49ers in a 49-26 rout. The Bolts also reached the AFC title game in the 1980 and 1981 seasons and again in 2007, losing by a touchdown or more in all three. While the Chargers have won 10 or more games six times in the last 20 years, they've won just five playoff games in that stretch, and their 12-19 playoff record ranks fourth-worst all-time. Will new coach Jim Harbaugh be able to end the drought?

 

 Tennessee Titans (1) 

 While other franchises have seen a chance at a championship slip through their grasp, none have come closer than the Titans did in 2000. With six seconds left in Super Bowl XXXIV and Tennessee trailing by seven, receiver Kevin Dyson caught a slant pass over the middle and was wrapped up by St. Louis Rams linebacker Mike Jones near the 1-yard line. Dyson stretched out his arm toward the goal line, but he was inches short. The play, known as "The Tackle" or "One Yard Short," became the enduring image of that game and the Titans' years-long quest for their first Lombardi Trophy.

 

 Atlanta Falcons (2) 

 While other teams on this list have reached more Super Bowls, none blew their chance at hoisting the Lombardi Trophy like the Falcons in 2017. Atlanta held a 28-3 lead over the New England Patriots in the third quarter of Super Bowl LI , when they boasted a win probability as high as 99.7%. That was before Tom Brady launched the defining comeback of his career, leading his team to the biggest comeback in Super Bowl history and the only overtime victory in the game's 57-year history. It was the second title game loss for the Falcons, who got blasted by the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XXXIII . Still, nothing compares to that loss in '17, and the team has reached the playoffs just once in seven seasons since.

 

 Carolina Panthers (2) 

 The Panthers have only been around since 1995, but they've reached the Super Bowl twice in their relatively brief existence. Both times, they were defeated by an all-time great quarterback. In 2004, Brady and the Patriots outlasted Carolina, 32-29, in  Super Bowl XXXVIII . Twelve years later, Peyton Manning led the Broncos to a 24-10 win over the 15-1 Panthers in Super Bowl 50 -- his second Super Bowl victory and the final game of his storied career. Despite those gutting losses, Carolina remains the only team on this list with a winning record in the postseason and one of just 13 teams with multiple Super Bowl appearances this century.

 

 Cincinnati Bengals (3) 

 The Bengals nearly worked their way off this list in 2022, when Joe Burrow led his team to Super Bowl LVI . However, the Bengals came up short against the Los Angeles Rams, 23-20. That marked Cincinnati's first Super Bowl appearance since 1989, when Montana led his 49ers to their second Super Bowl victory over the Bengals in an eight-year span -- with both games decided by five or fewer points. The Bengals were among the title favorites entering the 2023 season before Burrow suffered a season-ending right wrist injury.

 

 Buffalo Bills (4) 

 No team has fallen short more often than the Bills, who lost four consecutive Super Bowls from 1991 to 1994 -- a run memorialized by the ESPN 30 for 30 documentary " Four Falls of Buffalo ." The first was easily the most painful, as kicker Scott Norwood famously missed wide right on a 47-yard field goal in the final seconds to seal a 20-19 loss to the Giants in Super Bowl XXV . It would be the closest Buffalo came to a title, as they lost the next three Super Bowls by a combined 65 points (with none closer than 13 points). The cruelty of those losses is magnified by the fact that the Bills won the two final AFL championships (1964, 1965) before the introduction of the Super Bowl following…

title: 15 NFL players, coaches on the hot seat entering Week 6: Quinn, McDaniel, others
summary: What now for Mike McDaniel? Should the Commanders or Eagles consider coaching changes? Could Jacoby Brissett or Brian Thomas Jr. get traded?
full_text:
Week 6 is about the point where seats start getting hot around the NFL. Five games isn't a huge sample for coaches and players, but it's enough time to see with some confidence that preseason expectations or hopes aren't going to be met. It's enough time for fans to be frustrated and make their feelings known in stadiums and on social media.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 There's no joy in seeing anyone around the league lose their job or miss out on an opportunity, but it's also a reality that everybody who works for a team faces on an annual basis. Today, I'm going to run through some of the players and coaches on the proverbial hot seat after the first five weeks of the 2026 NFL season and break down what's going wrong and what might happen next.

 In no particular order, I'll hit on three head coaches, two coordinators and 10 players with questions about their futures with their current teams. And I'll begin with a coordinator for a winless team that entered the season with postseason aspirations.

 

 
 Jump to a player or coach: 
 McDaniel | Montgomery | Bland | Smack 
 Bowles | Quinn |  Sainristil | Sirianni 
 Sheppard | Hairston | Jeudy | Brissett 
 Smith | Thomas | Nix 

 
 

 

 Mike McDaniel, OC, Los Angeles Chargers 
 It seems natural to talk about what must be the most disappointing unit in football this season. And it's fair to note that, yet again, injuries have waylaid the Chargers on the offensive side of the ball. In last week's 23-17 loss to the Broncos , the Chargers were down their top two wide receivers ( Quentin Johnston and Ladd McConkey , the latter of whom was active but did not play a single snap) and their three best offensive linemen ( Joe Alt , Tyler Biadasz  and Rashawn Slater ). Justin Herbert 's lone touchdown pass went to Hayden Rucci , a tight end who was signed off Jacksonville's practice squad in mid-September.

 Even so, McDaniel's old employers in San Francisco have had plenty of injuries on offense and are still humming along just fine for the 49ers. Frankly, even before the injuries really slowed this offense down, things didn't look the way they were supposed to in Los Angeles. The Chargers haven't been able to run the ball all season, ranking 28th in EPA per play on designed rushes.

 McDaniel has been insistent on running into heavy boxes with limited success; the Chargers have faced a numbers disadvantage in the run game 36.2% of the time per NFL Next Gen Stats, which is the fifth-worst rate in the league. It's fine to run into loaded boxes if you trust your linemen to pull it off, but the Chargers are averaging 2.5 yards per carry and minus-0.32 EPA per play on those attempts while picking up first downs at the fifth-lowest rate in the NFL.

 What has to be more concerning for coach Jim Harbaugh, though, is the regression of Herbert. Through five weeks, Herbert is last among qualifying passers in Total QBR (26.6). By several notable metrics, Herbert has completely collapsed as a passer:

 

 Herbert's sack rate is up, and he leads the league in interceptions with seven. And while a couple of those have been the customary snaps in which a Chargers receiver is suddenly allergic to the football at the point of arrival and coughs it up to a defender, Herbert deserves plenty of blame for the problems the Chargers have had as games wear on. He has a 5.0 QBR in the fourth quarter, throwing four picks and taking a league-high five strip sacks. His fourth-down interception  against the Broncos last week was one of the worst throws you'll ever see Herbert make, a lowlight he seems adamant about challenging every week once the Chargers get behind late in games.

 There's usually not much benefit to making an in-season change at offensive coordinator, given that the positional coaches were likely brought in by that coordinator and would just be running the same scheme if they were promoted to the playcalling role. The most experienced assistant on McDaniel's staff is passing game specialist Adam Gase, which won't inspire much hope among Chargers fans.

 They do have Harbaugh, though, and there's a clear line that the offensive coordinator in Los Angeles can't cross. It's one thing to field a disappointing run game or fail to live up to expectations, but the offense can't break Herbert. If McDaniel can't turn things around, and Herbert continues to struggle badly, the Chargers might make a move sooner rather than later.

 

 
 

 David Montgomery , RB, Houston Texans 
 The latest in a series of offseason additions to try to fix a moribund Texans running game, Montgomery hasn't been able to transfer his successful three-year stretch in Detroit to Houston. Though the 2019 third-round pick scored three touchdowns in the Week 1 loss to the Bills , Montgomery has averaged just 2.7 yards per carry and posted a league-worst 23.1% success rate. You can help compensate for those issues with explosive runs, but Montgomery has just one gain of 10-plus yards across 52 carries this season.

 Montgomery left last week's win over the Titans in the first half with a groin injury , potentially opening up the door to a larger role for Woody Marks . The second-year pro had what qualifies as a great game on the ground for a Texans back, turning 15 carries into 62 yards while adding four catches for 23 yards as a receiver. The Texans have been hesitant to turn the lead role over to Marks, but Montgomery's struggles and the groin injury might leave them no choice.

 

 

 
 

 DaRon Bland , CB, Dallas Cowboys 
 Bland was a first-team All-Pro after he picked off nine passes in 2023, but the interceptions have dried up since then. He has just one INT across 24 games since the start of 2024. And when Bland isn't creating significant value with his takeaways, teams find it too easy to pick on him in coverage. He has allowed passer ratings north of 100  in coverage in each of the past three seasons, per Pro-Football-Reference.com, including a career-worst 126.2 mark this season.

 Jerry Jones and the Cowboys have had reasons to give Bland a long leash. Despite missing most of the 2024 season with a foot injury , the Cowboys gave their young corner a four-year, $90 million extension before the 2025 season. Bland missed more time last year before pronouncing himself to be all the way back this season ... but he has looked overmatched in coverage. Tez Johnson 's 64-yard catch against the Cowboys  in primetime last week came on a play where Bland was badly juked and fell to the ground like he was the child in one of those " dad crosses over baby " videos.

 The Cowboys didn't really have solutions to replace Bland on the outside at cornerback, but that has changed. Cobie Durant should be set to return from his hamstring injury in the coming weeks, while Joey Porter Jr . will be back in the lineup after missing the loss to the Buccaneers with an illness . When healthy, they should be the starters on the outside for Dallas. Bland could end up in the slot, but the Cowboys have been playing  Reddy Steward  there, and rookie safety Caleb Downs could move there once Jalen Thompson returns from his hamstring injury .

 Dallas restructured Bland's deal just before the season, which reduced his cap hit and made his contract more tradable. But it also creates more dead money if (or more realistically when) the Cowboys decide to move on from the 27-year-old cornerback. Bland is owed $13 million next year, and at the moment, it's only guaranteed for injury. The Cowboys don't want to be on the hook for that money, so it would hardly be a surprise if they took Bland out of the lineup altogether once Durant and Porter are back on the field to avoid triggering those guarantees, which would happen if Bland suffers a significant injury.

 

 
 

 Trey Smack , K, Green Bay Packers 
 Life is tough for rookie kickers. Coaches don't trust you. Fans want an excuse to turn on you. You might get only a handful of kicks to prove that you're an NFL-caliber…

title: Are Panthers positioned to add reinforcements before NFL trade deadline?
summary: Armed with draft capital and sitting at 2-2, Carolina has leverage unlike in years past. So what does it mean?
full_text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- The Carolina Panthers come out of their bye week with their best four-game record in five seasons. And at 2-2, the Panthers stand alone at the top of NFC South division race with four weeks until the annual NFL trade deadline Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

 With the Panthers sitting in an unprecedented position under the current front office, Carolina is in an interesting spot when it comes to consideration of midseason reinforcements. While several notable names -- including starting right tackle Taylor Moton (blood clot), starting defensive end Tershawn Wharton (neck) and top returner Trevor Etienne (ankle) -- are expected to make their 2026 debuts in short order, the Panthers could use improved depth at a few positions with injuries piling up. That's where the trade deadline could come into play, and Carolina is inarguably better positioned to add players than in years past, especially if the team finds a good fit on the market.

 

 Panthers general manager Dan Morgan has been methodical about parting with draft capital for incoming players during his tenure, which began in 2024. In fact, his first straight-up trade involving an outgoing pick for an incoming player -- without a player or pick swap -- happened less than two months ago, when Morgan traded a 2028 sixth-round pick to the Los Angeles Chargers in late-August for defensive lineman TeRah Edwards , who played in each of the Panthers' first four games before their Week 5 bye.

 The Edwards trade, while a minor deal, shows Morgan isn't going to be stubborn with his draft assets if it means he can upgrade a roster primed for a potential repeat division championship.

 Panthers coach Dave Canales said he and Morgan speak about potential roster moves "all the time."

 "I won't get into specific positions or anything like that, but Dan has done a great job of trying to look for opportunities that may present themselves to us to be able to challenge our roster in the right way," Canales said Tuesday. "We're always open, we're always looking. I'll pop into his office right after this meeting for about 15 or 20 minutes. And we may be watching [saying], 'Hey, let's take a look at this guy.' We may be watching a college player as he's starting to gather his evaluations, but always having those conversations, to be ready for what could be."

 While the Panthers have momentum coming off a Week 4 win against the Detroit Lions and quite a few talented players who are getting healthy, adding external talent could help push the team beyond the standard it set last season with an 8-9 playoff berth.

 Let's break down the ins and outs of the Panthers' outlook with less than four weeks before the trade deadline and ahead of their game Sunday at the Philadelphia Eagles ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ):

 
 

 Roster needs for Panthers entering Week 6 
 Carolina's injuries have established positional demands across the depth chart, even with several players eligible to return from injury before Nov. 10:

 Cornerback: Jaycee Horn (quad) and Mike Jackson (groin) are on injured reserve. They were replaced by rookie Will Lee III and special teams ace Akayleb Evans against the Lions in Week 4. And while Lee held his own, Evans was picked on relentlessly by Detroit quarterback Jared Goff to the tune of 12 completions for 208 yards and a touchdown on 16 throws.

 The Panthers could use an additional veteran presence with Horn and Jackson sidelined.

 Running back: The Panthers don't want to overload starting running back Chuba Hubbard , but he has already touched the ball 71 times in the first four weeks of the season. While that workload has been beneficial to the offense (390 total yards and five touchdowns), the Panthers have postseason aspirations and don't want to hinder Hubbard's late-season production on the way there.

 Etienne will return from an ankle injury this week, but he hasn't proved himself offensively in the NFL. And the early returns on AJ Dillon haven't been particularly glowing (46 yards on 19 total touches) as he has filled in for Jonathon Brooks , who is on injured reserve after undergoing core muscle surgery. A consistent pass-catching option out of the backfield would benefit the rotation. Maybe Etienne can become that option, and he'll have a decent runway to prove himself before the trade deadline.

 Defensive line: The Panthers plan to have Wharton back in the lineup shortly. However, while they've benefited from second-round pick Lee Hunter 's play, the Panthers' run defense has left a lot to be desired. Entering Week 5, Carolina ranks last in rushing yards allowed per carry (5.4) and 31st in rushing yards allowed per game (156.5).

 While those numbers are largely skewed by the Week 1 loss to the Chicago Bears , the unit has only held one rushing offense below 132 yards in four games. Wharton isn't known as a run defender and likely won't solve this issue. Nose tackle Cam Jackson (shoulder) was also placed on season-ending IR on Tuesday, so Morgan might need to look to add externally again.

 
 Panthers' draft capital for 2027 and 2028 
 The Panthers have eight draft picks coming their way in 2027, including an additional seventh-round pick (from the offseason trade of Andy Dalton to the Philadelphia Eagles) and a second fourth-round pick, which was upgraded from a fifth-round pick in a pick swap (with the Minnesota Vikings in the 2025 Adam Thielen trade).

 

 2027 draft inventory: 

 First round (1): Original pick 
 Second round (1): Original pick 
 Third round (1): Original pick 
 Fourth round (2): Original pick, additional pick from Minnesota 
 Fifth round (0): N/A (original pick traded to the Vikings) 
 Sixth round: Original pick 
 Seventh round (2): Original pick, additional pick from Philadelphia

 In 2028, the Panthers have six picks following the sixth-round swap for Edwards in August. All six are the Panthers' original picks.

 
 State of Panthers' salary cap 
 While the Panthers have an encouraging record, quality draft capital and clear needs at relatively attainable positions, their salary cap constraints could hold them back ahead of the deadline. According to the NFLPA, the Panthers have just $2.32 million in cap space (which ranks as second worst in the league behind the Los Angeles Rams with $1.78 million in space) as of Wednesday.

 The team has the ability to open up cap space with contract restructures, but that might not be the most sound strategy, even with the team looking to win now. While trading a future draft pick is one thing, pushing cap charges into the future, along with trading away that capital, might be hard to stomach for an organization that has largely balanced those scales under Morgan and executive vice president of football operations Brandt Tilis.

 The team could also look into releasing or waiving an underperforming player for salary cap space. That avenue would probably be the most likely strategy, as a cut player would also open up a spot for someone acquired via trade.

 
 Four games loom large for Carolina 
 The next four weeks will be a big factor in the Panthers' approach at the deadline. The team faces the Eagles (2-3) on Sunday and then has matchups against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) at home and the Green Bay Packers (3-2) on the road before hosting the Denver Broncos (3-2) in the final matchup before the deadline. If the Panthers are still hovering around .500, they'll have reason to pounce on a potential trade. They could also decide to make a move well before the deadline, as the Baltimore Ravens did with center Cam Jurgens and the  Houston Texans did with wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr . in the past week.

 Given the Panthers' salary cap situation, though, their outlook on trades might be more about short-term stopgaps toward the end of their rookie contracts or veterans with low base salaries rather than the grandiose long-term splashes. A blockbuster trade probably isn't in the cards, but if the Panthers can take advantage of…

title: Ranking all eight NFL divisions this season by strength: NFC North at No. 1?
summary: Why do we have the NFC North at No. 1 in our annual division power ranking -- even ahead of the mighty NFC West? And is the NFC South at the bottom of our list ... again?
full_text:
Every year around this time, we like to rank the NFL's divisions against each other. We have a tool that does that -- ESPN's Football Power Index -- but the powers that be also ask me to do it, which I take as license to disagree with FPI.

 One of my quiet personal obsessions is the idea that, at some point, a division will send all four of its teams to the playoffs in a given year. This has been possible only since 2020, when the NFL expanded the playoff field to seven teams from each conference, and we are 0-for-6. We've had divisions in which every team finished with a winning record -- most recently last season's NFC North. But it hasn't been enough to put all four teams in the postseason.

 So far in 2026, we have two divisions in which all four teams have winning records. And if the season ended right now -- after the  Seahawks lost to the Broncos  on Thursday night to kick off Week 6 -- all four of the teams in the NFC North would hold playoff spots. So there's hope, even though at this point the other one of those divisions (AFC North) would have just one playoff team.

 Because I'm mildly obsessed with this idea, I use it as a gauge for this exercise. It's not the only qualification, but I do tend to rate a division higher if it's close and I believe one has the better chance of pulling off the all-four. That's a bit of an explanation about the madness behind my method. Here are the rankings for you all to get upset about. Enjoy. (Note: FPI rankings are through Week 5.)

 

 
 Jump to a division ... 
AFC: East | West | North | South 
NFC: East | West | North | South 

 
 

 

 1. NFC North 
 Combined FPI rating: 6.0 (No. 2 of eight) 

 
 Detroit Lions : 2.1 (10th in the NFL) 
 Chicago Bears : 1.7 (12th) 
 Minnesota Vikings : 1.5 (13th) 
 Green Bay Packers : 0.7 (16th) 
 
 It was a tough call between this division and the NFC West, which has three teams in the FPI's top six while this one has only one in the top 10. But the premise here is that we want to know which division has the best chance of landing all four of its teams in the playoffs, and with apologies to the Cardinals, I believe that puts the NFC North up top. This division features three teams (Detroit, Chicago, Green Bay) with high-end offenses but shaky defenses and one team (Minnesota) with the best defense in the league but an offense that's still putting things together.

 

 At 5-0, the Vikings are still ranked 13th by FPI because of their 26th-ranked offense. But their defensive and special teams FPI both rank No. 1 overall, and if you look at the injury issues they've had on offense, it's not difficult to imagine that unit improving. The Packers are 10th in offensive FPI despite massive offensive line issues and a complete lack of a run game. Those issues feel less likely to improve than Minnesota's weaknesses, but it's not out of the question. And the eventual return of edge rusher  Micah Parsons should boost Green Bay's 19th-ranked defense.

 Chicago ranks 12th in FPI offense and defense, and it could get quarterback Caleb Williams back from injury in Week 6. Detroit is fourth in offensive FPI and 30th in defensive, and the Lions' playoff hopes rest on their ability to outscore the teams on their fourth-place schedule. I like their chances.

 

 
 

 2. NFC West 
 Combined FPI rating: 8.8 (No. 1 of eight) 

 
 San Francisco 49ers : 6.7 (first in the NFL) 
 Los Angeles Rams : 4.5 (third) 
 Seattle Seahawks : 3.5 (sixth) 
 Arizona Cardinals : minus-5.9 (30th) 
 
 Like everyone else who has assumed since the Myles Garrett trade that the Rams are an unstoppable force, FPI continues to leave me alone on the "Shouldn't we wait to see it first?" island. There is no way anyone who has watched them play this season truly believes the 2-3 Rams are the third-best team in the NFL. Yet there they sit by being fifth in offensive FPI, sixth in defensive FPI and, of course, that pesky 32nd in special teams. With nearly 30% of the season complete, they've allowed more points than they've scored. They've lost to all three teams they've played that have a winning record, and if not for the Eagles gifting them a  Week 4 win , they'd be 1-4. I'm willing to believe the Rams have what it takes to be one of the best teams in the NFL, but right now they are absolutely not.

 

 Meanwhile, the 49ers look elite despite being riddled with injuries. They're 5-0, second in offensive FPI and 10th in defensive FPI. They beat the Rams handily in the season opener and just won a knock-down, drag-out game against the Super Bowl champion Seahawks . Seattle (now 3-3) went into Thursday night's game ranked second in FPI defense and special teams -- but a troubling 14th in offense. If the Seahawks want a shot at repeating, they need to get the run game figured out the way they did as last season went along.

 The Cardinals rank 23rd in FPI's offensive rankings, dead last in defense and 29th in special teams. They are the main reason this division can't dream of putting all four teams in the playoffs, but again, the Rams have yet to show us anything this season that should make us think this division could get three.

 

 
 

 3. AFC North 
 Combined FPI rating: minus-2.5 (No. 5 of eight) 

 
 Cincinnati Bengals : 2.4 (eighth in the NFL) 
 Baltimore Ravens : 0.9 (15th) 
 Pittsburgh Steelers : minus-1.1 (19th) 
 Cleveland Browns : minus-4.7 (27th) 
 
 This is one of two divisions, along with the NFC North, in which all four teams have winning records. FPI doesn't particularly love any of them. It has Cincinnati's offense ranked sixth, Baltimore's offense 11th (though  Lamar Jackson 's absence is woven in there), Pittsburgh's offense 19th and Cleveland's offense 31st. Defensively, FPI ranks the Ravens 14th, Steelers 15th, Browns 16th and Bengals 18th, which is about as mediocre and closely bunched as you can get.

 Cincinnati's offensive ranking, combined with FPI's assessment of the 3-2 Bengals' remaining schedule as the easiest in the league, offers hope for Joe Burrow 's return to the postseason. Baltimore has the 4-1 first-place record and has yet to play a division game, so opportunity is there for the Ravens to take control. Jackson's left ankle injury  isn't believed to be long term, and they just beat the Falcons with Tyler Huntley anyway.

 FPI (and history) identify the Browns as the weak link here. They've been outscored by an average of 3.8 points per game but still have a 3-2 record. That's a testament to the job first-year coach Todd Monken is doing, but it certainly offers license to wonder how sustainable it is over the rest of the season. And the Steelers? Well, quarterback  Aaron Rodgers is flinging it, running back  Jaylen Warren is on a hot streak, and the defense looks better than it did last season. They also have the head-to-head win over the Bengals in their pockets (though they also lost to the Browns ). The Steelers are hard to figure, but they're even harder to count out.

 This division always feels like it has a chance to put at least three teams in the playoffs each season, and if the Browns keep overachieving, the North could make history.

 

 

 
 

 4. AFC West 
 Combined FPI rating: 1.8 (No. 3 of eight) 

 
 Kansas City Chiefs : 4.3 (fourth in the NFL) 
 Denver Broncos : 1.5 (14th) 
 Los Angeles Chargers : minus-1.3 (20th) 
 Las Vegas Raiders : minus-2.7 (22nd) 
 
 The Chiefs are back! FPI has them seventh in offense and eighth in defense after their bye week. And Patrick Mahomes  seems to be feeling all the way recovered from last season's major knee injury . After reaching the AFC Championship Game seven years in a row and winning three Super Bowls along the way, the Chiefs watched as two other AFC West teams made the playoffs last season. But they look like a good bet to resume their postseason streak at 4-0.

 Last year's No. 1 seed in the AFC, the Broncos, are 4-2. FPI has them ranked third in defense but 17th in offense. Early-season regression from quarterback Bo Nix…

title: NFL Week 6 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips
summary: Can the Titans, Chargers finally win? Stroud vs. Lawrence? There are 13 more games in Week 6, and we have picks, predictions and more for all of them.
full_text:
Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season is here, and there's a lot to look forward to. Can the Chargers and Titans  finally get their first win of the season? Can the Raiders get back on track against a fiesty Buffalo team? And there are plenty of division showdowns to watch: Texans-Jaguars and Ravens-Browns, just to name two.

 We're here to get you ready for the action. First, our NFL Nation reporters take you inside the locker room with the best thing they heard this week, and ESPN Research provides a key stat to know. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder makes a bold prediction for each matchup, fantasy analyst Eric Moody shares fantasy football intel and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado gives her  insights  for each contest. We also have Football Power Index (FPI) game projections, and Maldonado, Moody and Walder all give us final score picks for every game.

 Let's get into the full Week 6 slate, which culminates with the "Monday Night Football" matchup between the Commanders and 49ers on ESPN . (Game times are Sunday unless otherwise noted, and all odds are via Draftkings.)

 
 Jump to a matchup: 
 HOU-JAX | CHI-ATL | BAL-CLE 
 TEN-IND | NYJ-NE | NO-NYG 
 CAR-PHI | PIT-TB | ARI-LAR 
 LAC-KC | BUF-LV | DAL-GB 
 WSH-SF 

 Thursday: SEA-DEN 
 Bye: CIN , DET , MIA , MIN 

 
 

 What ESPN Analytics says ... 
 

 

 
 

 Texans (1-4) at Jaguars (4-1)  in London 
 9:30 a.m. ET | NFL Network | JAX -2.5 (42.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Texans: New WR  Marvin Harrison Jr . is playing , according to coach DeMeco Ryans. Harrison and QB  C.J. Stroud  will have an opportunity to recreate their fireworks from their college stint at Ohio State in 2021-22. Don't expect Harrison to play most of the offensive snaps, but there will be packages for him. -- DJ Bien-Aime 

 

 What we're hearing on the Jaguars: QB  Trevor Lawrence 's history against the Texans isn't great. They're the only division team against which he has thrown more interceptions (11) than touchdowns (eight) and has a completion percentage below 60% (57.8%). One reason to be optimistic for Sunday is that Lawrence leads the NFL in off-target percentage at 8.8%, meaning he's rarely making bad passes or throws that should be intercepted. His previous best off-target percentage was 15% last season, when he had the best season of his career. -- Michael DiRocco 

 Stat to know: The Jaguars have given up 608 passing yards on throws of 15-plus yards downfield this season, second most in the NFL behind the Lions (633). Stroud is one of two QBs to attempt a pass of 15-plus yards downfield at least 45 times in 2026. -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: Texans CB  Kamari Lassiter will record an interception. This is blind faith in a good player who has struggled mightily. But I think he turns it around and, as a result, leads Houston to an upset win. -- Walder 

 Injuries: Texans | Jaguars 

 Fantasy nugget: Stroud is a viable streaming option with four teams on a bye. The Jaguars have been tough on QBs, giving up only 14.0 fantasy points per game. But Stroud has scored at least 20 fantasy points in back-to-back games and averaged 19.9 fantasy points in five career games against Jacksonville. WR  Nico Collins remains his top target, and Stroud now has another familiar playmaker in Harrison. See Week 6 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: Since 2018, the under is 8-2 when the Jaguars play in London. Jacksonville's defense gives up only 2.9 yards per carry, giving Houston's struggling run game little room to improve. That forces Stroud to carry the offense behind protection that has given up 14 sacks. Meanwhile, Houston's 18 sacks and Jacksonville's injury at left tackle ( Anton Harrison ) could keep the Jaguars from efficient drives. Read more . -- Maldonado 

 Maldonado's pick: Texans 20, Jaguars 19 
 Moody's pick: Jaguars 24, Texans 20 
 Walder's pick: Texans 23, Jaguars 21 
 FPI prediction: JAX, 58.4% (by an average of 2.2 points)

 

 Matchup must-reads: WR Harrison will play for Texans on Sunday, coach says ... Jaguars WR Washington has the clutch gene  ... Harrison latest in Texans' quest to solve WR2 conundrum ... Jaguars' Coen to tweak playcalling after delay of game issues 

 
 

 Bears (3-2) at Falcons (2-3) 
 1 p.m. ET | Fox | CHI -1.5 (51.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Bears: QB Caleb Williams ' potential return from a hamstring injury would come with an injection of explosiveness and playmaking the Bears' offense has been lacking since Week 3. "He has tremendous talent, arm ability with his legs as well," WR Rome Odunze said. "So obviously, when you're missing a player like that on the field, you feel it." Chicago could benefit in a lot of areas from Williams' return, namely with his deep ball (12 passing touchdowns of 20-plus air yards, the most in the NFL since the start of 2025) and his play under duress. Including last season, Williams threw nine touchdowns to one interception when pressured. -- Courtney Cronin 

 What we're hearing on the Falcons: QB Michael Penix Jr . has the fourth-worst EPA per dropback (minus-0.7) in the league when pressured among QBs with at least 20 dropbacks. But with no pressure, Penix is fifth best in EPA per dropback (0.58). The Bears have generated only 52 pressures, the fifth-lowest total in the NFL despite blitzing at the seventh-highest rate (39.3%). -- Marc Raimondi 

 Stat to know:  Though the Bears (173.2) and Falcons (166.8) are the top two teams in average rushing yards per game, both teams also have stout run defenses. Atlanta ranks fourth in rushing yards allowed per game (80.2); Chicago ranks ninth (96.0). -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: Falcons CB Mike Hughes will give up more than 100 combined receiving yards to Bears receivers (Odunze, Luther Burden III and Kalif Raymond ). Hughes has struggled this season, giving up 1.5 yards per coverage snap -- much higher than average for an outside corner -- per NFL Next Gen Stats. -- Walder 

 

 Injuries: Bears | Falcons 

 Fantasy nugget:  Burden has had at least five targets in every game this season, but Chicago's QB struggles have limited him to only two games with double-digit fantasy points. He has a favorable matchup against a Falcons defense that has given up the sixth-most fantasy points per game to WRs. Burden should have a decent floor based on his target volume, and his ceiling would be even higher if Williams returns under center. See Week 6 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: Since 2022, the under is 6-0 when the Falcons are home underdogs of three points or fewer. Chicago's defense has allowed opponents to convert only 26% of third downs, giving both defenses a path to ending possessions before they turn into scoring opportunities. Read more . -- Maldonado

 Ravens (4-1) at Browns (3-2) 
 1 p.m. ET | Fox | BAL -5.5 (51.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Ravens: Baltimore's focus will be on containing QB Deshaun Watson , who is 2-0 against the Ravens as the Browns starter. "He can do damage when he squirms out of there," DT Nnamdi Madubuike said. Watson ranks second in the NFL with 111 yards rushing when pressured. Edge rusher  Trey Hendrickson ( finger ) is expected to return after sitting out two games for a Baltimore team that has hit quarterbacks 55 times this season (fifth most in the league). -- Jamison Hensley

title: Run game, defense power Broncos in OT win against Seahawks
summary: Behind two rushing touchdowns and a five-sack night, Denver holds off Seattle on "Thursday Night Football."
full_text:
DENVER -- In a season in which the Denver Broncos ' offense has struggled mightily to construct many scoring drives, let alone big plays, they used just enough small ones to grind out a 17-14 overtime victory over the Seattle Seahawks  on Thursday night in Empower Field at Mile High.

 In coach Sean Payton's second game since he took back playcalling duties from offensive coordinator Davis Webb , the Broncos put together a 16-play drive for their first touchdown of the game -- their longest drive of the season -- to go with a nine-play, 79-yard touchdown for their second one. Denver then survived without another scoring drive.

 

 Payton has preached a need for a reduction in "calories" in the offense as well as more physicality in the run game to make life easier on quarterback Bo Nix . All while the Broncos' defense, which was without All-Pro Pat Surtain II and safety Talanoa Hufanga in the secondary, continued its quarterback-harassing ways. Denver had its second consecutive game with five sacks and an overtime interception from Ja'Quan McMillian .

 The Broncos ran it more than they threw it in the Week 5 win against the  Los Angeles Chargers  and had the scale tipped squarely toward the run game most of the night against the Seahawks -- 26 runs compared to 27 pass attempts before Wil Lutz kicked the winning field goal.

 "It's special, that's what we sign up for," Lutz said. "If you don't want that moment, you're not made for it. You kind of saw how the game was unfolding and the chance it was going to come down to the field-goal unit.'"

 The victory might not have been suitable for framing, given the Broncos didn't score after the first quarter and had to survive an 11-point fourth quarter from the Seahawks, but it was enough by the wafer-thinnest of margins.

 It meant the Broncos have navigated the toughest six-game opening stretch of any team in the league, per ESPN Analytics, with wins against both teams from the NFC Championship Game last season as well as five teams that were in the postseason.

 "It was a real challenge for us and I like the way we handled it,'' outside linebacker  Nik Bonitto  said of the Broncos improving to 4-2.

 Here are the most important things to know from Thursday night for both teams:

 

 

 

 Denver Broncos (4-2) 
 Trend to watch: The Broncos, from Payton on down, probably have expended more energy, spoken more words, spent more time in thought and still more aspirin in the pursuit of faster starts in games. And yet they have finished every opening drive of every game -- including Thursday night -- with either a punt or a turnover (there were five punts and one interception in the season opener). And their Week 5 win against the Chargers was the only opening drive of a game to go even more than three plays.

 Stat to know: With Thursday's win, Payton's teams have now won 40 consecutive games when they had a double-digit lead at halftime. The Broncos led 14-3 at halftime. The last time a Payton team lost a game when it had a double-digit lead at halftime was Week 1 of the 2014 season when the  New Orleans Saints  led 20-10 at halftime and lost the game 37-34.

 What to make of the QB performance: Payton obviously meant what he said when he put himself back on the headset, that there would be "more balance" between run and pass to try to dial things down for Nix. Thursday's game was a low-risk, low-reward affair as Nix didn't have a completion longer than 16 yards and never really looked settled against a Seahawks pass rush that came in with a league-best 65.5% pass rush win rate. -- Jeff Legwold 

 Next game:  at  Arizona Cardinals  (Oct. 25)

 

 

 

 Seattle Seahawks (3-3) 
 The Seahawks' offense is officially broken. As a result, the defending champions are in serious trouble. In one of their most agonizing offensive showings since Mike Macdonald became their head coach in 2024, the Seahawks managed only 184 yards through the first three quarters, gave up five sacks of quarterback  Sam Darnold and turned the ball over three more times -- including interceptions in the fourth quarter and overtime.

 "I just think it's B.S for me to keep turning the ball over," said Darnold, who gave a mea culpa in the locker room postgame. "It's not fair to our defense, it's not fair to our special teams group, not fair really to the entire team. So I've got to be better that way."

 Adding to the inexplicability of it all is the fact the Broncos were missing their best defensive player in Surtain and another difference-maker in safety Talanoa Hufanga . It wasted a standout performance by Seattle's defense, which continues to keep the Seahawks in games despite their offensive struggles.

 First-year coordinator Brian Fleury's unit entered Week 6 ranked eighth in scoring, but that was buoyed by Seattle's defense and special teams, which have been covering for the offense's flaws -- too many turnovers, Darnold's inability to play decisively, the lack of a credible run game and breakdowns in pass protection.

 With the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers playing the one-win Washington Commanders at home Monday night, the Seahawks could be three games behind in the NFC West standings by the time Week 6 is over -- with one loss already to their division rival.

 

 What to make of the QB performance: After taking five sacks Sunday in a loss to the 49ers, Darnold made it clear this week that he needs to play more decisively. That still appeared to be an issue Thursday, with the quarterback bypassing open receivers and trying unsuccessfully to extend plays. At times, though, his pass protection gave him no chance. Darnold showed his mettle by leading a touchdown and field goal drive in the fourth quarter to bookend his fourth-quarter interception. But after entering this game ranked 29th in Total QBR, he now has as many picks as touchdown passes -- seven -- in the four games since he returned from a glute injury.

 Trend to watch: As good as Seattle's defense is, it can't keep teams out of the end zone in goal-to-go situations. The Seahawks' opponents have had nine of them over the first six games and have scored touchdowns on all of them -- including two by Denver on Thursday night. Not that you can fault Macdonald's unit for this one. After the Broncos' back-to-back long touchdown drives in the first half, Seattle's defense gave them nothing.

 Stat to know: This was  Jaxon Smith-Njigba 's fourth career game with at least 10 catches and 100 receiving yards, tying Tyler Lockett for most in team history. The league's leading receiver and the reigning AP Offensive Player of the Year (12 catches for 134 yards) entered Thursday having gotten 34.8% of the Seahawks' targets -- by far the largest target share of any NFL player. He had some help for a change, with  Rashid Shaheed  (66 yards) and  Cooper Kupp  (50 yards) both topping 50 receiving yards and combining for 18 targets.  -- Brady Henderson 

 Next game:  vs.  Kansas City Chiefs  (Oct. 25)

title: Colts RB Jonathan Taylor not fretting slower start than usual
summary: Taylor may have lower numbers than usual, but he's still in the top 10 in rushing yards and rushing TDs.
full_text:
INDIANAPOLIS -- The true indication of a player's greatness might be what kind of reaction comes when they produce average performances.

 Take Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor , for instance.

 He appeared for his scheduled media gathering with local reporters on Thursday, and the conversation quickly turned to the lack of the explosive plays for which he has become famous.

 "Explosive runs?" Taylor said. "You talking about the 40-, 50-yard touchdowns?

 "Everybody loves those."

 Taylor then pointed out that he registered a 20-yard run in last Sunday's loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers , one of his longest of the season. A fair point, but the retort might have had more impact if Taylor hadn't had two runs of 80 yards or longer just last season.

 The whole exchange was a good reminder of the lofty standards Taylor is held to. It's why his current 3.9-yard-per-rush average is somewhat alarming for a player who has averaged 4.8 yards per carry in his career. It's why his third-down conversion rate of 33.3% is noticeable, considering his career mark is 47.3%.

 

 And, perhaps more than anything, it's why it's so remarkable that Taylor hasn't posted a 100-yard rushing performance in 11 months. It's all a little jarring when the subject is a player who is one of the best rushers of his generation, one coming off a 1,585-yard season in 2025, when he matched a career-high 18 rushing touchdowns.

 "It's still early and obviously everyone wants to come out the gate fast, similar to how we did last year," he said. "But, like I mentioned, it's a long season. It's a very long season."

 The Colts (2-3) have not produced the offensive fireworks they thought were possible in 2026. They drew confidence from their fast start in 2025, when quarterback Daniel Jones and the passing game took off and Taylor ran past opponents. But in the latter stages of the season, after Jones was sidelined with an Achilles tear and the Colts became easier to defend, Taylor started to see slippage in his production.

 That has continued this season, with Jones off to a slow start after his recovery, with deep-threat receiver Alec Pierce sidelined by a recurrence of his heel injury and the Colts experiencing overall lethargy on offense.

 Indianapolis ranks 22nd in expected points added, 29th in yards per play (4.6) and 25th in third-down conversions (35.3%).

 The lack of explosive threats has made them easier to defend, and that has allowed Taylor to become the focal point of opposing defenses. The Steelers used a five-man defensive front at times in their win over Indianapolis. The Tennessee Titans , who visit the Colts on Sunday, will undoubtedly take a similar approach and emphasize stopping Taylor in their game plan. Tennessee ranks fourth against the run, allowing 3.5 yards per rush.

 

 To be clear, Taylor has still managed to be effective in 2026. He ranks 10th in rushing yards per game (79.6), with 398 rushing yards and six touchdowns. Those inside the organization emphasize that he is getting the most out of his runs.

 Running backs coach DeAndre Smith on Thursday said, "When you're elite like that, those guys actually get more [yardage] than what's actually blocked. So, it's always been the standard here that he'll make spectacular plays."

 Currently, the types of defensive tactics the Colts are seeing don't allow as many of those.

 "When you don't have to blitz and you can just play four guys up front, and do a lot of damage, then that keeps seven people back," Smith said. "You're trying to maneuver through several layers of a defense."

 Taylor is among the league's most patient runners, able to wait for blocks to materialize and for defenders to commit to an angle before making his devastating cuts. And he'll need to continue displaying patience in the grander sense, too, as he waits for the opportunities for the big plays he believes are coming.

 "It's about maybe squeezing out 1 or 2 extra yards," he said. "Now maybe that's 4.1 [yards per carry], maybe that's 4.2. Maybe you have a 50-yard touchdown, now it's at 4.5."

 He added, of those thrilling big plays, "Those will come. It's still early."

title: Chiefs still have faith in pass rush, despite going without a sack since Week 1
summary: Entering this week, the Chiefs ranked 27th in pass rush win rate and hadn't recorded a sack since Week 1.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Following their bye week, the Kansas City Chiefs returned to the training facility Tuesday, their first day in preparation for Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Chargers . Longtime defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo shared earlier this month that his first meeting with his players on Tuesday often includes him reminding them of where they must improve.

 "We like to have constructive criticism," Spagnuolo said then. "The good thing about this group is they're all pretty accountable. Even if I'm standing there and pointing something out, I see a lot of heads are shaking, [saying], 'Yeah, you're right.'"

 

 This week, one of the main areas for the Chiefs defense to address is the unit's lack of a single sack over the past month.

 The 4-0 Chiefs are hoping that statistical trend ends Sunday against a Chargers team that has struggled to properly protect quarterback Justin Herbert . One reason the Chargers are 0-5 is because Herbert has been sacked at least twice in every game. Without right tackle Joe Alt (neck), left tackle Rashawn Slater (right ankle), left guard Kayode Awosika (fibula) and backup guard Trevor Penning (concussion), Herbert was sacked five times last week in the Chargers' loss to the Denver Broncos .

 Entering this week, the Chiefs ranked 27th in pass rush win rate, generating pressure by beating the opponent's pass protection within 2.5 seconds just 45% of the time. The concern for the Chiefs after their most recent game, a comeback win over the Las Vegas Raiders , is that quarterback Kirk Cousins , who they pressured on just 34.6% of his dropbacks, was the least mobile passer they have faced so far this season.

 "We've done a good job of keeping the quarterback busy back there, though, with pressure, which is important," coach Andy Reid said Monday. "Hands down, we want to have sacks. But the pressure on the quarterback ends up being an important thing, and I think our guys have been generating that."

 In the Chiefs' overtime win against the Indianapolis Colts , quarterback Daniel Jones was able to defeat pressure with quick completions, most of which were made in the middle of the field. Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis , who was sacked nine times in two games before facing the Chiefs, used his legs to escape pressure from pass rushers such as Chris Jones , George Karlaftis and rookie R Mason Thomas .

 Against the Raiders, Jones was quick to give his assessment of why Cousins wasn't sacked.

 "In order to win, you can't beat yourself," Jones said. "I think a lot of times we've made costly penalties that put us back."

 Late in the fourth quarter, Cousins was in the process of trying to get the Raiders to rally from an 11-point deficit. Just before the two-minute warning, Cousins was swarmed in the backfield by Karlaftis, Thomas and defensive end Ashton Gillotte . The problem, however, was that the sack was nullified by a holding penalty from nickel cornerback L'Jarius Sneed .

 

 Cousins was then able to finish the drive with a touchdown, the byproduct of him barely evading Thomas, who attempted a strip sack. But Cousins was able to scramble out of the pocket and throw a 20-yard touchdown pass to tight end Brock Bowers . While the Raiders celebrated, Thomas displayed his disappointment by putting both of his hands on his helmet.

 "We're motivated and we're all trying to work all together," Karlaftis said after the game. "We weren't happy with the results of last year and our numbers aren't there yet, but we're trying to affect the quarterback and have an impact on the game.

 "Up front, we felt like we had some MOBPs -- missed opportunities [for] big plays. We'll get better as the season goes on."

 Last season, the Chiefs' ineffective pass rush was one of their biggest issues. The defense recorded just 35 sacks, the fifth fewest in the league. Entering Sunday's game against the Chargers, the Chiefs have just three sacks, which is tied with the Dolphins for the league's fewest.

 "I think our D-line did a good job of finding ways to make some pressures," linebacker Nick Bolton said after the game. "We've got to finish. We can take some of those points off the board."

 

 Through four games, opponents have used similar tactics to thwart the Chiefs' defensive line. Jones has been double-teamed on most clear passing downs. Karlaftis, who is known for his strength and tenacity, leads the Chiefs with 10 quarterback hits despite not having a sack.

 Spagnuolo wants his pass rushers to be better on first- and second-down snaps, which should lead to more advantageous rushing situations on third down. The Raiders, though, were able to keep Cousins' jersey clean in the first half by utilizing play-action passes on those early downs. Cousins completed nine of his 13 play-action passes for 133 yards and a touchdown, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 "You create movement for the quarterback and get him open spaces for him to throw the ball," Jones said of the Raiders' play-action passes. "You bring the linebackers down and you've got to respect the run game. It opens up areas for the tight ends to get the ball. They did it a lot earlier in the game, and they were very successful with it. We had to adjust in the second half because they were operating under it so well."

 Of course, the Chiefs know much of their pass rush will be determined by how much their rookies, Thomas and defensive tackle Peter Woods , can contribute as the season progresses. One of the Chiefs' offseason goals was providing better support to Jones and Karlaftis. Woods and Thomas became the Chiefs' first pair of defensive linemen selected in the first and second rounds of the same draft since 2002.

 Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott , a second-year player, is also expected to return to the pass-rush rotation later this season after recovering from a torn ACL in his right knee.

 Above all, Jones is not worried. He emphasized how close the Chiefs were to sacking Cousins. He also expects the Chiefs will have plenty of opportunities to redeem themselves by hitting, wrapping up and bringing the quarterback down to the turf. Those opportunities, the Chiefs hope, start to occur Sunday against Herbert and the Chargers.

 "I think we don't waver from what we've been doing," Jones said. "We've done a lot of good and put a lot of good [plays] on film. A win is more important than a sack -- and sacks will come if we continue to do what we do."
