title: Bring on the blitz! Changing the identity of the Giants' defense
summary: The Giants' uptick in blitzing could be correlated to Brian Burns being out with injury.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- No Brian Burns ? Not a problem for the time being for the New York Giants . Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has found a workaround without the team's top rusher. He's now bringing the blitz at the levels of former defensive coordinator Wink Martindale. 

 Wilson has called for more than four rushers on 56.6% of the opposition's dropbacks the past two weeks after Burns was lost for the season with a torn ACL in his right knee in Week 3. That is second only behind the blitz-happy Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings . This after the Giants blitzed 23.1% of the time over the first three weeks, 26 th most in the NFL during that span. 

 "Dennard does a great job," coach John Harbaugh said. "He's got pretty much every blitz known to man in the system."

 The Giants found something Sunday against the Washington Commanders and quarterback Jayden Daniels that worked, leading to a surprising tie . Wilson kept going to the well. He sent a defensive back as a blitzer on 15 of Daniels' 37 dropbacks (41%), their second-highest DB blitz rate in the past 10 seasons.

 New York sacked Daniels three times when sending DB blitzes, two of which came from cornerback Dru Phillips .

 "It's definitely a fun thing to do," Phillips said. "But it was cool to get out there and blitz a little bit."

 

 Overall, Daniels was 2-of-7 passing for 23 yards with five sacks under pressure in the contest. The blitzing worked. It also worked the previous week against Arizona's Jacoby Brissett , especially on the goal-line stand in the final seconds when the Giants sent a blitz on three of the final four plays to secure a victory.

 Brissett and Daniels combined completed just 45.7% of their passes against the blitz in the two games.

 The Giants seem to suggest the sudden uptick in blitzing has something to do with playing without Burns, who had 16.5 sacks last season. His replacement, Kayvon Thibodeaux , isn't that level of a pass rusher. He has a pass rush win rate of 6.6%, which is 137 th out of 142 qualifying rushers.

 But it also has something to do with the opponent. The Giants played against veterans Dak Prescott and Matthew Stafford the first two weeks of the season. There was much more hesitation blitzing such accomplished passers.

 "It's a great week-to-week game-planning mindset. Whether it has to do with Brian Burns being out or not, could be, but it's also who you're playing, [the] quarterback and those kind of things, or what the game situation calls for," Harbaugh said. "I think in this game [vs. Washington] you saw probably more [cover] zero all-out pressure blitzes from two teams in the fourth quarter and the fifth quarter than you'll ever see again, probably. I mean, every play pretty much was zero blitz by both teams, it seemed like. So, that's probably going to drive the numbers up a little bit game situation wise.

 "But we feel like we would consider ourselves probably a blitzing team generally, but we also consider ourselves a cover defense, too. We think we play zone-match [coverage] well. We think we play man [coverage] well. We think we can do all those things. We want to keep it moving on people."

 This week's opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox). Saints QB Tyler Shough has been just a touch above average against the blitz, with a 0.1% completion percentage above expectation (CPOE). He has five touchdown passes and two interceptions against the blitz.

 Wilson isn't about to simply commit to all-out blitzing just because Burns is out. Or with his current top edge rusher Abdul Carter dealing with a minor calf injury. The quarterback and opponent matters. 

 "Yeah, it'll be a mixture of both," he said. "I think that we've always had pressures in our system. You know, like I say, the first two games this season, we played quarterbacks that feast off of pressure, knowing where to go. I think it's always matchup dependent. It's how the guys are playing. It's rhythm of the game. It's feel of the game. It's the ability to adjust during the game. We always have pressures up. So, we'll use them when we have to and be smart and educated about it."

 Wilson's track record doesn't show a heavy lean on the blitz. His Titans defense blitzed just 22.8% of dropbacks over the previous two seasons, the 22 nd- highest rate. He sent DB blitzes 9.3% of dropbacks, which was 25 th over that span.

 Perhaps that changes a bit with the Giants short-handed on pass rushers. It might be the best way for them to survive.

 "Dennard has a way of cooking things up, but it's definitely not I would say a consistent thing. It's a week-by-week thing off of, I guess what we're seeing and how we feel," Phillips said. "So, you just go out there and if they send me I'm going to try my best to go get there and everything but the percentage is just it goes off the flow of the game."

title: WR Garrett Wilson deems Patriots matchup a 'big-ass game' for Jets
summary: New York knows its first divisional game means a lot for the standings.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When it comes to recent AFC East history, the New York Jets are like the orange ghost named Clyde in the "Pac-Man" arcade game -- the most erratic of the four ghosts, the one always lagging in the pursuit of Pac-Man.

 The Jets have finished last seven times in the past 10 seasons, in large part because they've been dominated within their own division. Their 13-47 divisional record over that span, including a staggering 4-26 on the road, is easily the worst in the NFL and 19 games behind the next-closest AFC East opponent, the Miami Dolphins (32-28).

 It's no wonder their division-title drought is older than rookie sensation David Bailey . They last won the AFC East in 2002, the year before Bailey was born.

 Every year sparks new hope, this notion that the Jets -- finally free of the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick vice grip -- will rise up and put up a legitimate fight against the New England Patriots , Buffalo Bills and Dolphins (though Miami looks down and out this year).

 

 And it never happens.

 Well, here they go again, preparing for their first divisional game, Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ) against the Patriots (3-2) at Gillette Stadium.

 There's a good vibe around the Jets (2-3), coming off a win and an eight-sack performance against the  Cleveland Browns . Now there's an opportunity to make a statement that things are going to be different, that Clyde is reprogrammed and no longer wandering aimlessly around the maze.

 In coach Aaron Glenn's first year, the Jets went 0-6 in the division.

 "There's a premium on this one because it is our first one [in the division]," wide receiver Garrett Wilson said Wednesday. "I don't know how to exactly put it, but it's a big-ass game."

 Since Wilson's arrival in 2022, their divisional record is 6-18, with the three most recent wins coming against a backup quarterback (Miami's Tyler Huntley , 2024, Week 18), a quarterback on the verge of being benched (New England's Jacoby Brissett , 2024, Week 3) and another backup (New England's Bailey Zappe , 2023, Week 18).

 True, they did defeat Buffalo's Josh Allen in the 2023 opener, but that victory will forever be tarnished by  Aaron Rodgers ' season-ending Achilles injury.

 From 2020 to 2022, the Jets lost 15 straight in the division.

 

 As a rookie, Wilson heard about the Patriots' dominance, how they owned the rivalry with a 12-game winning streak at the time. Wilson noticed how it weighed on the Jets' organization. It ballooned to 15 games before the Jets finally ended the misery in the 2023 season finale. Now Wilson wants the current rookies to understand the importance of the AFC East games.

 "To put yourself in the hunt, it's how did you stack up with the teams you play twice a year?" he said. "And this is our first one."

 There's an old saying in football, that divisional games count more than all others. Makes sense, especially when you consider the tiebreaking criteria. There's also symbolism, meaning: If you can't handle the playground bullies in your own neighborhood, how do you expect to do it crosstown?

 It's fitting that the Jets play their first divisional game in Foxborough because -- let's be honest -- it's where they get pushed around the most.

 Before their win over Zappe & Co. in the 2023 finale -- Belichick's final game as the Patriots' coach -- the Jets had gone 12 seasons without a victory at Gillette. It came in the 2010 AFC Divisional playoffs, probably their best moment as a franchise since Super Bowl III in 1969.

 Since then, they're 1-14 in Foxborough, including six losses by 14 or more points. So yes, a win Sunday would be massive for Glenn, who is trying to establish credibility for the franchise.

 

 "We really don't focus on what happened in the past when it comes to us -- we just focus on what's happening right now -- but yes, division games are definitely crucial," Glenn said. "Sometimes people say they count as two games, but the only thing that we're focused on is, this is the one game that we have to play, this is the one game we want to win, this is the one game that we're prepared for and look to win."

 The Patriots with Brady and Belichick had a stranglehold on the division for two decades. When they split up in 2020, it figured to create parity in the AFC East. The Jets, for one, have failed to capitalize on the opening -- four last-place finishes and a 6-30 division record. The Robert Saleh- Zach Wilson -Rodgers era was a bust, and now they're one-plus season into the Glenn regime.

 Meanwhile, the Patriots, after a brief post-Brady/Belichick swoon, reinvented themselves with coach Mike Vrabel and quarterback Drake Maye .

 "I think it means the world," nickelback Jarvis Brownlee Jr . said of Sunday's matchup. "I think it means everything to this team, this organization, that if we go over there to the defending division champs and get a dub, man, I think that'd be awesome."
